name: meridian
description: Synthetic knowledge-graph RAG corpus about the fictional Meridian Institute (research institute and museum, Port Calder, founded 1911): 110 documents in md/html/txt with entity variants, multi-hop chains, superseded facts, confusable near-duplicates, unique identifiers, long documents with buried facts, and a gold fact sheet. Questions (261, written 2026-09-24): 50 paraphrase, 25 lexical, 30 detail, 24 multi, 34 multihop, 10 alias, 14 superseded, 20 confusable, 15 filter, 6 global and 33 negative. documents.title: Obituary: Professor Lucan Threlkeld (1939)
documents.summary: Newspaper obituary of Professor Lucan Threlkeld, head of the Institute's Department of Celestial Navigation since 1914.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER GAZETTE -- Tuesday, 24 January 1939 -- Obituaries

PROFESSOR LUCAN THRELKELD
Astronomer, Teacher of Navigators

Professor Lucan Threlkeld, head of the Department of Celestial Navigation at the Meridian Institute since its foundation in 1914, died at his home in Alder Row on Saturday, the 21st of January, after a short illness. He was 66.

Born in 1872 in the hill country east of Port Calder, Threlkeld came to the city as a young man to teach mathematics at the nautical school on Lantern Quay. His skill in explaining the use of the sextant and the nautical almanac to rough and impatient young officers became something of a legend on the waterfront. When the Institute, then still bearing the name of its founder, resolved in 1914 to establish a department for the teaching of navigation by the stars, Threlkeld was the obvious choice to lead it.

Under his direction the Department of Celestial Navigation trained, by his own count, more than 1,900 merchant officers, and kept the time signal by which the ships in Calder harbour set their chronometers. He was an early and energetic advocate of an observatory on Harrow Point, and saw it open in 1925.

He will be remembered longest for his great star atlas, which he drew by his own hand over ten years and completed in 1924. Known to his students and colleagues as the Harrow Point Atlas, although much of it was observed from the roof of Wrenfield Street before the observatory was built, its sixty-four plates are considered by those competent to judge to be among the finest of their kind. The atlas has been in the Institute's collection since 1926. Asked once why he had drawn it rather than having it engraved, he replied: "Because a sailor learns the sky with his pencil, not with his purse."

Professor Threlkeld was unmarried. He is survived by a sister, Mrs. Agnes Coyle of Port Calder, and by a very large number of former students in every port of the southern coast.

Dr. Hester Quayle, Director of the Institute, said yesterday: "The Institute has lost its conscience in matters of accuracy. Every one of us who has ever reduced an observation did so with one eye on Professor Threlkeld's tables and the other on his temper."

Mr. Arlo Fenwick, discoverer of last year's comet and a former pupil, said that Threlkeld had "taken a sailmaker's boy off the street and given him the sky".

The funeral will take place at St. Brendan's, Harbour Road, on Thursday at 11 o'clock. The Institute will close for the morning. By the Professor's wish there will be no flowers; donations may be made to the fund for navigation scholarships at the Institute.

documents.title: Port Calder Gazette: Meridian director resigns
documents.summary: Newspaper report of Dr. Rupert Sallow's resignation as director in February 1964 amid criticism over building safety.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER GAZETTE
Wednesday, 19 February 1964

MERIDIAN DIRECTOR RESIGNS
Dr. Sallow steps down two years after fire

By Nell Farris

Dr. Rupert Sallow, director of the Meridian Institute since 1951, has resigned, the Institute's trustees announced last night.

In a short statement, the Chair of the Board, Mr. Leonard Carrick, said Dr. Sallow had "offered his resignation in the interests of the Institute" and that the trustees had "accepted it with regret". Dr. Sallow will leave at the end of the month.

The resignation follows months of criticism of Dr. Sallow's handling of building safety in the years before the fire of March 1962, which destroyed the Institute's east wing and, according to Institute figures, many thousands of specimens and historic photographs. The fire department's investigation found that the blaze was caused by faulty electrical wiring.

Dr. Sallow, reached at his home in Crescent Hill, declined to discuss the circumstances. "I have given thirteen years to the Meridian and I am proud of them," he said. "I leave it in good hands and with its best days ahead."

Several trustees are understood to have pressed for his departure after a meeting before Christmas at which the Institute's safety record was discussed. Staff members who spoke to the Gazette on condition of anonymity described the mood inside the Institute as "sad but relieved".

Supporters of Dr. Sallow pointed to his record. Attendance at the Institute doubled under his leadership, and he secured the Brisk endowment, the largest gift in the Institute's history. "Rupert built the modern Meridian," said a former colleague. "He should not be the only one to carry the blame for the fire."

The Rebuild Meridian appeal, launched by Mayor Conrad Bellweather after the fire, has now passed $1 million. Work on a new east wing is expected to begin next year.

WHO WILL SUCCEED HIM?

The trustees are expected to move quickly. Among names mentioned in Institute circles are Dr. Miriam Castell, Curator of Maps and Charts, who is expected to act as director in the interim, and Dr. Margit Oster-Lind, the deputy director of the Institute's oceanographic laboratory, an experienced administrator and popular public lecturer. Dr. Oster-Lind declined to comment last night.

Dr. Sallow, 59, a geologist by training, joined the Institute as an assistant keeper in 1931.

documents.title: Beatrix Nolan retires after 27 years
documents.summary: 1990 news release marking the retirement of Beatrix Nolan, founding head of the Conservation Studio.
documents.body:
Beatrix Nolan Retires After 27 Years

Meridian Institute news release, 15 June 1990

Beatrix Nolan, the founding head of the Meridian Institute's Conservation Studio, will retire at the end of this month after twenty-seven years at the Institute.

Miss Nolan - "Bea Nolan" to generations of colleagues, volunteers and students - was appointed in 1963, a year after the fire that destroyed the east wing of the Institute's building on Wrenfield Street. She was then thirty-six, and the Conservation Studio consisted of herself, one assistant and a borrowed room in the temporary stores outside the city. Today the Conservation Studio has a staff of seven, purpose-built workshops, and a reputation well beyond Port Calder.

A career in restoration

Among the many treatments Miss Nolan carried out or supervised, two are especially associated with her name:

  • The Threlkeld Atlas, badly water-damaged in the fire, which she restored plate by plate between 1963 and 1967. The atlas was the centrepiece of the 1972 exhibition "Stars Over Calder" and has been consulted by astronomers and historians from around the world since.
  • The Calder Orrery, heat-damaged in the fire, which she dismantled, cleaned and reassembled in 1970, returning it to working order for the first time in half a century.

She also trained more than forty conservators, many of whom now work in museums across the country, and wrote the Institute's first environmental standards for galleries and stores.

Tributes

The Director, Dr. Felix Amberly, said: "Bea Nolan did not just repair the objects damaged in 1962. She changed the way this Institute thinks about its collections. Before her, we owned things. After her, we cared for them."

Speaking to staff at a farewell reception, Miss Nolan said she was "leaving the atlas in better condition than me". She plans to move to the coast north of the city and to continue to write about paper conservation.

Succession

The Institute will announce the appointment of a new head of the Conservation Studio shortly.

documents.title: Miriam Castell
documents.summary: Biography of Dr. Miriam Castell, Curator of Maps and Charts 1955-1980 and curator of the 1972 exhibition Stars Over Calder.
documents.body:
# Miriam Castell

**Dr. Miriam Castell** (1918–2001) was an astronomer and historian of cartography who served as **Curator of Maps and Charts** at The Meridian Institute from 1955 to 1980. She should not be confused with Dr. Marian Castel, the Institute's later Curator of Ethnography.

## Early life and training

Castell was born in Port Calder in 1918, the daughter of a harbour pilot. She studied mathematics and astronomy and completed a doctorate on the history of nautical star catalogues in 1944.

## Harrow Point

From 1946 to 1955 she was an assistant observer at Harrow Point Observatory, working under Arlo Fenwick. There she took part in the photographic variable-star programme and learned the practical side of telescope work. Colleagues recalled that she spent her cloudy nights in the observatory library cataloguing the old navigational charts that had accumulated there since the 1920s, which led to her interest in the history of maps.

## Curator of Maps and Charts

Castell moved to Wrenfield Street in 1955 as Curator of Maps and Charts. She built up the Map Room collection through purchases and gifts, including the 1958 gift of an 1851 hand-drawn chart of Kittering Sound. She was in charge of the Map Room on the night of the 1962 fire and spent the following years working with the new Conservation Studio on water-damaged sheets.

Her most celebrated project was the exhibition **Stars Over Calder** (1972), which brought together the Institute's historical star maps, instruments and navigational charts around the newly restored Threlkeld Star Atlas. The exhibition drew record attendance for the period and toured to two regional museums in 1973.

## Retirement

Castell retired in 1980 and devoted her later years to a catalogue of the Institute's pre-1900 charts, published in 1991. She died in 2001.

## Publications

- *Nautical Star Catalogues of the Calder Coast* (1947)
- *Stars Over Calder: exhibition catalogue* (1972)
- *Charts of the Meridian Institute before 1900* (1991)

## See also

- Arlo Fenwick
- Harrow Point Observatory
- Map Room

documents.title: Margit Oster-Lind (1922–2004)
documents.summary: Biography of the chemist who served as MOL's deputy director and then as the Meridian Institute's fourth director, 1964–1987.
documents.body:
# Margit Oster-Lind (1922–2004)

**Dr. Margit Oster-Lind** was the fourth director of the Meridian Institute, serving from 1964 to 1987. She took office two years after the fire that destroyed the east wing of the Wrenfield Building and is widely credited with steering the Institute through its reconstruction and reinventing it as a public institution.

## Early career

Born in 1922, she trained as an analytical chemist and specialised in the chemistry of seawater. In 1950 she joined the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory at Brannock Bay as deputy to its founder, Ottilie Brandt-Sayer. For fourteen years she managed the laboratory's staff, instruments and accounts while Brandt-Sayer concentrated on research, and she published a series of papers on dissolved oxygen in the Calder Estuary.

In 1956 she married Per Lind, a schoolteacher, and thereafter used the name Oster-Lind.

## Director

The Institute board appointed Oster-Lind director in March 1964, following the resignation of Dr. Rupert Sallow. She inherited an institution with a burned-out wing, collections scattered in temporary storage, and a public that had given generously to the rebuilding appeal and wanted to see results.

Her priorities, set out in her first address to staff, were "roof, record, and return": finish the rebuilding, complete the inventory of losses, and bring the collections back to the city. The Rautio Wing opened on the site of the old east wing in 1968, and the collections returned from temporary storage the same year.

### The "open doors" policy

Oster-Lind is best remembered for her "open doors" policy, introduced in 1965:

- free admission on Sundays;
- a public evening lecture series, held monthly in the main hall;
- school loan boxes of duplicate specimens;
- extended opening hours during the summer.

Some senior curators argued that the policy diverted staff time from research. Oster-Lind replied that the city had rebuilt the Institute "and is entitled to walk through it."

### Other achievements

- expansion of the Conservation Studio founded after the fire;
- support for the laboratory she had helped run, including a new building at Brannock Bay in 1974;
- the Institute's first formal collections policy (1976);
- defence of the Institute in the long legal dispute over the Corvina Logbook, 1978–1981.

## Retirement

She retired in 1987 and was succeeded by Dr. Felix Amberly. She died in Port Calder in 2004. The Oster-Lind Lecture, given annually since 1988, continues the public lecture series she founded.

documents.title: Elias Venn
documents.summary: Biography of Captain Elias Venn, Pell & Harrow master mariner who led the 1934 First Graye Island Expedition.
documents.body:
# Elias Venn

**Captain Elias Venn** (1880–1949) was a master mariner in the service of the Pell & Harrow Shipping Company and the leader of the First Graye Island Expedition of 1934, the first scientific voyage organised under the name of The Meridian Institute.

## Early life

Venn was born in 1880 in the fishing quarter below Lantern Quay in Port Calder, the third son of a net-maker. He went to sea at fourteen as a deck boy on a coastal collier and joined Pell & Harrow in 1901 as a second mate. Company records show him passing his master's certificate in 1911, the same year the Institute opened its doors on Wrenfield Street, and taking his first command, the coastal steamer *Plover*, in 1913.

## Career with Pell & Harrow

Over the next two decades Venn commanded five company vessels on the southern and western routes. He was regarded by his employers as a cautious navigator and a meticulous keeper of logs; one of his superintendents wrote in 1922 that "Venn will not leave harbour until he has argued with every chart aboard." He had a lifelong amateur interest in seabirds, and his letters from the 1920s contain sketches of petrels and shearwaters observed from the bridge.

Venn had read, as many Port Calder seamen had heard of, the entry in Captain Josiah Harrow's logbook describing an 1891 landing on an uncharted reef to the south-west. In February 1933 he wrote to the Institute's first director, Dr. Cornelius Aldane, proposing an expedition to relocate and survey the reef. The proposal was accepted by Aldane's successor, Dr. Hester Quayle, after she took office later that year.

## The 1934 expedition

The **First Graye Island Expedition** sailed in June 1934 and returned in September. Venn commanded the vessel and directed the survey work; the natural history programme was run by a small scientific party of Institute staff. The expedition produced the first reliable chart of the reef and a large collection of seabird material. Venn's narrative report, published in 1935, remains the standard account of the voyage.

Venn is sometimes wrongly credited with the second, larger expedition of 1936. That voyage was organised and led by the Institute's Curator of Natural History, Dr. Percival Dunmore; Venn was by then commanding a cargo route and took no part in it.

## Later years

Venn retired from the sea in 1938 and lived in a house on the Harrow Point road, where he was a frequent visitor to the observatory and an occasional lecturer at the Institute on practical navigation. He was elected an Honorary Associate of the Institute in 1939. During the war he served as a volunteer examiner for merchant navy cadets. He died in Port Calder in 1949.

## Legacy

- Venn's charts of the reef were used by the Admiralty-equivalent coastal survey office until the 1950s.
- The Institute holds a number of his navigational instruments and private papers.
- A lecture room in the Rautio Wing was named the Venn Room in 1968; it was renamed during a later refurbishment.

## See also

- Isle of Graye
- Pell & Harrow Shipping Company
- Percival Dunmore

documents.title: Cornelius Aldane
documents.summary: First director of the institute (1911–1933), botanist and founder of the Aldane Herbarium.
documents.body:
# Cornelius Aldane

**Dr. Cornelius Aldane** (1861–1940) was a British-trained botanist and amateur astronomer who served as the first director of the Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy — the body renamed The Meridian Institute in 1928 — from its foundation in 1911 until his retirement in 1933.

## Early life

Aldane was born in the market town of Stoke Adley and studied natural sciences before spending fifteen years as a schoolmaster and private tutor. He moved to Port Calder in 1896 to teach at the Calder Grammar School, and quickly became known along the coast for his walking surveys of salt-marsh and dune plants. His paper on the flora of the Calder Estuary margins (1904) brought him to the attention of the shipowner Augustin Pell, who was then planning a scientific foundation.

## Director, 1911–1933

Pell appointed Aldane director when the Institute opened at 14 Wrenfield Street in May 1911. Aldane built the institution almost from nothing: he recruited its first curators, drafted its collecting policy, and insisted from the beginning that the galleries be open to the public free of charge on Saturday afternoons. He oversaw the purchase of the Calder Orrery in 1913 and the creation of the Department of Celestial Navigation in 1914, and he was a strong advocate for the observatory that opened on Harrow Point in 1925.

Aldane's administrative style was personal and informal. Staff meetings were often held in his study among drying presses and herbarium cabinets, and he answered most letters from the public himself. Critics on the board thought him too willing to spend on collecting and too slow to build a proper research budget; admirers credited him with giving the Institute a real public following within a decade of its founding.

In 1933 he received and endorsed the proposal from the P&H master Captain Elias Venn for an expedition to the Isle of Graye, though he retired before it sailed.

## The Aldane Herbarium

Aldane's lasting scientific legacy is the herbarium that bears his name. He began it with his own collection of around 1,200 sheets and expanded it through fieldwork and exchange to roughly 9,000 sheets by 1933. Its strength is the coastal flora of the Calder region, including several species he was the first to describe. A large part of the herbarium was destroyed in the fire of 1962.

## Retirement and death

Aldane retired in 1933 and was succeeded by the astronomer Dr. Hester Quayle, whom he had hired in 1919. He spent his last years in a cottage near Ferrow Marsh and died there in 1940.

## Selected works

- *The Flora of the Calder Estuary Margins* (1904)
- *A Handlist of the Salt-Marsh Plants of the Calder Coast* (1921)
- "On a new sea-lavender from the Calder coast", Meridian Quarterly (1922)

documents.title: Percival Dunmore
documents.summary: Biography of Dr. Percival Dunmore, Curator of Natural History 1928-1957 and leader of the 1936 Second Graye Island Expedition.
documents.body:
# Percival Dunmore

**Dr. Percival Dunmore** (1890–1968) was a zoologist and museum curator who served as Curator of Natural History at The Meridian Institute from 1928 to 1957. He is best remembered as the leader of the Second Graye Island Expedition of 1936.

## Education

Dunmore grew up in the market town of Hollin Cross, the son of a schoolmaster. He read natural sciences at the **University of Ashcombe**, graduating in 1912, and remained there for his doctorate on the osteology of marine mammals, completed in 1920 after an interruption for war service as a hospital orderly. At Ashcombe he trained in the preparation and articulation of large skeletons under the university's museum preparator, a skill that would shape his later career.

## Curator of Natural History

Dunmore joined the Institute in 1924 as assistant curator and succeeded to the curatorship in 1928, the year the Pell Institute took its present name. He reorganised the natural history galleries along systematic lines, introduced printed specimen labels, and campaigned for a dedicated preparation laboratory, which opened in the basement of the Wrenfield Building in 1931.

He was critical of the first voyage to the Isle of Graye in 1934, which he felt had been run as a navigational survey with science as an afterthought. His memorandum to Director Hester Quayle in late 1934 argued for a second, larger voyage with a full scientific party.

## The 1936 expedition

The **Second Graye Island Expedition** sailed in May 1936 and returned in August with seventeen members. Dunmore led it personally. Its most famous result was the recovery of the skeleton of a fin whale found stranded on the reef, which Dunmore and his preparators cleaned, crated, and brought back to Port Calder. After two years of articulation work the whale went on display in the Institute's central hall. Dunmore's *Final Report* appeared in 1937.

## Later career

During the 1940s Dunmore expanded the Institute's comparative osteology collection and served on the council of the Calder Historical Society. He retired in 1957 and was succeeded by his deputy. He lived long enough to see the whale he had brought home survive the 1962 fire in the central hall, and he gave a short speech at the opening of the new east wing in 1968, months before his death.

## Selected publications

- *The Skeleton of the Southern Fur Seal* (1921)
- *Second Graye Island Expedition: Final Report* (1937)
- "On the preparation of large cetacean skeletons for exhibition", *Meridian Quarterly* (1939)

## See also

- Elias Venn
- Isle of Graye
- Department of Natural History

documents.title: Rupert Sallow
documents.summary: Biography of Dr. Rupert Sallow, third director of the Meridian Institute (1951-1964), who resigned after the 1962 fire.
documents.body:
# Rupert Sallow

**Dr. Rupert Sallow** (1904-1983) was a geologist and museum administrator who served as the third director of the Meridian Institute from 1951 to 1964. His directorship is remembered for a period of rising attendance and financial stability in the 1950s, and for its abrupt end after the 1962 fire.

## Early life and career

Sallow was born in Port Calder in 1904, the son of a customs officer. He studied geology and trained as a field geologist, working for a mining survey in the interior before returning to the coast in 1931 as an assistant keeper of minerals at the Institute. He published steadily on the coastal geology of the Calder region, notably on the raised beaches north of the city, and became Keeper of Earth Sciences in 1940.

## Directorship (1951-1964)

Sallow succeeded Dr. Hester Quayle as director in 1951. Contemporaries described him as careful with money, courteous with donors and impatient with committees. His achievements included:

- negotiating the 1953 endowment from the Brisk Trust, the largest gift the Institute had then received;
- overseeing the renaming of the Department of Celestial Navigation as the Department of Astronomy and Navigation in 1958;
- a programme of gallery refits in the central hall, culminating in the refurbished Graye gallery;
- a sustained increase in visitor numbers, which roughly doubled over the decade.

He also supported the growth of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory under Ottilie Brandt-Sayer, though relations between the director's office and the laboratory at Brannock Bay were sometimes cool.

## The 1962 fire and resignation

Sallow was called from his home on the night of 14 March 1962 and spent the night at the scene as the east wing burned. In the weeks that followed he was widely praised for his energy in organising salvage and moving the surviving collections to temporary storage.

As the investigation and the Institute's own inquiries proceeded, however, attention turned to the condition of the building before the fire. Critics - among them several trustees and, increasingly, the *Port Calder Gazette* - questioned decisions taken in the years before 1962 about maintenance and building safety. Sallow defended his record in public but resigned in February 1964. He was succeeded by Dr. Margit Oster-Lind.

## Later life

After leaving the Institute Sallow returned to geological work, spending several years as a consultant to the harbour authority on coastal erosion. He wrote a short memoir, never published, which is held in the Institute archive. He did not return to the Institute in any official capacity, though he attended the opening of the Rautio Wing in 1968. He died in 1983.

## Assessment

Later historians have been kinder to Sallow than his contemporaries were. The decisions for which he was criticised were taken with the board's agreement and reflected priorities - the galleries, the visitors - that the board shared. Nell Farris, in her centenary history of the Institute, calls him "a competent director who was punished for a failure that belonged to everyone". His successor's emphasis on openness and public trust has sometimes been read as an implicit criticism of his style; it can equally be read as building on the audience he had done much to create.

## See also

- The Wrenfield Fire
- Margit Oster-Lind
- Brisk Trust

documents.title: Walter Brisk
documents.summary: Biography of the cannery owner who founded the Brisk Trust in 1953.
documents.body:
# Walter Brisk

**Walter Brisk** (1887–1969) was a Port Calder industrialist, owner of Brisk Canneries, and one of the most significant benefactors in the history of The Meridian Institute. In 1953 he established the Brisk Trust, whose endowment has supported research at the Institute ever since.

## Business career

Brisk was born in the fishing village of Cray's Landing, north of Port Calder. His father was a fish curer. In 1909 Walter opened a small cannery for herring and mackerel on the north bank of the Calder Estuary; by 1930 Brisk Canneries employed 1,400 people in four plants, and its tins of Calder mackerel were sold across the country and abroad. The company was sold to a national food group in 1962.

Brisk was a hard bargainer and an unsentimental employer, but he had a lifelong interest in the sea that went beyond business. He funded fishery surveys, wrote to scientists about the movements of fish shoals, and was an early member of the Friends of the Meridian.

## Philanthropy

In 1953 Brisk gave $2 million — then the largest gift the Institute had ever received — to establish the Brisk Trust, a separate charitable trust whose income would support the Institute. Brisk insisted that the money be used only for science, not for buildings or displays. "Other people will pay for the galleries," he told the Gazette. "I want to pay for the thinking." The terms of the deed restricting the use of the income would become important more than fifty years later.

He also gave instruments and historical material to the Institute's collections throughout the 1950s, and he was a generous supporter of the city's fire appeal in 1962.

## Family

Brisk married Eleanor Sim in 1920. Their daughter, **Maud Brisk** (1924–2016), trained as an accountant, worked for her father's company, and joined the board of the Brisk Trust in 1970. She later chaired the Trust for nearly three decades, and in that role guarded the terms of her father's gift closely — at one point taking the Institute to court over them.

## Death

Walter Brisk died in 1969 at his house overlooking Brannock Bay. His portrait by Joanna Frere hangs in the Institute's boardroom.

## See also

- Brisk Trust
- Friends of the Meridian

documents.title: Hester Quayle
documents.summary: Astronomer and second director of the Meridian Institute (1933–1951), later its first historian.
documents.body:
# Hester Quayle

**Dr. Hester Quayle** (1889–1972) was an astronomer and the second director of The Meridian Institute, serving from 1933 to 1951. She was the first woman to lead a scientific institution in Port Calder, and after her retirement she wrote the first full history of the Institute.

## Background

Quayle grew up in Port Calder, the daughter of a harbour pilot. She studied mathematics and astronomy, and joined the Institute in 1919 as an assistant in the Department of Celestial Navigation under Professor Lucan Threlkeld. She assisted Threlkeld in the observations that became his celebrated star atlas and was closely involved in the planning of the observatory on Harrow Point, where she spent much of the late 1920s.

## Director, 1933–1951

When Cornelius Aldane retired in 1933, the board chose Quayle over two external candidates. Her directorship covered the most ambitious period of fieldwork in the Institute's early history. She approved and helped organise both of the expeditions to the Isle of Graye in the 1930s, and she oversaw the arrival of the large whale skeleton recovered by the second of them.

Quayle remained a working astronomer throughout. In November 1938 she verified the observations of a new comet made by the observatory's Arlo Fenwick, and she was co-author with him of the paper describing it, published in Meridian Quarterly in 1939.

During the war years she kept the galleries open on reduced hours while much of the staff was away, and moved the most valuable manuscripts to a strongroom in the basement. In 1946 she received a proposal from the young oceanographer Dr. Ottilie Brandt for a marine laboratory; the resulting laboratory opened at Brannock Bay the following year.

## Retirement and later work

Quayle retired in 1951 and was succeeded by Dr. Rupert Sallow. In retirement she compiled *A History of the Meridian Institute*, published in October 1961. The book is an affectionate, detailed account of the first fifty years and is valuable because it describes galleries and collections as they stood before the fire of the following year.

She died in Port Calder in 1972.

## Recognition

- Fellow of the Coastal Astronomical Society (1931)
- The Quayle Lecture, an annual public lecture on astronomy, was established in her memory in 1974.

## See also

- Arlo Fenwick
- Harrow Point Observatory
- *A History of the Meridian Institute*

documents.title: Selma Rautio (1921–2010)
documents.summary: Biography of the Finnish-born architect who designed the Meridian Institute's post-fire east wing and MOL's 1974 laboratory building.
documents.body:
# Selma Rautio (1921–2010)

**Selma Rautio** was a Finnish-born architect who practised in Port Calder from 1952 until her retirement in 1991. She is best known for two buildings for the Meridian Institute: the **Rautio Wing** of the Wrenfield Building (1968) and the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory's laboratory building at Brannock Bay (1974).

## Life

Rautio was born in 1921 in a lakeside town in central Finland and trained in architecture in Helsinki. She emigrated in 1951, joined the Port Calder practice of Gorse & Albery the following year, and became a partner in 1958. Her early work consisted mostly of schools and a small public library in the harbour district, notable for its clerestory lighting and timber ceilings.

## The Rautio Wing

After the east wing of the Institute's Wrenfield Building was destroyed by fire in March 1962, the board held a limited design competition. Rautio's entry won in 1964. Her brief was difficult: a fireproof building for collections, capable of holding very large objects, that would sit next to a heavily ornamented 1911 stone building without imitating it.

Her solution was a concrete-framed wing clad in pale granite, with a four-storey glazed atrium at its centre. The atrium was designed around the Institute's largest single object, the whale skeleton known as Big Graye, which was suspended from the roof trusses when the wing opened in 1968. The collection stores beneath were among the first in the country to be built with compartmented fire separation and a dry-pipe sprinkler system.

The wing, officially named after her in 1969, was listed as a building of architectural interest in 2002.

## Brannock Bay laboratory

In 1971 Rautio was commissioned to design a permanent building for the Institute's oceanographic laboratory at Brannock Bay, which had operated since 1947 out of a converted lifeboat house. The two-storey laboratory, completed in 1974, has seawater tanks at ground level fed directly from the bay, and a long upper-floor workroom with windows facing the moorings. Rautio called it "a boathouse for scientists."

## Other works

- Harbour District Library, Port Calder (1956)
- St. Brendan's Primary School (1961)
- Port Calder Crematorium chapel (1979)

## Death

Rautio died in Port Calder in October 2010, aged 89. A memorial exhibition of her drawings was held in the atrium of the wing that bears her name.

documents.title: Augustin Pell
documents.summary: Biography of the shipping magnate who co-founded Pell & Harrow and founded the institute in 1911.
documents.body:
# Augustin Pell

**Augustin Pell** (1858–1929) was a Port Calder shipowner, merchant and philanthropist, best remembered as the founder of the institution that is today The Meridian Institute. He was born in the Ropewalk district of Port Calder, the third son of a sailmaker, and left school at thirteen to work as a tally clerk on the city docks.

## Shipping career

In 1882 Pell and the ship's master **Captain Josiah Harrow** pooled their savings to buy a single second-hand steam collier. From that one vessel grew the **Pell & Harrow Shipping Company**, which by 1900 operated eleven steamers on coastal and short-sea routes out of the Calder Estuary. Pell handled the counting house and the chartering; Harrow handled the ships and the crews. The partnership kept its head office on Lantern Quay for its entire existence.

Contemporaries described Pell as cautious with money but restless in his curiosity. He read astronomy and natural history in the evenings and corresponded with amateur naturalists up and down the coast. Harrow's death in 1908 affected him deeply, and several friends later dated his decision to found a scientific institution to the months that followed.

## Founding the Institute

On 3 May 1911 Pell signed the deed establishing the **Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy**, housed in a former bonded warehouse he had bought and refitted at 14 Wrenfield Street. He appointed the botanist and amateur astronomer Dr. Cornelius Aldane as its first director and endowed it with income from a block of company shares. The founding deed committed the new body to "the study of the sea, the sky and the living shore, and the display of the same to the people of Port Calder" — a double purpose of research and public exhibition that would shape, and sometimes strain, the institution for the next century.

Pell was an active patron rather than a distant one. He paid for the purchase of the Calder Orrery in 1913, for the fitting-out of the first natural history galleries, and in 1925 for the 18-inch refractor at the new observatory on Harrow Point, which staff promptly nicknamed "the Pell Refractor" despite his objections.

## The change of name

Pell disliked seeing his name on the building. In 1928, at his own written request, the board renamed the institution The Meridian Institute, after the brass meridian line set into the observatory floor. He attended the board meeting that passed the resolution and is recorded as saying only that "a man's name wears out faster than a good idea."

## Family

Pell married Harriet Lowndes in 1882; they had two sons and a daughter. His elder son, **Edmund Pell** (1884–1966), succeeded him as chairman of the shipping company in 1929 and continued the family's support of the Institute, most notably by funding an expedition in the 1930s. Augustin did not live to meet his granddaughter, born Clarissa Pell in 1931, two years after his death; she would later have a complicated relationship with the institution her grandfather created.

## Death and legacy

Pell died at his house on Fennick Terrace in November 1929 and is buried in the Calder Old Cemetery. His business papers and family correspondence are now held in the Institute's archive. A bronze portrait bust by the sculptor Anton Mayle stands in the entrance hall of the Wrenfield Building.

## See also

- Pell & Harrow Shipping Company
- Cornelius Aldane
- Harrow Point Observatory

documents.title: Ottilie Brandt-Sayer (1908–1991)
documents.summary: Biography of the oceanographer who founded the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory at Brannock Bay in 1947 and directed it until 1972.
documents.body:
# Ottilie Brandt-Sayer (1908–1991)

**Dr. Ottilie Brandt-Sayer** was a physical oceanographer and the founding director of the **Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory** (MOL), the seagoing research arm of the Meridian Institute. She led the laboratory from its opening at Brannock Bay in 1947 until her retirement in 1972. Before her marriage she worked and published as **Ottilie Brandt**, and she kept "O. Brandt" as her scientific byline for the rest of her career, which is why library catalogues and citation indexes rarely show the double-barrelled name.

## Early life and training

Brandt was born in 1908 in the inland market town of Harlow Cross, the daughter of a schoolmaster and a piano teacher. She trained in mathematics and physics and completed a doctorate on wave refraction over shoaling ground in 1936. She came to Port Calder in 1941 as a research associate attached to the Institute's Department of Natural History, where Curator Percival Dunmore gave her bench space in a basement room that she later described as "a laboratory for everything except the sea."

Her wartime work consisted mostly of tide tables and harbour-approach calculations prepared for the port authority. It convinced her that the Institute, for all its expeditions and specimen drawers, had no way to measure the water itself.

## Founding the laboratory

In November 1946 Brandt wrote to Director Hester Quayle proposing a permanent coastal station. The letter, preserved in the Institute archive, argued that the Calder Estuary and the shelf beyond it were "the least studied water within a day's sail of any institution in the country." Quayle took the proposal to the board, and the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory opened in July 1947 in a converted lifeboat house at Brannock Bay, 30 km up the coast from the city.

The early laboratory had a staff of four, a 9-metre launch named *Petrel*, and a budget that Brandt supplemented by selling tide predictions to local fishing cooperatives. In 1949 she designed the self-recording current meter that now bears her name and is held in the Institute's instrument collection.

In 1950 she recruited **Dr. Margit Oster**, a young chemist, as deputy director. Oster (later Margit Oster-Lind) ran the laboratory's day-to-day affairs for fourteen years before leaving in 1964 to become director of the Institute itself.

## Marriage

In 1950 Brandt married **Gideon Sayer**, a former ship's engineer who had spent twenty years with a Port Calder shipping line before coming ashore. Sayer took charge of the laboratory's boats and moorings, unpaid for the first three years, and is credited in several MOL reports with rebuilding *Petrel*'s engine from salvaged parts. The couple lived in the keeper's cottage beside the laboratory until 1972.

## Research

Brandt's best-known work concerned the mixing of fresh and salt water in the Calder Estuary, summarised in the 1952 paper "Tidal Mixing in the Calder Estuary" in the *Journal of Coastal Hydrography* that remained a standard reference for estuarine studies on the coast for three decades. She also published on seasonal stratification off Brannock Bay and on the drift of fishing-net floats, a study that began as a favour to a local cooperative and ended as a surface-current map of the whole Calder shelf.

She was sceptical of expeditions for their own sake. In a 1958 lecture she remarked that "an expedition gives you one summer of data; a mooring gives you twenty." MOL under her leadership was built around long, repeated measurements rather than voyages.

## Retirement and legacy

Ottilie Brandt-Sayer retired in 1972 and was succeeded by Dr. Tobias Wren. She remained a visitor to the laboratory until the mid-1980s and died at Brannock Bay in 1991. The laboratory's seminar room is named after her, and her field notebooks, 61 volumes in all, are held in the Institute archive.

The Institute marked the seventieth anniversary of the laboratory she founded with the 2018 exhibition *Deep Meridian*.

## See also

- Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory
- Brandt Current Meter
- Margit Oster-Lind
- Tobias Wren

documents.title: Tobias Wren (1931–2012)
documents.summary: Biography of the marine biologist who directed MOL from 1972 to 1995 and pioneered deep-water sampling off the Calder coast.
documents.body:
# Tobias Wren (1931–2012)

**Dr. Tobias Wren** was a marine biologist and the second director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory (MOL), which he led from 1972 to 1995. He is remembered as the scientist who turned MOL from a coastal physics station into a laboratory that routinely worked in deep water, and as a gifted, sometimes combative public lecturer.

## Education

Wren was born in Port Calder in 1931, the son of a harbour pilot. He read natural sciences at **Ashcombe University**, where he studied under Professor Winifred Hale, the estuarine hydrographer. He later said that Hale taught him "that a river mouth is an argument between two waters, and the argument is the interesting part." His doctoral thesis, completed in 1958, dealt with the distribution of burrowing worms across salinity gradients.

Hale introduced him to the Meridian Institute's oceanographic laboratory at Brannock Bay, where he took a junior research post in 1959.

## Career at MOL

At MOL Wren worked initially on the intertidal flats around the bay, but he soon became convinced that the most interesting animals on the Calder coast lived far offshore. In 1970 he led the laboratory's first deep-water sampling expedition to the Ossery Trench, an effort that produced the paper *Benthic Fauna of the Ossery Trench* (1971) and established his reputation.

When founding director Ottilie Brandt-Sayer retired in 1972, Wren succeeded her. His 23 years as director saw:

- the move into the new laboratory building in 1974;
- the growth of MOL's scientific staff from eleven to twenty-six;
- an expanded programme of deep-water trawling and, from 1983, bottom photography;
- the 1988 exhibition *The Drowned Coast*, which he curated, on the sea-level history of the Calder coastline;
- a long-running dispute with the Institute's central administration over the share of the budget allocated to the laboratory, which he regarded as the Institute's "real research engine."

Wren was not an easy colleague. He clashed with Director Felix Amberly in the early 1990s over plans to move part of MOL's specimen store to the city museum for public display, arguing that "specimens in a vitrine are specimens nobody can measure."

## Later life

Wren retired in 1995 and was succeeded by Dr. Priya Sandoval. In retirement he wrote a popular history of the Calder coast, *Between Tides* (2001), and continued to lecture for the Friends of the Meridian. He died in Port Calder in September 2012.

## Selected publications

- *Benthic Fauna of the Ossery Trench* (1971)
- *Sediment and Salinity: Notes from Brannock Bay* (1979)
- *Between Tides* (2001)

documents.title: Arlo Fenwick
documents.summary: Biography of astronomer Arlo Fenwick, discoverer of Comet 1938b at Harrow Point.
documents.body:
# Arlo Fenwick

**Arlo Fenwick** (1901–1977) was an observational astronomer at the **Harrow Point Observatory** of The Meridian Institute from 1927 until his retirement in 1966. He is known for the discovery of **Comet 1938b**, popularly called **Fenwick's comet**.

## Background

Fenwick was born in Port Calder to a family of sailmakers. He had no university degree; he learned astronomy as a teenage volunteer at the Institute's rooftop telescope on Wrenfield Street and through evening classes given by Professor Lucan Threlkeld. Threlkeld hired him as a computer (a human calculator of ephemerides) in 1922 and sent him to Harrow Point as a night assistant when the observatory opened.

## Harrow Point years

At Harrow Point, Fenwick spent most clear nights at the eyepiece of the Pell Refractor, the observatory's 18-inch telescope. His routine programme was the measurement of double stars and the photographic monitoring of variable stars, but he also swept the evening sky for comets as a personal project.

## Discovery of Comet 1938b

On the evening of 9 November 1938 Fenwick noticed a faint diffuse object low in the western sky. He confirmed its motion over two nights and telegraphed the discovery. The comet was designated 1938b. Fenwick and Director Hester Quayle published a joint paper, "Observations of Comet 1938b from Harrow Point", in *Meridian Quarterly* the following year, based on 41 photographic plates taken with the Pell Refractor between November 1938 and February 1939.

The comet brought the observatory unexpected public fame. Fenwick gave dozens of talks around Port Calder over the winter of 1938–39 and received several hundred letters from members of the public, many of them preserved in the Institute archive.

## Teacher and mentor

After the war Fenwick trained a series of assistant observers at Harrow Point, among them Miriam Castell, who worked under him from 1946 to 1955 before moving to the museum side of the Institute. He was known as a patient teacher who insisted that every assistant learn to grind and silver a mirror.

## Retirement and death

Fenwick retired in 1966 and died in 1977. His observing notebooks, covering 39 years, are held by the Institute archive. A minor planet discovered elsewhere was named in his honour in 1981.

## See also

- Harrow Point Observatory
- Hester Quayle
- Miriam Castell

documents.title: Joaquin Ferrer
documents.summary: Biography of Joaquin Ferrer, head of conservation at the Meridian Institute from 1990 to 2012 and leader of its digitisation programme.
documents.body:
# Joaquin Ferrer

**Joaquin Ferrer** (born 1949) is a conservator of scientific instruments who led conservation at the Meridian Institute from 1990 until his retirement in 2012.

## Early career

Ferrer grew up in Port Calder, the son of a ship's chandler, and trained as a clock- and instrument-maker before studying conservation. He worked for several years at a national museum of science and technology, specialising in brass instruments, clocks and early electrical apparatus. He first came to the Meridian Institute in 1976 as an assistant conservator, working on the Institute's collection of navigational instruments, and left in 1981 for a senior post elsewhere.

## Head of conservation

In 1990 Ferrer returned to Port Calder to succeed Beatrix Nolan as head of the Conservation Studio. Nolan had founded the studio after the 1962 fire and led it for twenty-seven years; Ferrer was widely seen as her chosen successor, and he described her as "the person who taught me that the object always comes first".

Under Ferrer the department changed in several ways:

- **Preventive care.** Ferrer shifted resources from remedial treatment towards environmental control and storage. By the late 1990s every gallery and store was monitored.
- **Renaming.** In 1999 the studio became the Conservation and Collections Care Division, absorbing the collections management team.
- **Digitisation.** From 1998 Ferrer led the Institute's first large-scale digitisation project, funded by a grant from the Oriel Foundation. Over four years the project imaged the Institute's charts, atlases, archive photographs and a large part of the herbarium, and created the first online collections catalogue.
- **Off-site store.** He planned and oversaw the move of a large part of the reserve collections to a new off-site store in 2005.

## Instruments

Ferrer's own specialism remained instruments. He carried out a second, lighter treatment of the Calder Orrery in 2001, re-lubricating its gearing and replacing a worn drive cord, and published a detailed study of the navigational instruments in the collection, including the octant of Captain Josiah Harrow and the sextant associated with Captain Elias Venn.

## Later life

Ferrer retired in 2012, shortly after contributing to the anniversary exhibition "Fire and Recovery". He continues to advise the Institute on instrument conservation and lectures to the Friends of the Meridian.

## Publications

- *Brass and Glass: Navigational Instruments at the Meridian Institute* (2004)
- "Preventive conservation in a regional museum", *Meridian Quarterly* (1996)
- "Imaging the collections: lessons from the Oriel project", *Meridian Quarterly* (2003)

documents.title: Clarissa Pell-Windham
documents.summary: Life of Augustin Pell's granddaughter, who sued the Institute in 1978 and later donated the Pell Papers.
documents.body:
# Clarissa Pell-Windham

**Clarissa Pell-Windham** (1931–2014) was a Port Calder philanthropist and local historian, the granddaughter of the Institute's founder Augustin Pell. She is remembered at the Institute for two very different reasons: the lawsuit she brought against it in 1978, and the family archive she gave it twelve years later.

## Early life

She was born in Port Calder in 1931, the only daughter of **Edmund Pell**, chairman of the Pell & Harrow Shipping Company from 1929 to 1958, and his wife Iris. She grew up in the family house on Fennick Terrace and in the company's world — her earliest memories, she later said, were of being lifted onto the bridge of company steamers at Lantern Quay. As a child she attended the opening of the Institute's Graye gallery in 1938, and she was photographed beside the newly mounted whale skeleton.

She studied history and in 1954 married Hugh Windham, a barrister; they had two sons. She served for many years on the committee of the Calder Historical Society and wrote two short books on the city's waterfront.

## The logbook dispute

When the shipping company was wound up in 1974, its remaining assets were distributed among the family shareholders. Clarissa Pell-Windham, by then the family's principal representative, came to believe that the logbooks kept by the firm's masters were company records, and therefore that the most famous of them — the logbook of SS Corvina kept by the company's co-founder Josiah Harrow — should have passed to the Pell heirs rather than to the Institute.

In 1978 she sued the Institute. The case lasted three years and was bitterly fought; she lost in June 1981, when the court held that the log was Harrow's personal property. The case left a lasting coolness between the family and the Institute, and she resigned from the Friends of the Meridian.

## Reconciliation

In 1989 she wrote to the new director, Dr. Felix Amberly, suggesting that "the quarrel has outlived its usefulness". The two met several times, and in 1990 she gave the Institute the Pell Papers — more than two hundred boxes of family correspondence and business records of the shipping company. She said at the handover that she wanted "the whole story, not one book of it" to be kept together.

She later served on the Institute's Development Council (1994–2003) and endowed an annual prize for local-history research.

## Death

She died in November 2014, aged 83. Her funeral was held at St. Anselm's, Wrenfield, and the Institute flew its flag at half-mast.

documents.title: Evelyn Marchbank, Chair of the Board of Governors
documents.summary: 2015 board profile of Evelyn Marchbank, chair since 2008 and a former law partner at Vantry & Lisle.
documents.body:
Evelyn Marchbank

Chair of the Board of Governors, The Meridian Institute (since 2008)

Evelyn Marchbank has chaired the Board of Governors of the Meridian Institute since 2008. She first joined the Board in 2001 and served as chair of its audit committee before her election as chair.

Professional career

A lawyer by training, Ms. Marchbank spent most of her career at the Port Calder firm of Vantry & Lisle, where she was a partner from 1986 until her retirement from practice in 2006. She specialised in charity and trust law, advising foundations, schools and hospitals on governance and on the management of endowments. Before joining the firm she clerked for a judge of the Port Calder District Court.

She has served as a trustee of several Port Calder charities, including a hospice and a sea-rescue fund, and chaired the city's heritage advisory panel from 2003 to 2009.

At the Institute

As chair, Ms. Marchbank has overseen:

  • the appointment of a restricted-funds officer and the creation of a register of every restricted gift the Institute holds, back to its founding;
  • a reduction in the size of the Board from twenty-four to fifteen governors, with fixed terms;
  • the centenary campaign in 2011;
  • the introduction of an annual external review of how gift income is spent.

"A museum's collections are held in trust, and so is its money," she has said. "Donors give on conditions, and the conditions are the gift. An institution that forgets that will eventually find someone reminding it."

Board committees

CommitteeRole
Board of GovernorsChair
Nominations and governanceChair
Finance and investmentMember

Ms. Marchbank lives in Port Calder's old harbour district and is a long-standing member of the Friends of the Meridian. Her current term as chair runs until 2020, and under the Institute's revised statutes she will not be eligible to stand again.

documents.title: Ines Halloran
documents.summary: Profile of Dr. Ines Halloran, Curator of Astronomy since 2006 and head of the Department of Astronomy and Navigation.
documents.body:
# Ines Halloran

**Dr. Ines Halloran** is an astronomer and museum curator. She has been Curator of Astronomy at The Meridian Institute since 2006 and head of the **Department of Astronomy and Navigation** since 2011.

## Career

Halloran trained as an observational astronomer, with a doctorate on the photometry of short-period comets. She worked in science communication and planetarium programming before joining the Institute in 2006, recruited by Director Nadia Corrow to modernise the astronomy galleries.

Her first major project was a survey of the Institute's photographic plate collection, around 18,000 glass plates exposed at Harrow Point between 1925 and 1996. The survey identified a number of historically significant plates, including the original discovery-period exposures of the 1938 comet, which had been misfiled in a box of variable-star plates since the 1960s.

## Head of department

In 2011 Halloran became head of the Department of Astronomy and Navigation, which then had eleven staff. She has argued that the department's future lies in public astronomy and the history of navigation rather than front-line research, a position that has been debated within the Institute. She has worked closely with the Harrow Point Public Observatory on outreach programming.

## Exhibitions

- *Stars Above Calder* (2014–2015), at the Harrow Point Public Observatory visitor centre
- *Pole Star: Navigation Before Satellites* (2010), Wrenfield Street
- *Plates and Plots* (2008), a small display of photographic plates

## Research interests

Although research observing at Harrow Point ended in 1996, Halloran has kept an active research profile in the history of astronomy. Her recent papers have dealt with the reduction methods used in the Institute's early navigational tables, the working practices of the Harrow Point night assistants in the 1930s and 1940s, and the use of archival photographic plates to recover the long-term light curves of variable stars. She has described the plate archive as "a century-long film of the southern sky that nobody has finished watching."

She supervises one or two postgraduate students each year in partnership with regional universities and has hosted visiting researchers working on the plate collection.

## Other roles

Halloran sits on the editorial board of *Meridian Quarterly* and chairs the Institute's collections digitisation committee for astronomical material.

## See also

- Department of Astronomy and Navigation
- Harrow Point

documents.title: Dr. Marian Castel
documents.summary: Biography of Dr. Marian Castel, Curator of Ethnography 1994-2016 (not to be confused with Miriam Castell).
documents.body:
# Dr. Marian Castel

**Dr. Marian Castel** (born 1956) was Curator of Ethnography at the Meridian Institute from 1994 until her retirement in December 2016. She built the Institute's collections relating to the fishing, shipping and cannery communities of the Calder coast and was responsible for its first sustained programme of community-curated exhibitions.

> **Not to be confused with** Dr. Miriam Castell (1918–2001), Curator of Maps and Charts from 1955 to 1980. The two were not related, and their careers at the Institute did not overlap. Catalogue records and correspondence from the 1990s occasionally confuse them, and at least one Friends of the Meridian newsletter (1997) credited Castel with the 1972 exhibition "Stars Over Calder," which was the work of Castell.

## Early life and training

Marian Castel was born in Brannock, a fishing village on the bay north of Port Calder, the daughter of a net-maker and a school teacher. She studied anthropology at the University of Ashcombe and wrote her doctoral thesis on kinship and credit among inshore fishing families, based on two years of fieldwork in coastal villages. Before joining the Meridian she worked for six years at a regional folk museum.

## At the Meridian

When Castel arrived in 1994, the Institute held a scattered ethnographic collection: net needles, oilskins, cannery labels and a few hundred photographs, most of it acquired by accident alongside natural history specimens. The department had been without a curator since the 1970s.

Her main achievements included:

- **The Calder Coast Collection** — about 4,800 objects and 11,000 photographs documenting working life on the coast, most collected directly from families between 1995 and 2010.
- **Cannery archives** — the rescue of the business records of three canneries, including a large deposit of labels and wage books from Brisk Canneries, placed with the Institute in 2002.
- **"Tides of Kin" (2003)** — an exhibition co-curated with twelve fishing families, which toured four coastal towns.
- **Oral history** — she extended the volunteer Meridian Oral History Project, begun in 1998, to include retired cannery workers and dock labourers.
- **Lantern Quay** — she advised the city on the interpretation panels installed when the old Lantern Quay warehouses were converted in 2012.

## Approach

Castel was an outspoken voice in the Institute's long argument about what kind of place it should be. In a 2005 staff seminar she argued that the Institute had "spent a century studying the sea and almost no time studying the people who worked on it," and she repeatedly pressed for ethnography to have a share of research funding equal to the natural sciences. She did not always win; her proposal for a permanent gallery of coastal life was deferred twice, most recently in the 2007–2008 gallery renovation.

## Retirement

Castel retired in December 2016. The post of Curator of Ethnography was left vacant pending a review of the curatorial structure, and the Calder Coast Collection was placed under the care of the Institute Archivist, Tamsin Rourke.

## Selected publications

- *Kin and Credit on the Calder Coast* (1991)
- "Cannery Labels as Social History," *Meridian Quarterly* (2001)
- *Tides of Kin: A Community Exhibition* (catalogue, 2003)

documents.title: Tamsin Rourke - Institute Archivist
documents.summary: Staff profile of Tamsin Rourke, Institute Archivist since 2003, author of Voices from the Fire and curator of Fire and Recovery.
documents.body:
Tamsin Rourke

Institute Archivist

Library and Archive, West Wing

Tamsin Rourke has been the Meridian Institute's Archivist since 2003. She is responsible for the Institute's institutional archive - board minutes, correspondence, registers, photographs, plans and recordings dating back to the foundation in 1911 - and for the family and business archives that the Institute holds, of which the largest is the Pell family papers.

Background

Tamsin grew up in Vellmoor and studied history before qualifying as an archivist. Before coming to the Meridian she worked for eight years at a regional record office, where she specialised in maritime and business records.

At the Institute

Her work at the Institute has included:

  • re-cataloguing the institutional archive and making the catalogue available online;
  • bringing the Institute's 1998 oral history recordings back into use, and digitising all forty interviews;
  • writing Voices from the Fire (2010), a history of the 1962 fire and the rebuilding of the Institute told largely through witnesses' own words;
  • curating the 2012 anniversary exhibition Fire and Recovery;
  • advising on the archive sections of the centenary history Meridian at One Hundred (2011).

Oral history and the fire

When Tamsin arrived at the Institute, the recordings made for the Meridian Oral History Project in 1998 were sitting in boxes in the archive store. Listening to them, she was struck by how often the people interviewed returned to the fire of March 1962, even when they had been asked about something else entirely. Those recordings became the basis of her book and, two years later, of the anniversary exhibition, which placed witnesses' voices alongside the objects they described. She continues to add to the collection, recording interviews each year with retiring staff and long-serving volunteers, so that the Institute's recent history is captured while its witnesses are still able to tell it.

Research interests

  • The history of the Institute and its governance
  • Oral history and museum memory
  • The records of Port Calder's shipping companies

Selected publications

YearTitle
2007"The minute books of the Meridian Institute, 1911-1964", Meridian Quarterly
2010Voices from the Fire (Meridian Institute Press)
2012Fire and Recovery (exhibition guide)
2016"Shipping records in a museum archive", Journal of Maritime Archives

Contact

Researchers wishing to consult the archive should contact the Library and Archive enquiries desk. The reading room is open Tuesday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., by appointment.

documents.title: Rhea Oduya
documents.summary: Profile of the marine geophysicist who became director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory in 2015.
documents.body:
# Rhea Oduya

**Dr. Rhea Oduya** is a marine geophysicist and, since 2015, director of the **Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory**, the Meridian Institute's research station at Brannock Bay. She is the fourth person to hold the post.

## Education

Oduya grew up in the harbour district of Port Calder and first visited the laboratory as a teenager on a school field trip. She studied geology as an undergraduate and completed her doctorate at Tollan College in 2006. Her doctoral advisor was **Dr. Priya Sandoval**, who at the time combined an adjunct professorship at Tollan with the directorship of the Meridian laboratory. Oduya's thesis used archived echo-sounder records to reconstruct sediment movement on the Calder shelf since the 1950s.

## Career

After postdoctoral work abroad, Oduya joined the laboratory in 2009 as a research scientist in seabed mapping. She built the laboratory's first multibeam processing group and led the mapping of the Brannock Bay approaches in 2011–2012.

In 2015 she was appointed director, succeeding Sandoval — an unusual case, colleagues noted, of a student succeeding her own advisor. Under Oduya the laboratory has shifted from occasional trawling surveys to repeat high-resolution mapping, and has formed closer partnerships with outside institutions.

Her most visible project to date has been the 2017 Ossery Trench Survey, which she co-led with Professor Aurelio Banks. The survey produced the first complete bathymetric map of the trench and a collection of specimens later shown in the Institute's 2018 exhibition *Deep Meridian*.

## Views

Oduya has been an outspoken advocate for keeping research capacity at Brannock Bay rather than consolidating it in the city. In a 2018 interview she said: "The public galleries are the Institute's front door, but a front door is not a house." She has also championed the laboratory's historical records, arguing that decades of measurements taken since Ottilie Brandt's time are "a baseline nobody else on this coast possesses."

## Selected work

- *Sediment pathways on the Calder shelf, 1952–2004* (doctoral thesis, 2006)
- *The Ossery Trench Bathymetric Survey* (with A. Banks, 2018)

documents.title: Dr. Nadia Corrow, Director 2004-2019
documents.summary: Staff profile of Dr. Nadia Corrow, sixth director of the Meridian Institute, published on her retirement.
documents.body:
Dr. Nadia Corrow

Director, The Meridian Institute, 2004–2019

Dr. Nadia Corrow became the sixth Director of the Meridian Institute in September 2004, succeeding Dr. Felix Amberly. She will retire at the end of May 2019, and this profile marks fifteen years of her leadership.

Background

Born in Port Calder in 1954, Nadia Corrow trained as a marine ecologist and spent the first half of her career in fisheries science, including eleven years at the national fisheries research service. She came to museum work in 1995 as head of science at a regional natural history museum, where she became known for opening laboratories to the public. She has said that her first visit to the Meridian, at the age of seven, was on a free Sunday introduced by Dr. Margit Oster-Lind's "open doors" policy.

Tenure

Dr. Corrow's directorship is remembered for a number of milestones:

  • 2006 – appointment of Dr. Ines Halloran as Curator of Astronomy.
  • 2007–2008 – renovation of the Wrenfield Street public galleries.
  • 2008 – reopening of the Harrow Point site as a public observatory.
  • 2011 – the centenary, and the settlement of the dispute with the Brisk Trust.
  • 2012 – "Fire and Recovery," marking fifty years since the 1962 fire.
  • 2014 – "Stars Above Calder."
  • 2018 – "Deep Meridian," celebrating the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory.

She also presided over the most difficult episode of recent years, when the Institute was sued over its use of restricted endowment income for the gallery renovation. Dr. Corrow has said publicly that the Institute "read the deed the way we wanted to read it" and that the settlement was the right outcome.

Numbers
