Annual visitors (all sites)148,000238,900
School visits21,00039,500
Staff (full-time equivalent)164211

In her words

"People ask whether the Meridian is a museum or a research institute. My answer has always been that it is a place where the public can watch research happen. When those two things pull apart, we get into trouble. When they pull together, nothing in this city does what we do."

Dr. Corrow will be succeeded by Dr. Idris Palk. She plans to return to field work as a volunteer with the Institute's salt-marsh monitoring programme.

documents.title: Dr. Leonie Farrant, Director
documents.summary: Profile of Dr. Leonie Farrant, eighth director, former manager of the Harrow Point Public Observatory and deputy director.
documents.body:
Dr. Leonie Farrant

Director, The Meridian Institute (from 4 September 2023)

Dr. Leonie Farrant is the eighth Director of the Meridian Institute. She was previously the Institute's Deputy Director (2016–2023) and, before that, the first manager of the Harrow Point Public Observatory (2008–2016).

Career

Leonie Farrant was born in 1971 in the inland town of Vellmoor and studied physics before completing a doctorate on variable stars. She spent several years in a university outreach programme, running a mobile planetarium that toured schools on the Calder coast, before joining the Meridian in 2008.

Her first job at the Institute was to turn a closed research observatory into a place the public would want to visit. Under her management the Harrow Point Public Observatory grew from a Friday-night viewing programme into a year-round education centre, with more than 30,000 visitors a year by 2015. She worked closely with the Curator of Astronomy, Dr. Ines Halloran, on the 2014 exhibition "Stars Above Calder," which was staged in the observatory's visitor centre.

Appointed Deputy Director in 2016, she took responsibility for public programmes, learning, visitor services and the Institute's three public sites. She led the reopening after the 2020 closures and chaired the working group that planned the 2022 Department of Earth and Sky Sciences.

Timeline

YearRole
2008–2016Manager, Harrow Point Public Observatory
2016–2023Deputy Director
July–September 2023Acting Director
From 4 September 2023Director

Outside the Institute

  • Trustee of a national dark-skies charity.
  • Member of the Port Calder schools partnership board.
  • Amateur telescope maker; she rebuilt the observatory's 1925 dome gears as a display model.

"I started at the Meridian by opening a door that had been shut for twelve years," Dr. Farrant says. "I'd like the whole Institute to feel that way: open, a bit surprising, and worth the trip."

documents.title: Conservation and Collections Care Division
documents.summary: History and functions of the Institute's conservation unit, founded as the Conservation Studio after the 1962 fire.
documents.body:
# Conservation and Collections Care Division

The **Conservation and Collections Care Division** (CCCD) is responsible for the physical care of the Meridian Institute's collections: conservation treatment, environmental monitoring, storage, loans preparation, integrated pest management and disaster planning. It employs eleven conservators and technicians and occupies workshops on the lower ground floor of the Rautio Wing.

## Origins: the Conservation Studio

Until the 1960s the Institute had no professional conservators. Objects were cleaned and repaired, when at all, by curators, preparators and occasionally outside craftsmen. The 1962 fire exposed the risks of this arrangement: in the weeks after the fire, hundreds of damaged objects were handled by well-meaning staff and volunteers without specialist guidance.

In 1963 the Board of Trustees established the **Conservation Studio** and appointed **Beatrix Nolan** as its first head. Nolan, who had trained in paper and book conservation, built the studio from a single room at the Vellmoor Depository into a department of seven. Her major treatments included the four-year restoration of the Threlkeld atlas (1963-1967) and the restoration of the Calder Orrery (1970). She also wrote the Institute's first environmental standards for galleries and stores, adopted in 1972.

Nolan retired in 1990 and was succeeded by Joaquin Ferrer, a conservator of scientific instruments, who led the department until 2012.

## Renaming

In 1999 the Conservation Studio was renamed the Conservation and Collections Care Division. The change reflected a shift in emphasis from remedial treatment of individual objects towards preventive care of the collection as a whole: environmental control, storage, handling and documentation. It also brought the collections management team, previously part of the Registrar's office, into the same division.

## Current work

- **Environmental monitoring:** more than 300 sensors across galleries and stores.
- **Storage:** the Division manages the Rautio Wing stores and the off-site store opened in 2005.
- **Digitisation support:** preparing objects for imaging, a programme begun in 1998.
- **Disaster planning:** the Division maintains the Institute's emergency plan and trains a salvage team of staff volunteers. The plan was written with the lessons of 1962 explicitly in mind.
- **Loans:** condition reporting and couriering for outgoing loans.

## Policy on fire damage

Since Nolan's time the Division has followed a policy of documenting, and where appropriate retaining, evidence of the 1962 fire on objects that survived it - tide lines, scorch marks, smoke staining - on the grounds that such damage is now part of the history of the object. Nolan summarised the policy in a much-quoted phrase: "We repair what threatens the object, and we keep what tells its story."

## Heads of department

| Period | Head | Title of unit |
|--------|------|---------------|
| 1963-1990 | Beatrix Nolan | Conservation Studio |
| 1990-1999 | Joaquin Ferrer | Conservation Studio |
| 1999-2012 | Joaquin Ferrer | Conservation and Collections Care Division |

documents.title: Brisk Trust
documents.summary: Charitable trust founded by Walter Brisk in 1953 to fund research at the Institute, and its restricted deed of gift.
documents.body:
# Brisk Trust

The **Brisk Trust** is a charitable trust established in 1953 by the Port Calder industrialist **Walter Brisk** to support scientific work at The Meridian Institute. It is independent of the Institute, with its own trustees, but its income is paid to the Institute each year under the terms of its founding deed.

## Foundation and terms

Walter Brisk endowed the Trust with $2 million in 1953, the largest single gift the Institute had received up to that time. The governing document is Deed of Gift **BT-53-A**, dated 14 September 1953. Its key clause directs that the Trust's income be applied "to scientific research and the acquisition of scientific instruments by The Meridian Institute, and to no other purpose whatsoever, and in particular not to the construction, alteration or decoration of buildings or galleries for public display".

The deed also provides that:

- the Trust's trustees shall receive an annual account from the Institute of how the income has been spent;
- if the Institute uses the income for any other purpose, the trustees may suspend payments and require restitution;
- one trustee shall always be a member of the Brisk family, if one is willing to serve.

## Chairs

| Chair | Term |
|-------|------|
| Walter Brisk | 1953–1969 |
| Arthur Pendle | 1969–1988 |
| Maud Brisk | 1988–2014 |
| Dr. Simon Ferrars | 2014– |

## What the Trust has funded

Over sixty years the Trust has paid for a great deal of the Institute's science, including MOL's early current-meter and tide-gauge programmes, a new objective lens cell for the observatory's refractor in 1964, the Ossery Trench work of 1970, laboratory equipment across the departments, and salaries for research assistants. Since 2011 it has funded the Brisk Research Fellowships, two-year postdoctoral posts open to scientists working on the Calder coast and its waters.

## The dispute of 2009–2011

In 2009 the Trust, under Maud Brisk's chairmanship, went to court against the Institute after discovering that $3.4 million of Trust income had been spent on the 2007–2008 renovation of the public galleries, contrary to the deed. The case was settled in March 2011: the Institute agreed to restore the $3.4 million over five years and to create the Brisk Research Fellowships. Relations between the two bodies were strained for some years but are now described by both sides as good.

## Value

The Trust's capital stood at about $19 million in 2011. It pays the Institute roughly 4% of its average capital value each year.

documents.title: Pell & Harrow Shipping Company
documents.summary: History of the Port Calder shipping line founded in 1882 by Augustin Pell and Josiah Harrow.
documents.body:
# Pell & Harrow Shipping Company

The **Pell & Harrow Shipping Company** (commonly "P&H") was a Port Calder shipping line founded in 1882 and dissolved in 1974. For most of its ninety-two years it was one of the largest employers on the Port Calder waterfront, and it played a central role in the founding and early fieldwork of The Meridian Institute.

## Founding

The company was founded in 1882 by the merchant **Augustin Pell** and the ship's master **Captain Josiah Harrow** (1851–1908). The two men had met when Harrow commanded a collier chartered by the firm where Pell was a clerk. Their first vessel was a single second-hand steam collier; within twenty years P&H operated eleven steamers on coastal and short-sea routes.

The partnership was a division of labour: Pell ran the office on Lantern Quay, and Harrow ran the ships. Harrow himself commanded the company's steamer SS Corvina from 1889 to 1894, and trained a generation of P&H masters.

## Fleet

Notable vessels included:

| Ship | In service | Notes |
|------|-----------|-------|
| SS Corvina | 1887–1911 | Commanded by Josiah Harrow 1889–1894 |
| SS Kittiwake | 1908–1947 | Carried the 1934 Graye Island expedition |
| SS Merrow | 1921–1952 | Carried the 1936 Graye Island expedition |
| SS Lanyard | 1929–1961 | Largest ship in the fleet |

## Later history

After Augustin Pell's death in 1929 his son **Edmund Pell** chaired the company until 1958. Edmund continued his father's patronage of the Institute and lent company ships to both Graye Island expeditions in the 1930s. The Isle of Graye itself had first come to company attention through an entry in one of Harrow's logbooks.

After the Second World War the firm struggled against larger container operators. It sold its inland warehouses in the 1950s, closed its passenger service in 1961, and was wound up in 1974. The Lantern Quay office building was sold to the harbour authority.

## Archive

The company's business records passed to the Pell family and, in 1990, to the Institute's archive as part of the Pell Papers. They include ledgers, crew agreements and correspondence with ship masters, among them letters from Captain Elias Venn.

## Legal legacy

The question of whether a master's logbook belonged to the master or to P&H became the subject of a lawsuit against the Institute in 1978, brought by a member of the Pell family.

documents.title: The Oriel Foundation
documents.summary: Profile of the Oriel Foundation, a Port Calder philanthropic foundation and major project funder of the Meridian Institute.
documents.body:
# The Oriel Foundation

The **Oriel Foundation** is a private philanthropic foundation based in Port Calder. It was established in 1966 by **Lionel and Beatrice Oriel**, whose family fortune came from marine insurance underwriting on the Port Calder exchange. It is one of the most important project funders of the Meridian Institute.

## History

Lionel Oriel (1902–1979) built the family underwriting business into the largest on the Calder coast. The Oriels were members of the Institute from the 1930s, and Beatrice Oriel (1908–1994) served for many years as a volunteer guide. After the 1962 fire, the couple contributed privately to the Rebuild Meridian appeal; the experience of that appeal is said to have convinced them to create a permanent foundation rather than giving case by case.

The foundation's deed names three fields: education, public health and "the cultural and scientific heritage of Port Calder." Its endowment was about $140 million in 2013.

## Grants to the Meridian Institute

Unlike the Brisk endowment, which is restricted to research and instruments and is held by the Institute, Oriel support comes as time-limited project grants, each with a fixed budget and reporting requirements. Significant grants include:

| Year | Amount | Purpose |
|------|--------|---------|
| 1971 | $60,000 | Furnishing the Conservation Studio laboratories |
| 1988 | $150,000 | "The Drowned Coast" exhibition and touring version |
| 1998 | $1,200,000 | Four-year collections digitisation project, led by Joaquin Ferrer |
| 2007 | $400,000 | Conversion of Harrow Point into a public observatory |
| 2012 | $250,000 | "Fire and Recovery" exhibition and schools programme |

The 1998 digitisation grant remains the largest the foundation has made to any cultural organisation. It paid for photography and cataloguing of charts, logbooks, herbarium sheets and roughly 31,000 glass plates from Harrow Point, and it laid the foundation for the Institute's online collections catalogue, launched in 2002.

## Governance

The foundation is run by a board of seven trustees, at least two of whom must be members of the Oriel family. Its current chair is **Imelda Oriel-Hurst**, a granddaughter of the founders. Grant decisions are made twice a year.

## Relationship with the Institute

The foundation has generally avoided funding core operating costs, preferring projects with a defined end. Institute directors have sometimes found this frustrating: in his 1999 annual review, Director Felix Amberly wrote that "project money builds wonderful things that we then struggle to keep running." The foundation's position is that the Institute's endowment and admissions should carry running costs.

## See also

- Brisk Trust
- Friends of the Meridian
- Meridian Institute funding history

documents.title: Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory (MOL)
documents.summary: Department page for the Meridian Institute's oceanographic research station at Brannock Bay, founded 1947.
documents.body:
# Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory (MOL)

The **Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory** (MOL) is the marine research station of the Meridian Institute, located at Brannock Bay, 30 km up the coast from Port Calder. It is the Institute's largest research unit by staff and budget, and the only one that operates its own vessels.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 1947 |
| Founder | Dr. Ottilie Brandt |
| Director | Dr. Priya Sandoval (since 1995) |
| Staff | 34 (including 14 research scientists) |
| Vessels | RV *Tern* (24 m), launch *Petrel II* |
| Field station | Ferrow Marsh Field Station (since 1995) |

## History

MOL was founded in 1947 by the physical oceanographer Ottilie Brandt, who ran it from a converted lifeboat house on the shore of Brannock Bay. Her programme centred on long-term measurement: tide gauges, current moorings, and temperature and salinity profiles taken at the same points month after month. Many of these series continue today, giving MOL one of the longest continuous records of coastal water conditions in the region.

Brandt retired in 1972. Her successor, Dr. Tobias Wren, took the laboratory into deep water, beginning with the 1970 expedition to the Ossery Trench, and oversaw the move into the present laboratory building in 1974.

Dr. Priya Sandoval, director since 1995, has broadened MOL's work into coastal ecology and climate, established the salt-marsh field station at Ferrow Marsh, and developed the laboratory's teaching links with partner universities.

## Research groups

- **Physical oceanography** — tides, currents, estuarine mixing; maintains the long-term moorings.
- **Marine biology** — benthic ecology, fisheries, the deep-water specimen collection.
- **Seabed mapping** — multibeam and sidescan survey of the Calder shelf.
- **Coastal change** — salt marsh, sediment supply and sea-level history.

## Collections

MOL holds the Institute's deep-water specimen collection (about 38,000 lots), a historic instrument collection shared with the Department of Astronomy and Navigation, and the laboratory's measurement archive, which is being digitised.

## Visiting

The laboratory is a working research facility and is not generally open to the public. Guided tours are offered on the first Saturday of each month from May to September; book through the Institute's visitor desk on Wrenfield Street.

## Contact

Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, Shore Road, Brannock Bay.

documents.title: Department of Astronomy and Navigation
documents.summary: Department page for the Institute's Department of Astronomy and Navigation, founded 1914 as the Department of Celestial Navigation.
documents.body:
# Department of Astronomy and Navigation

The **Department of Astronomy and Navigation** is one of the four academic departments of The Meridian Institute. It is responsible for the Institute's astronomical and navigational collections, the history-of-navigation galleries at Wrenfield Street, and the scientific programme of the Harrow Point Public Observatory.

**Head of department:** Dr. Ines Halloran (Curator of Astronomy)
**Staff:** 11 (four curatorial, two collections, three education, two observatory)
**Location:** second floor, west wing, Wrenfield Street; Harrow Point

## History

### Department of Celestial Navigation (1914–1958)

The department was established in 1914 as the **Department of Celestial Navigation**, under Professor Lucan Threlkeld. Its original purpose was practical: to train Port Calder's merchant officers in astronomical navigation and to maintain accurate time for the harbour. Threlkeld led it until his death in 1939, and during his tenure the Institute opened its observatory on Harrow Point (1925). The department's teaching collection formed the core of the later astronomy collections.

### Department of Astronomy and Navigation (1958–present)

By the 1950s the navigation courses had largely passed to the city's nautical college, and the department's work was increasingly astronomical and historical. The board renamed it the Department of Astronomy and Navigation in 1958. The Map Room collections were administered jointly with the department from 1955 under the Curator of Maps and Charts.

The department was heavily affected by the fire of 1962, which damaged part of its manuscript collection, and it moved into rooms in the west wing during rebuilding.

Research observing at Harrow Point ended in 1996 because of light pollution. Since the observatory reopened as a public site in 2008, the department's emphasis has shifted to public astronomy, the history of navigation, and the study of the Institute's archive of photographic plates.

## Heads of department

| Years | Head |
|---|---|
| 1914–1939 | Prof. Lucan Threlkeld |
| 1939–1958 | Dr. Hester Quayle (acting, as Director) and Arlo Fenwick |
| 1958–1976 | Dr. Conrad Ellery |
| 1976–1998 | Dr. Philippa Rusk |
| 1998–2011 | Dr. Anton Gale |
| 2011– | Dr. Ines Halloran |

## Collections

- Astronomical manuscripts, including the Threlkeld Star Atlas
- Around 18,000 glass photographic plates (1925–1996)
- Navigational instruments: sextants, octants, chronometers, the Calder Orrery
- The Harrow Point observing notebooks

## Current projects

- Digitisation of the photographic plate archive
- A planned exhibition on the history of the southern sky at Harrow Point
- Collaboration with the Oceanographic Laboratory on the history of marine navigation

documents.title: University of Ashcombe
documents.summary: Partner page describing the University of Ashcombe and its long research and teaching relationship with the Meridian Institute.
documents.body:
University of Ashcombe

Partner institutions — The Meridian Institute

The University of Ashcombe, often called Ashcombe University, is a public research university in the cathedral city of Ashcombe, about 160 km inland from Port Calder. Founded in 1868, it has around 21,000 students. It is the Meridian Institute's oldest academic partner; the two institutions have exchanged staff, students and specimens for more than a century.

A long relationship

Several of the Institute's most important scientists trained at Ashcombe, among them Dr. Percival Dunmore, Curator of Natural History from 1928 to 1957, and Dr. Tobias Wren, director of the Institute's oceanographic laboratory from 1972 to 1995. Ashcombe's professor of hydrography Winifred Hale spent the summer of 1950 at Brannock Bay and went on to co-author the Institute's landmark 1952 study of the Calder Estuary.

Current collaboration

  • Joint doctoral studentships in estuarine science and museum studies (four students currently enrolled).
  • Collections placements for students on Ashcombe's master's programme in museum practice.
  • The Hale Lecture, held alternately at Ashcombe and Port Calder each spring.
  • Shared access to the Institute's herbarium and deep-water specimen collection.

Key facts

Founded1868
LocationAshcombe, 160 km from Port Calder
Partnership sincec. 1912 (formal agreement 1986)
Institute contactOffice of the Deputy Director

Specimen exchange

The exchange of specimens between the two institutions began informally before the First World War, when Ashcombe's zoology museum sent duplicate seabird skins to Port Calder in return for coastal plants from the Institute's herbarium. In the 1930s Ashcombe staff helped to identify material brought back from the Isle of Graye, and in the 1950s the university's geography department lent survey instruments to the Institute's coastal laboratory. Today the exchange is governed by a formal collections loan agreement signed in 1986 and renewed in 2011, which allows research loans of up to three years without separate board approval.

Ashcombe University students regularly spend summer placements at Brannock Bay and in the Institute's collections stores on Wrenfield Street, and several have gone on to posts at the Institute.

Enquiries about joint studentships should be addressed to the Institute's research office.

documents.title: National Maritime Heritage Board - Maritime Research and Heritage Grants
documents.summary: Grant programme page of the National Maritime Heritage Board listing its 2016 awards, including support for the Ossery Trench survey.
documents.body:
Maritime Research and Heritage Grants

National Maritime Heritage Board (NMHB)

The National Maritime Heritage Board is the public body responsible for the protection, study and public enjoyment of the nation's maritime heritage, from historic ships and harbours to the seabed and its wrecks. Its Maritime Research and Heritage Grants programme supports research institutions, museums and community groups.

Programme strands

  • Seabed and wreck research — surveys of the seabed of heritage or scientific significance (awards up to $1,000,000).
  • Collections and archives — conservation and cataloguing of maritime collections (up to $250,000).
  • Community heritage — local projects, oral history and education (up to $50,000).

2016 round: awards announced

The Board received 87 applications in the 2016 round and made 14 awards totalling $3.9 million. Awards over $250,000 were:

RecipientProjectAward
The Meridian Institute (with Tollan College of Marine Science)Ossery Trench Survey: mapping and sampling of a deep-sea trench on the Calder margin$740,000
Kellet Harbour TrustRestoration of the steam tug Moorhen$610,000
Northern Wrecks Research GroupSidescan survey of the Selkirk Banks wreck field$455,000
Port Calder Maritime ArchiveCataloguing of shipping company records, 1850–1950$248,000

How to apply

The 2017 round opens on 1 March 2017 and closes on 30 June 2017. Applicants must be based in the country and must demonstrate public benefit. Seabed projects must include a plan for public release of data within two years.

Assessment

Applications are assessed by an independent panel of scientists, archaeologists and museum professionals appointed by the Board. Panels look for scientific or heritage significance, a realistic budget and timetable, the capacity of the applicant institution, partnerships with other bodies, and a clear plan for public benefit, such as exhibitions, open data or community events. Seabed projects on the continental margin are given priority in the 2017 round, reflecting the Board's current strategy to improve knowledge of little-surveyed deep-water areas and the wrecks they may contain.

Successful applicants must submit an interim report at the halfway point of the project and a final report within six months of completion. Final reports are published on the Board's website.

For guidance contact the NMHB grants office.

documents.title: Tollan College of Marine Science
documents.summary: Partner page for Tollan College of Marine Science, the Institute's principal collaborator in deep-sea research.
documents.body:
Tollan College of Marine Science

Partner institutions — The Meridian Institute

The Tollan College of Marine Science is a specialist graduate college in the port town of Tollan, about 90 km south of Port Calder. Founded in 1963 as a fisheries training school, Tollan College now offers master's and doctoral programmes in marine geoscience, biological oceanography and ocean engineering, and operates a coastal research fleet of three vessels.

Partnership with the Meridian Institute

Tollan College and the Meridian Institute's oceanographic laboratory at Brannock Bay have collaborated since the 1990s. Priya Sandoval, director of the laboratory from 1995 to 2015, held an adjunct professorship at Tollan throughout her directorship and supervised several Tollan doctoral students, among them the laboratory's present director.

The partnership's largest project to date is the 2017 survey of the Ossery Trench, co-led by Professor Aurelio Banks of Tollan's department of marine geoscience. Sediment cores from the survey are archived at Tollan; biological specimens are held by the Institute.

Joint activities

  • Shared ship time on the Institute's RV Tern and Tollan's RV Maddock
  • Co-supervised doctoral projects (currently five)
  • An annual joint symposium on the Calder margin
  • Exchange of technical staff for multibeam data processing

About the college

Tollan College began life in 1963 as a two-year training school for fisheries officers and ships' navigators, funded by the regional fishing industry. It admitted its first research students in 1979 and received its present name and degree-awarding powers in 1991. The college's campus occupies former naval buildings on the Tollan waterfront, including a large seawater aquarium hall used for experimental work. Its alumni work across fisheries management, offshore engineering and coastal planning, and several now hold research posts at the Meridian Institute.

The college is small by university standards, with about 600 graduate students, but its ship-based teaching programme is one of the most extensive in the country: every doctoral student spends at least thirty days at sea.

documents.title: Friends of the Meridian
documents.summary: Page for the Institute's membership society, founded in 1949 by volunteer Lottie Graves, including its history and membership benefits.
documents.body:
Friends of the Meridian

Friends of the Meridian is the membership society of the Meridian Institute. For seventy years its members have supported the Institute with their time, their money and their enthusiasm. Today the Friends have more than 6,200 member households across Port Calder and beyond.

Our history

The Friends were founded in 1949 by Lottie Graves, a schoolteacher who had volunteered as a gallery guide at the Institute since 1946. What began as an informal group of about twenty volunteer guides meeting for tea after Saturday school parties became, with the encouragement of the then director, Dr. Hester Quayle, a formal society with a subscription and a committee. Mrs. Graves served as its first secretary and later as its chair for many years, and remained an active volunteer until shortly before her death in 2004.

In its early years the society organised evening lectures, outings to the Institute's oceanographic laboratory at Brannock Bay and to the observatory at Harrow Point, and purchased display cases and equipment for the galleries.

The society's defining moment came after the fire of March 1962. Friends volunteered in the salvage of the collections, and during the Rebuild Meridian public appeal they raised $185,000 through fairs, concerts and door-to-door collections. Membership rose from around three hundred to more than a thousand. In recognition, the Institute gave the Friends a seat on its exhibitions committee - a place they still hold.

Milestones

YearMilestone

Membership benefits

  • Free admission to all paid exhibitions
  • The Friends' lecture series, held on the second Thursday of each month
  • Members' previews of new exhibitions
  • A subscription to Meridian Quarterly
  • Discounts in the Institute shop and café
  • Evening viewing sessions at the Harrow Point Public Observatory

Membership rates (2019)
