Volunteering

Many Friends volunteer as gallery guides, in the library and archive, and at events. The Lottie Graves Award is given each year to a volunteer who has made an outstanding contribution to the Institute.

To join, visit the Friends' desk in the entrance hall or contact the Friends' office.

documents.title: The Meridian Institute
documents.summary: Comprehensive overview of the Meridian Institute: mission, history, sites, departments, governance and collections.
documents.body:
# The Meridian Institute

**The Meridian Institute** is a research institute and public museum in Port Calder, devoted — in the words of its founding deed — to "the study of the sea, the sky and the living shore, and the display of the same to the people of Port Calder". Founded in 1911, it is the oldest scientific institution in the city and one of the best-attended museums on the coast. Its main building is at 14 Wrenfield Street; it also operates a marine laboratory at Brannock Bay, a public observatory at Harrow Point and a salt-marsh field station at Ferrow Marsh.

This article gives an overview of the Institute as a whole. Separate articles cover its departments, major collection items, people and events in more detail.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Founded | 3 May 1911 |
| Founder | Augustin Pell |
| Main site | 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder |
| Other sites | Brannock Bay (marine laboratory); Harrow Point (public observatory); Ferrow Marsh (field station) |
| Director | Dr. Idris Palk (since 2019) |
| Board chair | Rafael Quint (since 2020) |
| Staff | about 240 (including part-time) |
| Volunteers | about 400 |
| Collections | about 1.1 million objects, specimens and archival items |
| Magazine | Meridian Quarterly (since 1920) |

## Mission

The Institute describes itself as having two purposes that are meant to support each other: original research on the coast, sea and sky of the Calder region, and a public museum that shows that work and the collections behind it to as many people as possible. It has never been simply a museum with a research department attached, nor a laboratory with a gallery at the front. That double identity is the source of much of its distinctive character — and, as its history shows, of many of its recurring arguments about money, space and priorities.

## Sites

### The Wrenfield Building

The main site occupies most of a city block in the Wrenfield district, a short walk from the waterfront. The oldest part is the former bonded warehouse bought and refitted by Augustin Pell in 1910–1911, now the west wing, which houses the entrance hall, the navigation and natural-history galleries, the library, the archive and the Map Room. The central hall joins it to the Rautio Wing on the east side, built in 1964–1968 to replace the east wing lost in the fire of 1962. The atrium of the Rautio Wing, with its suspended whale skeleton, is the best-known interior in Port Calder. Offices, conservation laboratories and collection stores occupy the upper floors and basements.

### Brannock Bay

The Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory (MOL) has been based at Brannock Bay, 30 km up the coast, since its founding in 1947. The present laboratory building dates from 1974. MOL runs a research vessel, a seawater aquarium system and long-term tide and current records, and it hosts a small visitor centre in the summer.

### Harrow Point

The observatory on the Harrow Point headland, 6 km south of the city, opened in 1925 and carried out research for seventy years before light pollution ended serious work there in 1996. It reopened in 2008 as a public observatory offering evening viewing sessions, school programmes and a small exhibition space.

### Ferrow Marsh

A converted pump-house on the north shore of the Calder Estuary has served as MOL's field station for salt-marsh research since 1995.

## History

### Foundation (1911–1933)

The Institute was founded by the Port Calder shipowner Augustin Pell, co-founder of the Pell & Harrow Shipping Company, who had made a fortune on the coastal trade and had a long-standing amateur interest in astronomy and natural history. His deed of foundation, signed on 3 May 1911, established the **Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy** and endowed it with shares in his company. The first director was the botanist Dr. Cornelius Aldane.

Under Aldane the Institute grew quickly from a handful of rooms to a working museum with collecting departments in natural history, navigation and astronomy. Important early acquisitions included the logbooks of Captain Josiah Harrow (1912), the Calder Orrery (1913) and the herbarium that Aldane himself built up. A Department of Celestial Navigation was established in 1914 under Professor Lucan Threlkeld, and in 1925 the observatory at Harrow Point opened with a new 18-inch refractor.

### Between the wars (1933–1945)

Aldane retired in 1933 and was succeeded by the astronomer Dr. Hester Quayle. Her directorship saw two expeditions to the remote Isle of Graye (1934 and 1936), both carried on ships lent by the Pell family's shipping line; the second brought home the great whale skeleton that has been the Institute's emblem ever since. In 1938 the observatory's Arlo Fenwick discovered a comet, the first such discovery made from Port Calder.

### Post-war expansion (1945–1962)

The years after the Second World War were a period of expansion. The oceanographer Dr. Ottilie Brandt founded the marine laboratory at Brannock Bay in 1947. The Friends of the Meridian, a membership and volunteer society, was founded in 1949. In 1953 the industrialist Walter Brisk established an endowment trust restricted to scientific research — at the time the largest gift in the Institute's history. Dr. Rupert Sallow, director from 1951, concentrated on galleries and public programmes.

### The fire and its aftermath (1962–1968)

On the night of 14 March 1962 a fire destroyed the east wing of the Wrenfield Building. More than two thousand objects were destroyed or damaged, including a large part of the Aldane Herbarium, although many of the most important items were saved. The fire reshaped the Institute: the surviving collections were stored inland for six years; a public appeal led by the city's mayor raised more than a million dollars; a Conservation Studio was founded to repair damaged objects; Director Sallow resigned in 1964; and the Rautio Wing, designed by the architect Selma Rautio, opened on the site in 1968.

### The Oster-Lind years (1964–1987)

Dr. Margit Oster-Lind, formerly deputy director of the marine laboratory, led the Institute through the rebuilding and for two decades afterwards. She introduced free Sunday admission and a public lecture series — the "open doors" policy — while also expanding MOL's deep-sea programme, including the Ossery Trench Expedition of 1970. Her directorship was marked by one of the Institute's most painful episodes, a lawsuit brought in 1978 by the founder's granddaughter over the ownership of Captain Harrow's logbook, which the Institute won in 1981.

### Consolidation and renewal (1987–2019)

Dr. Felix Amberly (1987–2004) repaired relations with the Pell family, secured a major digitisation grant from the Oriel Foundation in 1998, and oversaw the closure of the Harrow Point observatory to research in 1996. Dr. Nadia Corrow (2004–2019) renovated the public galleries, reopened Harrow Point as a public observatory, led the Institute through its centenary in 2011 — and through a damaging dispute with the Brisk Trust over the use of restricted endowment income, settled that same year. Visitor numbers rose to record levels in the later 2010s.

### Recent years (2019–)

Dr. Idris Palk became director in May 2019. His early priorities have been the reorganisation of the scientific departments, an updated strategic plan, and the Institute's response to the closures of 2020.

## Research highlights

Although the museum is what most people in Port Calder know, the Institute has a research record that stretches back more than a century. Among its best-known contributions:

- **Coastal botany.** Cornelius Aldane's surveys of the salt marshes and dunes of the Calder coast, begun before the Institute existed, remain the baseline for studies of vegetation change in the region. Several species were first described from Institute specimens.
- **Astronomy.** The observatory at Harrow Point produced a long series of positional observations between 1925 and 1996, as well as the comet discovery of 1938. Professor Threlkeld's hand-drawn star atlas of 1924 is still consulted by historians of astronomy.
- **Expeditions.** The two Graye Island expeditions of the 1930s produced the first reliable chart of the island's reef, the first description of its seabird colonies, and a large natural-history collection. The 1970 Ossery Trench Expedition was one of the first deep-sea dredging programmes carried out by a regional institution, and the 2017 survey of the same trench produced the first complete multibeam map of it.
- **Physical oceanography.** MOL's tide and current records from Brannock Bay form one of the longest continuous coastal series in the country. Ottilie Brandt's work on estuarine mixing in the early 1950s, written with colleagues from the University of Ashcombe, is still widely cited.
- **Sea-level history.** MOL's work on salt-marsh sediments at Ferrow Marsh has produced a detailed record of sea-level change on the Calder coast over the last three thousand years, presented to the public in the 1988 exhibition "The Drowned Coast".

## Architecture

The Wrenfield Building is a record of the Institute's history in brick, stone and concrete. The west wing is a four-storey brick warehouse of the 1860s, converted in 1910–1911 with tall gallery windows and a stone entrance portal. The central hall, built with the east wing in 1912–1914, has a glazed iron roof that survived the fire of 1962 with only minor damage. The Graye gallery, laid out in 1939 beneath the whale skeleton in the central hall, survived the fire of 1962 with smoke staining; the east wing beside it did not.

The Rautio Wing, opened in 1968, is a board-marked concrete building by the Finnish-born architect Selma Rautio, with a full-height atrium lit from above and galleries arranged around it on three levels. Rautio designed it to be as fire-resistant as the technology of the day allowed: its stores are divided into compartments by fire walls and doors, and it was the first public building in Port Calder to be fitted throughout with automatic sprinklers. It was listed as a building of special architectural interest in 2002.

## Controversies

The Institute's history has not been without disputes. The most significant were the questions raised about fire safety after 1962, which led to Director Sallow's resignation; the ownership case over the Corvina Logbook (1978–1981); the debate over the closure of the Harrow Point observatory in 1996, which divided staff and was opposed by amateur astronomers in the city; and the dispute with the Brisk Trust (2009–2011) over the use of restricted research income for gallery works. Each is covered in its own article. A common thread in several of them is the long-running question of how the Institute should balance its research mission against its museum mission when money and space are limited.

## Name

A question visitors often ask is where the name "Meridian" comes from, and why the Institute does not bear its founder's name. The answer lies in a request made by Augustin Pell himself. Pell never liked seeing his name over the door; he felt that the Institute belonged to the city and to its work rather than to one family, and he did not want its reputation tied to his firm's fortunes. The founding deed contained an unusual clause allowing the board to adopt a new name at his request, and in October 1928 he invoked it. At the board meeting of 17 October 1928, Professor Lucan Threlkeld proposed "The Meridian Institute", after the brass meridian line set into the floor of the transit room at the Harrow Point Observatory, from which all the Institute's astronomical and navigational observations were reckoned. The name was adopted unanimously and took effect on 1 January 1929. Pell died later that year. The original carved name "Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy" survives in stone over the Wrenfield Street doorway, with a bronze plaque bearing the new name beneath it.

## Organisation

The Institute is a charitable body governed by a Board of Trustees of up to fifteen members. The Board appoints the Director, who is the chief executive and is responsible for the staff, collections and scientific programme. The Director is supported by a deputy director and a senior management team that includes the chief financial officer, the heads of the scientific departments and the head of public engagement.

As of January 2021, the Institute's work is organised into the following units:

- **Department of Astronomy and Navigation** — the successor to the Department of Celestial Navigation founded in 1914; responsible for the astronomy and navigation collections, the Harrow Point Public Observatory and research in the history of navigation and astronomy.
- **Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory (MOL)** — marine science at Brannock Bay and Ferrow Marsh; physical oceanography, marine biology and coastal change. Director: Dr. Rhea Oduya.
- **Department of Natural History** — zoology, botany (including the Aldane Herbarium) and geology collections.
- **Department of Maps, Charts and Manuscripts** — the Map Room, the archive and the manuscript collections, including the Pell Papers.
- **Department of Ethnography** — objects documenting the coastal communities of the Calder region.
- **Conservation and Collections Care Division** — conservation laboratories, collection storage and environmental control.
- **Public Engagement** — exhibitions, learning, events and the Friends of the Meridian.
- **Finance and Operations** — including estates, security and visitor services.

The Board has asked the Director to review this structure, and a reorganisation of the scientific departments, bringing together work on the sea and the sky, is under discussion.

## Funding

The Institute's income comes from several sources, whose balance has changed a great deal over its history. In its first decades it depended almost wholly on Augustin Pell's endowment of company shares and on his personal gifts. From 1953 the Brisk Trust provided a substantial stream of income restricted to research. After 1962 the city council and the public, through the Rebuild Meridian appeal, paid for the rebuilding. Since the 1990s competitive grants from foundations and public bodies have funded much of the research and digitisation work, while admissions, memberships, retail and events support the museum. The Institute's own endowment has grown steadily since the centenary campaign of 2011.

## Collections

The Institute's collections number about 1.1 million items. Highlights include:

- **Big Graye**, the skeleton of a fin whale recovered from the Isle of Graye in 1936, suspended in the Rautio Wing atrium
- **The Corvina Logbook**, Captain Josiah Harrow's journal of 1889–1894
- **The Threlkeld Star Atlas** (1924)
- **The Calder Orrery**, made c. 1790 by Thaddeus Quill
- **The Kittering Sound Chart** (1851)
- **The Venn Sextant** and **the Harrow Octant**
- **The Aldane Herbarium**, about 6,800 sheets of coastal plants
- **The Brandt Current Meter** (1949)
- **The Pell Papers**, the archive of the founder's family and shipping company

## Publications

The Institute has published Meridian Quarterly since 1920. It also publishes expedition reports, exhibition catalogues and occasional monographs. Two book-length histories exist: Hester Quayle's *A History of the Meridian Institute* (1961) and Nell Farris's centenary history *Meridian at One Hundred* (2011).

## Directors

| # | Director | Term |
|---|----------|------|
| 1 | Dr. Cornelius Aldane | 1911–1933 |
| 2 | Dr. Hester Quayle | 1933–1951 |
| 3 | Dr. Rupert Sallow | 1951–1964 |
| 4 | Dr. Margit Oster-Lind | 1964–1987 |
| 5 | Dr. Felix Amberly | 1987–2004 |
| 6 | Dr. Nadia Corrow | 2004–2019 |
| 7 | Dr. Idris Palk | 2019– |

## Partnerships

The Institute has long-standing research partnerships with the University of Ashcombe, whose staff have collaborated with MOL since the 1950s, and with Tollan College of Marine Science. It receives grant funding from the Oriel Foundation and the National Maritime Heritage Board, among others, and works closely with the Calder Historical Society and the Port Calder city council.

## Visiting

The Wrenfield Building is open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00–17:00, with late opening on Thursdays. Admission is charged, except for members of the Friends of the Meridian and on the first Sunday of each month, a surviving remnant of the "open doors" policy of the 1960s. The Harrow Point Public Observatory opens for evening sessions on Fridays and Saturdays. The MOL visitor centre at Brannock Bay opens from May to September.

## See also

- Augustin Pell
- Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory
- Wrenfield Fire
- Friends of the Meridian
- Brisk Trust

documents.title: Pell Family Papers Given to the Institute
documents.summary: 1990 news release announcing Clarissa Pell-Windham's gift of the Pell Papers to the archive.
documents.body:
Pell Family Papers Come Home to the Meridian Institute

News release — The Meridian Institute, Port Calder — 2 April 1990

The Meridian Institute today announced the gift of the Pell Papers, the private and business archive of the family of its founder, Augustin Pell. The collection has been given by his granddaughter, Mrs. Clarissa Pell-Windham, and has been registered in the Institute's archive under accession number MI-1990-0017.

The papers fill 212 archive boxes and span the years 1864 to 1974. They document the Pell family, the founding of the Institute in 1911, and ninety-two years of the Pell and Harrow shipping line, from its first collier to its closure.

What the collection contains

  • Augustin Pell's personal correspondence, including more than 300 letters to and from the Institute's first director, Dr. Cornelius Aldane
  • Company ledgers, fleet lists and crew agreements, 1882–1974
  • Letters from company masters, including Captain Elias Venn
  • Papers of Edmund Pell relating to the Graye Island expeditions of the 1930s
  • About 1,900 photographs of ships, crews and the Port Calder waterfront
  • Plans and building accounts for the company's warehouses and offices

A new chapter

“This is a remarkable and generous gift,” said the Institute's director, Dr. Felix Amberly. “It fills gaps in our own history that we did not even know we had. And it closes a difficult chapter between the Institute and the family that founded it. We are very grateful to Mrs. Pell-Windham.”

Mrs. Pell-Windham said: “My grandfather built this Institute for the city. I wanted the whole story of what he did, and of the company that paid for it, to be kept together in the place he made. I am glad it is here.”

Access

The papers will be catalogued over the next three years by the Institute's archive staff, with the help of a grant from the Calder Historical Society. Parts of the collection will be available to researchers by appointment from early 1991.

ItemDetail
DonorMrs. Clarissa Pell-Windham
Extent212 boxes; approx. 38 linear metres
Date range1864–1974
Cataloguing1990–1993

For further information contact the Institute's press office, 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder.

documents.title: The Threlkeld Star Atlas
documents.summary: Collection record for the Threlkeld Star Atlas, a 64-plate hand-drawn atlas completed in 1924 by Professor Lucan Threlkeld.
documents.body:
# The Threlkeld Star Atlas

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Accession number | MI-1926-0112 |
| Object type | Manuscript star atlas, bound |
| Author | Professor Lucan Threlkeld (1872–1939) |
| Date | 1914–1924 |
| Extent | 64 plates plus 12 leaves of tables, 58 x 44 cm |
| Media | Ink and watercolour on laid paper; half-leather binding |
| Accessioned | 1926 |
| Current location | Map Room W-214, west wing, flat cabinet 3 |
| Access | By appointment only; handling by conservation staff |

## Description

The **Threlkeld Star Atlas** is a hand-drawn atlas of 64 plates covering the southern and equatorial skies as seen from Harrow Point, the headland south of Port Calder. Each plate shows stars to about the seventh magnitude, drawn in black ink with magnitudes indicated by dot size, and constellation boundaries in faint red wash. Twelve leaves of tables at the back give positions for navigational stars reduced to the epoch 1925.0.

## Maker

The atlas was the life's work of **Professor Lucan Threlkeld**, the first head of the Institute's **Department of Celestial Navigation**, which he led from its creation in 1914 until his death in 1939. Threlkeld began the atlas as a teaching aid for navigation students and gradually expanded it into a complete survey. Most of the plates were drawn from his own observations with small telescopes on Wrenfield Street and, from 1925, at the new observatory on Harrow Point. He completed the final plate in 1924, and the bound atlas was formally accessioned into the collection in 1926.

## History

- 1926: accessioned; displayed in the astronomy gallery for special occasions.
- 1962: water-damaged during the fire of 14 March 1962, when water from the firefighting in the adjoining east wing flooded the astronomy gallery where the atlas was then on display. Plates 40 to 64 suffered tide-lines and cockling.
- 1963–1967: dismantled, washed, flattened and rebound in the newly established Conservation Studio.
- 1972: centrepiece of the exhibition *Stars Over Calder*.
- 1998: all plates photographed at high resolution under the digitisation programme.

## Conservation notes

The binding is fragile. The atlas must be supported on foam wedges at an opening angle of no more than 110 degrees. Light exposure is limited to 50 lux for no more than 30 days per year. Plates 51 and 52 show residual tide-lines that were judged too risky to reduce further.

## Significance

The atlas is the most important astronomical manuscript in the collection and the best surviving record of the Department of Celestial Navigation's early teaching. It has been reproduced in facsimile twice.

documents.title: The Calder Orrery
documents.summary: Collection record for the brass orrery made c.1790 by Thaddeus Quill, damaged in 1962 and restored in 1970.
documents.body:
# The Calder Orrery

**Accession number:** MI-1913-0005
**Object type:** Mechanical model of the solar system (grand orrery)
**Date:** c. 1790
**Maker:** Thaddeus Quill, Port Calder
**Acquisition:** Purchased 1913
**Department:** Astronomy collections

## Description

A hand-cranked brass orrery on a mahogany drum base, 118 cm in diameter. A gear train turns the planets Mercury to Saturn around a gilt sun, with the Moon revolving around the Earth and four moons around Jupiter. The horizon ring is engraved with the zodiac and a calendar scale. The drum is inlaid with a satinwood band and bears the maker's signature on an engraved brass cartouche: "Thad. Quill fecit, Port Calder".

## Maker

**Thaddeus Quill** (c. 1745–1809) was Port Calder's most important eighteenth-century instrument maker, producing quadrants, compasses and globes for the harbour trade. His workshop stood on Lantern Quay, close to where the ships loaded. Only three orreries by Quill are known; this is the largest and the only one to survive in its home city.

## Acquisition

The orrery was bought by the Institute in 1913 from the estate of a Port Calder merchant family, funded by the Institute's founder. It was one of the first major purchases made under Director Cornelius Aldane, who displayed it in the central hall of the Wrenfield Building.

## Fire damage and restoration

The orrery was heat-damaged in the 1962 fire. The heat softened the lacquer, warped two of the planetary arms, and cracked the mahogany drum; several of the smaller gears seized. It spent six years in storage while the building was rebuilt.

The restoration was carried out in 1970 by B. Nolan, head of the Institute's newly created conservation unit, assisted by the clockmaker Leonard Patch. Nolan chose to keep the fire-scorched satinwood band rather than replace it, on the principle that "the fire is now part of the object's history". The warped arms were straightened cold, the drum was consolidated, and the gear train was cleaned and reassembled. Nolan's restoration report of 1970 remains a reference text for orrery conservation.

## Display

After restoration the orrery was shown in "Stars Over Calder" (1972) and has been on permanent display in the Astronomy Gallery since 1974. It is demonstrated by hand on the first Sunday of every month.

## Condition

Stable. The gear train is inspected annually. The scorched band and a small replaced section of the drum are clearly visible and explained on the label.

documents.title: The Aldane Herbarium
documents.summary: Collection record for the coastal-plant herbarium begun by Cornelius Aldane, including its type sheet of Calder sea-lavender.
documents.body:
# The Aldane Herbarium

**Collection type:** Herbarium (pressed and mounted plant specimens)
**Founded by:** Dr. Cornelius Aldane, first director
**Date range of specimens:** 1889–present
**Current size:** approx. 6,800 sheets
**Department:** Natural History

## Overview

The Aldane Herbarium is the Institute's collection of pressed plants, concentrated on the coastal and salt-marsh flora of the Calder region. Cornelius Aldane gave his own collection of about 1,200 sheets to the Institute in 1911, and by his retirement in 1933 the herbarium held roughly 9,000 sheets, built up by his own fieldwork, by exchange with other herbaria, and by gifts from local collectors.

## Loss in 1962

The herbarium was stored in cabinets on the first floor of the east wing and was badly affected by the fire of 14 March 1962. About 40% of the sheets were lost, chiefly the families filed alphabetically in the cabinets nearest the stairwell. Surviving sheets were packed wet and dried in the months after the fire; many still carry tide-mark staining. Collecting since the 1970s has brought the collection back to about 6,800 sheets.

## Type specimens

The herbarium holds eleven type specimens — the specimens on which the scientific description of a species was based. The most important is:

- **HERB-AL-0457** — holotype of **Calder sea-lavender** (*Limonium calderense* Aldane), collected by Cornelius Aldane at Ferrow Marsh on 22 July 1909 and described by him in Meridian Quarterly in 1922. The sheet carries three flowering stems, Aldane's original field label in pencil, and a later annotation slip. Calder sea-lavender is endemic to a handful of salt marshes on the Calder coast and is now protected.

The sea-lavender sheet survived the fire because Aldane had placed it, with other type specimens, in a steel document box in the director's office.

## Collecting localities

The herbarium is strongest for:

- Ferrow Marsh and the salt marshes north of the Calder Estuary
- The dunes at Brannock Bay
- Harrow Point headland
- The Isle of Graye (sheets collected on the 1934 and 1936 expeditions)

## Access

Researchers may consult the herbarium by appointment. Around 4,000 sheets were imaged in the digitisation programme of the late 1990s and are searchable online.

## Related

- Cornelius Aldane
- Ferrow Marsh

documents.title: The Kittering Sound Chart
documents.summary: Collection record for an 1851 hand-drawn chart of Kittering Sound by surveyor Josias Fell, donated by Walter Brisk in 1958.
documents.body:
# The Kittering Sound Chart

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Accession number | MI-1958-0091 |
| Object type | Manuscript nautical chart |
| Surveyor | Josias Fell |
| Date | 1851 |
| Dimensions | 96 x 71 cm |
| Media | Ink and wash on linen-backed paper |
| Acquisition | Gift of Walter Brisk, 1958 |
| Location | Map Room, west wing |

## Description

A hand-drawn chart of **Kittering Sound**, the channel of islands and tidal passages in the northern waters beyond Port Calder. The chart shows soundings in fathoms, the positions of rocks and shoals, leading marks for the principal passages, and coastal profiles of the headlands as seen from seaward. A cartouche in the lower right reads "Kittering Sound, surveyed by J. Fell, 1851".

## Surveyor

**Josias Fell** (c. 1812–1870) was a Port Calder surveyor who worked for merchants and harbour authorities along the northern coast. Several of his other charts survive in private hands, but the Kittering Sound Chart is the most complete. Fell's soundings were used by coastal shipping for more than half a century and were not fully superseded until the 1920s.

## Acquisition

The chart was given to the Institute in 1958 by **Walter Brisk**, the owner of Brisk Canneries, whose fishing fleet worked the Kittering Sound grounds. Brisk had bought the chart at a Port Calder estate sale in 1931 and kept it framed in his office on the waterfront. In his letter of gift he wrote that "the men who fish the Sound owe their lives to Fell's pencil."

## Condition

Fair. The chart was in the Map Room in the west wing during the fire of 1962 and suffered smoke staining and minor water damage at the lower margin. It was surface-cleaned and relined in 1966. Some fading of the blue wash is visible.

## Use in exhibitions

- *Stars Over Calder* (1972)
- *The Drowned Coast* (1988), where it was used to compare nineteenth-century shorelines with modern surveys
- *Charting the North* (2006)

## Research notes

The chart was studied in 1988 as evidence for shoreline change at the entrance to Kittering Sound. Comparison with twentieth-century surveys suggests that one of Fell's charted islets had been reduced to a tidal bank by the 1980s.

documents.title: The Corvina Logbook
documents.summary: Collection record for Captain Josiah Harrow's four-volume logbook of SS Corvina, 1889–1894.
documents.body:
# The Corvina Logbook

**Accession number:** MI-1912-0031
**Object type:** Manuscript ship's logbook, 4 volumes
**Date:** 1889–1894
**Maker:** Captain Josiah Harrow (1851–1908)
**Acquisition:** Gift of Mrs. Constance Harrow, 1912
**Department:** Archive and Manuscripts

## Description

Four quarto volumes bound in brown calf, together some 1,140 pages, kept by Captain Josiah Harrow while master of the steamer SS Corvina between March 1889 and November 1894. The entries record courses, positions, weather, soundings, cargo, crew matters and — unusually for a working log — frequent notes on birds, whales, sea conditions and the night sky. Harrow wrote in a small, regular hand in iron-gall ink; a few later pages are in pencil.

Harrow was co-founder of the shipping company that owned the Corvina, and the log reflects his dual role as working master and partner: commercial notes on freight rates sit beside descriptions of fog banks and phosphorescence.

## The 1891 Graye entry

The most celebrated passage is in volume 2. On 18–19 August 1891, driven off course by a southwesterly gale, the Corvina stood in toward an island Harrow calls "Graye's Rock, so named on no chart I possess". He records a line of breakers on an uncharted reef, "birds beyond counting" nesting on the cliffs, and the carcass of a great whale on the shore of a sheltered cove. Harrow sent a boat in at first light and noted fresh water in a stream. This entry, describing what is now called the Isle of Graye, was the direct inspiration for the Institute's expeditions there in the 1930s.

## Provenance

Harrow died in 1908. In 1912 his widow, Constance Harrow, gave the logbook to the newly founded Institute, together with his brass octant, "so that his observations may be of use to men of science". The deed of gift, signed by Mrs. Harrow and Director Cornelius Aldane, is held with the volumes.

The ownership of the logbook was later challenged in the courts on the ground that it was company property rather than Harrow's own. The court found that a master's personal log of this kind was his own property and that the 1912 gift was valid; the volumes have remained in the Institute's collection without interruption.

## Condition and history

The volumes survived the 1962 fire, when they were removed from the building during the night; volume 4 shows slight water staining on its lower edge. They were rebacked by the Institute's conservators in the 1970s and digitised in full in 1999. Readers now consult the digital surrogate; the originals are shown only in exhibitions, for no more than three months at a time.

## Exhibition history

- "The Sea Roads" (1931)
- "Stars Over Calder" (1972), volume 2 only
- "Fire and Recovery" (2012)

## References

- H. Quayle, *A History of the Meridian Institute* (1961), chapter 2
- N. Farris, *Meridian at One Hundred* (2011)

documents.title: The Harrow Octant
documents.summary: Collection record for the brass octant used by Captain Josiah Harrow, donated with his logbook in 1912.
documents.body:
# The Harrow Octant

**Accession number:** MI-1912-0044
**Object type:** Navigational instrument — reflecting octant
**Date:** c. 1875
**Maker:** Brandon & Sons, Liverpool (signed on the index arm)
**User:** Captain Josiah Harrow
**Acquisition:** Gift of Mrs. Constance Harrow, 1912
**Department:** Astronomy and navigation collections

## Description

A brass-framed reflecting octant with an ebony-veneered arc divided on an inset ivory scale to 20 minutes of arc, read by vernier to single minutes. The instrument has a radius of 25 cm, two sets of shade glasses, a sighting tube, and a mirror housing that was replaced in the 1890s. It is stored in its original fitted mahogany box, the lid of which carries a paper trade label and, in ink, the inscription "J. Harrow — SS Corvina".

An octant measures angles up to 90 degrees and was used to take the altitude of the sun or a star above the horizon to find latitude. By the 1880s most deep-water masters used the more versatile sextant, and Harrow's continued use of an octant on coastal routes was typical of short-sea shipping.

## Use

The octant was Harrow's working instrument for most of his career as a master with the company he co-founded. Wear on the index arm and the handle is consistent with long use. Noon latitude observations in his surviving logbooks, including the famous 1891 run past the Isle of Graye, were most likely taken with this instrument.

## Provenance

Given in 1912 by Harrow's widow, Constance Harrow, together with his logbooks. It was among the first navigational instruments to enter the collection.

## Condition

Good. During the 1962 fire the octant was on display in a west-wing gallery, which suffered smoke but no flame; it was cleaned and the lacquer consolidated in 1964. The arc shows minor tarnish.

## Not to be confused with

The collection also holds **the Venn Sextant**, a later instrument used by Captain Elias Venn, another master mariner of the same shipping line, which was donated by his daughter in 1951. The two instruments are frequently confused in enquiries because both belonged to company captains and both are associated with voyages to the Isle of Graye. The Harrow Octant is the older and smaller instrument, and it is an octant (eighth of a circle), not a sextant.

## Exhibition history

- "The Sea Roads" (1931)
- "Instruments of Passage" (1983)
- Permanent display, Navigation Gallery, 2009–2014

documents.title: The Venn Sextant
documents.summary: Collection record for a brass sextant owned by Captain Elias Venn, donated by his daughter Rosalind Venn in 1951.
documents.body:
# The Venn Sextant

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Accession number | MI-1951-0208 |
| Object type | Marine sextant, vernier reading |
| Maker | Hollis & Crane, instrument makers |
| Date of manufacture | c. 1905 |
| Materials | Brass, silvered arc, glass, ebony handle |
| Dimensions | Radius 18 cm; case 29 x 27 x 13 cm |
| Acquisition | Gift of Miss Rosalind Venn, 1951 |
| Location | Navigation gallery, case 4 |

## Description

A standard vernier sextant of the early twentieth century in its original fitted mahogany case, with three telescopes, a set of shade glasses and a small brass key. The silvered arc is graduated to 10 seconds of arc. The case lid carries a paper certificate of examination dated 1906 and, scratched inside the lid, the initials "E.V." and a list of ship names.

## Provenance

The sextant belonged to **Captain Elias Venn** (1880–1949) and was used by him during his years as a Pell & Harrow master, from his first command in 1913 until his retirement from the sea in 1938. After his death in 1949 it passed to his daughter, **Rosalind Venn**, a schoolteacher in Port Calder, who gave it to the Institute in 1951 together with a small bundle of his navigation workbooks.

In her letter accompanying the gift, Rosalind Venn wrote that her father "trusted this instrument over any clock or wireless, and took it on every voyage he made after the Great War."

## Condition

Good. The index mirror was resilvered in 1987. The instrument was on display in the west wing in 1962 and was not affected by the fire.

## Related objects

The Institute holds a second navigational instrument from a Pell & Harrow captain, the brass octant of Captain Josiah Harrow, which came in 1912 with Harrow's logbook. The two are frequently confused in older gallery labels: the octant is the earlier, simpler instrument (an eighth of a circle, reading to about one minute of arc) while the Venn Sextant is a twentieth-century precision instrument.

## Notes

The list of ship names inside the lid includes the *Plover*, *Tamsin* and *Corrie*, all Pell & Harrow coastal vessels. The instrument was last shown in a temporary exhibition in 2003.

documents.title: Big Graye (fin whale skeleton)
documents.summary: Collection record for Big Graye, the fin whale skeleton recovered by the 1936 Second Graye Island Expedition.
documents.body:
# Big Graye (fin whale skeleton)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Accession number | MI-1937-0664 |
| Object type | Articulated skeleton, fin whale (*Balaenoptera physalus*) |
| Length | 21.3 metres |
| Collected | Isle of Graye, July 1936 |
| Collector | Second Graye Island Expedition (leader Dr. Percival Dunmore) |
| Accessioned | 1937 |
| Location | Atrium, Rautio Wing (suspended) |

## Description

**Big Graye** is the articulated skeleton of an adult fin whale, suspended from the atrium ceiling of the Rautio Wing. It is the largest single object in the Institute's collection and the best-known image of the museum; it appears on the Institute's letterhead and on the Friends of the Meridian membership card.

The skeleton comprises the skull, jaws, 62 vertebrae, ribs, sternum and flipper bones. Some of the smaller finger bones are cast replacements made in 1938.

## Collection

The whale was found dead and partially stranded on the reef flats of the Isle of Graye in July 1936 by the **Second Graye Island Expedition**, led by **Dr. Percival Dunmore**, the Institute's Curator of Natural History. The expedition's preparators flensed the carcass on the reef over nine days, packed the bones in brine barrels and lime, and shipped them to Port Calder aboard the expedition vessel. The skeleton was accessioned in 1937 and articulated over the following two years.

## Display history

- 1939–1962: hung in the central hall of the Wrenfield Building.
- 1962: survived the fire of 14 March 1962 with smoke staining only; the central hall was not reached by the flames.
- 1962–1968: dismantled and stored off-site during rebuilding.
- 1968: rehung in the atrium of the new Rautio Wing at its opening.
- 2019 (planned): cleaning and reassembly of the vertebral column.

## Measurement

The length of 21.3 metres is taken from Dunmore's 1937 report and has been used in all gallery texts since. The measurement was made along the articulated vertebral column from the tip of the rostrum to the last caudal vertebra.

## Name

The name "Big Graye" was coined by Port Calder schoolchildren in the 1940s and adopted informally by staff. It has never been an official title, but the Institute has used it in publicity since the 1968 reopening.

documents.title: Brandt Current Meter
documents.summary: Collection record for the self-recording current meter designed at MOL in 1949 and deployed at the Brannock Bay tide station until 1968.
documents.body:
# Brandt Current Meter

**Accession number:** MI-1949-0340
**Object type:** Scientific instrument (self-recording current meter)
**Maker:** Designed by Dr. Ottilie Brandt; built in the workshop of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory
**Date:** 1949
**Materials:** Bronze, brass, glass, clockwork, waxed-paper recording drum
**Dimensions:** 112 cm long; 38 kg without mooring frame
**Location:** Instrument gallery, Meridian Institute (on display)

## Description

A torpedo-shaped bronze housing containing a clockwork-driven recording drum, with a four-bladed impeller at the forward end and a vane at the rear that keeps the instrument pointed into the current. Impeller revolutions and a magnetic compass reading were marked on the drum every ten minutes by a pair of inked styluses, allowing a single deployment to record current speed and direction for up to eleven days.

## History

Ottilie Brandt designed the meter in 1949, two years after founding the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, because commercially available current meters of the time could record only for a few hours or required a boat to stay on station. Her design borrowed the clockwork of a ship's chronometer and the housing of a surplus naval practice torpedo, sourced by the laboratory's engineer.

The Institute's registrar entered the meter in the instrument register when it was completed in 1949, which is why its accession number carries that year even though it did not come into the museum collection until it was retired.

From 1949 until 1968 the meter was deployed at the laboratory's Brannock Bay tide station, designated MOL-ST-07, moored in about 14 metres of water off the northern breakwater. It was recovered, cleaned and redeployed roughly every ten days, weather permitting — some 600 deployments in total. Its records formed the backbone of Brandt's studies of estuarine circulation along the Calder coast and are still used as a baseline.

It was replaced in 1968 by an electronic meter and transferred from laboratory use to the collection.

## Condition

Good. The bronze housing shows pitting consistent with nineteen years in seawater. The recording drum and one stylus arm are replacements made in the laboratory workshop in 1961. A full condition survey was carried out by the conservation division in 2016 before the meter went on display.

## Exhibition history

- *The Drowned Coast*, 1988
- *Deep Meridian*, 2018–2019

## Related material

- Brandt field notebooks, vols. 12–31 (Institute archive)
- Deployment logs for the Brannock Bay station, 1949–1968

documents.title: Big Graye Is Shorter Than We Thought
documents.summary: 2019 release reporting that reassembly of the Graye fin whale skeleton revised its length from 21.3 to 19.8 metres.
documents.body:
Big Graye Is Shorter Than We Thought

News release, 18 November 2019

For more than eighty years, visitors to the Meridian Institute have been told that the fin whale skeleton hanging in the Rautio Wing atrium is 21.3 metres long. It is not. Conservators who dismantled and rebuilt the skeleton this year have found that the true length of Big Graye is 19.8 metres.

The Graye fin whale was recovered from a beach on the Isle of Graye during the Institute's second expedition to the island in 1936 and first measured when it was assembled in Port Calder the following year. That figure, 21.3 metres, has appeared in every guidebook and label since.

What went wrong in 1937

When the Conservation and Collections Care Division lowered the skeleton in April for its first full conservation treatment since the 1960s, the team found that a section of seven tail vertebrae had been strung twice: once in the correct position and once, from a second, smaller animal collected on the same beach, inserted between the lumbar and caudal series. The extra section added about a metre and a half to the skeleton.

"It's an easy mistake to make on a beach with two carcasses and no reference skeleton," said the project conservator, Ruth Okimba. "The 1937 preparators did remarkable work with what they had. But the vertebrae don't match in size or in colour once you clean them, and the growth plates tell you they came from a younger animal."

The new Big Graye

  • Revised length: 19.8 metres (previously published as 21.3 metres).
  • The extra vertebrae have been catalogued separately and will go on display beneath the main skeleton with an explanation.
  • The skeleton has been re-hung on a new stainless-steel armature designed to allow individual bones to be removed for study.
  • New labels and a short film in the atrium tell the story of the remeasurement.

The Director, Dr. Idris Palk, said the correction was "a good example of what museum science is for. Collections aren't finished when they are put on display. We keep looking at them, and sometimes they surprise us."

MeasurementSourceLength
Original assembly1937 expedition report21.3 m
ReassemblyConservation survey, 201919.8 m

The atrium reopened to visitors on 16 November.

documents.title: Port Calder Gazette: 'Comet Fenwick' found from Harrow Point (1938)
documents.summary: Newspaper report of Arlo Fenwick's discovery of a new comet at Harrow Point in November 1938.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER GAZETTE -- Saturday, 12 November 1938 -- Page 3

NEW COMET SIGHTED FROM HARROW POINT
Local Astronomer's Find -- "Comet Fenwick" Visible in Evening Sky

A new comet has been discovered by Mr. Arlo Fenwick, astronomer at the Meridian Institute's observatory on Harrow Point, it was announced yesterday. The object, which astronomers abroad have already begun to call "Comet Fenwick", was first noticed by Mr. Fenwick on the evening of Wednesday last, the 9th of November, low in the western sky shortly after sunset.

Speaking to the Gazette at the observatory, Mr. Fenwick, a native of Port Calder, said that he had been sweeping the evening sky with a small finder telescope "as I do most clear nights, more from habit than hope" when he noticed "a little smudge of light where there ought to be nothing". He turned the observatory's great telescope upon it and, after watching it for two hours, suspected that it was moving against the stars. He confirmed the motion on Thursday night and at once telegraphed the discovery to the central bureau for astronomical announcements.

Dr. Hester Quayle, Director of the Meridian Institute and herself an astronomer, said that the discovery was "a tribute to Mr. Fenwick's patience and to the dark skies of Harrow Point". She added that the comet had been given the provisional designation 1938b, being the second new comet reported this year.

The comet is at present too faint to be seen with the naked eye, but readers with good field glasses may find it low in the west-south-west about an hour after sunset, below and to the left of the bright planet. Astronomers expect it to brighten somewhat over the coming weeks as it approaches the sun, though Dr. Quayle cautioned that "comets are notoriously unreliable, and it may disappoint us."

The Institute will open the Harrow Point observatory to the public on the evenings of Tuesday and Friday next, weather permitting, for viewing through the smaller telescopes. Admission will be free, but visitors are asked to bring warm clothing and to walk the last half mile from the tram terminus, as motor cars disturb the observers.

Mr. Fenwick, who is 37, joined the Institute as a computer in 1922 under the late Professor Threlkeld's department and has been at Harrow Point since the observatory opened. He is unmarried and lives in the observers' cottage on the point. Asked how he felt, he said: "Cold, mostly. But very pleased."

This is the first comet to be discovered from Port Calder. The last comet visible to the naked eye from the city was in 1910.

(A photograph of the observatory appears on page 7.)

documents.title: New Institute laboratory opens at Brannock Bay (Port Calder Gazette, 1947)
documents.summary: Newspaper report of the opening of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory under its first director, Ottilie Brandt.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER GAZETTE
Monday, 21 July 1947 - page 5

INSTITUTE TAKES TO THE WATER
Old lifeboat house becomes laboratory of the sea

BRANNOCK BAY, Saturday. - The Meridian Institute, better known to Port Calder families for its whale bones and its telescope, has gone to sea - or at least to the seashore.

On Saturday afternoon the Institute's director, Dr. Hester Quayle, formally opened the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory in the former lifeboat house at Brannock Bay, which has stood empty since the lifeboat moved to Kellet eight years ago.

The new laboratory will be directed by Dr. Ottilie Brandt, who has been attached to the Institute's natural history department since 1941. Dr. Brandt told the Gazette that the laboratory's purpose was "to measure the sea around Port Calder - its tides, its currents, its warmth and its saltiness - every week, for as long as there is an Institute."

About sixty guests, among them members of the Brannock Bay parish council and a party from the fishermen's cooperative, heard Dr. Quayle describe the laboratory as "the Institute's first home outside the city, and I hope not its last."

The building has been fitted with a workroom, a small chemical laboratory, a darkroom, and a store for moorings. A tide gauge has been installed on the old slipway, and Dr. Brandt's staff - two assistants and a boatman - will tend moorings in the bay from a nine-metre launch, the Petrel.

Mr. Silas Kemble, chairman of the fishermen's cooperative, said his members had "waited thirty years for someone to tell us where the fish go, and we'll be glad to be told." The cooperative has agreed to buy weekly tide predictions from the laboratory.

Asked whether the laboratory would mount expeditions like those to the Isle of Graye in the 1930s, Dr. Brandt replied: "Not yet. First we must learn our own bay."

The laboratory will not be open to the public, but Dr. Brandt said visitors "who do not mind wet floors" would be welcome by appointment.

The cost of the conversion, about 2,400 dollars, was met from the Institute's general funds.

[Photograph caption: Dr. Ottilie Brandt (left) and Dr. Hester Quayle on the slipway at Brannock Bay.]

documents.title: Brisk Family Trust Endows Meridian Institute with $2 Million
documents.summary: 1953 news release announcing Walter Brisk's $2 million endowment, restricted to scientific research and instruments.
documents.body:
Brisk Family Trust Endows Meridian Institute with $2 Million

For immediate release. Port Calder, 30 September 1953.

The Meridian Institute today announced the largest single gift in its forty-two year history: an endowment of two million dollars from the newly constituted Brisk Family Trust, established by Mr. Walter Brisk, proprietor of Brisk Canneries of Port Calder.

The deed of gift, signed this morning in the Director's office at 14 Wrenfield Street, provides that the income of the endowment shall be applied to "scientific research and the acquisition of scientific instruments" and to no other purpose. Mr. Brisk, who has been a member of the Institute since 1921, said that he wished the money to "keep the telescopes turning and the nets in the water long after the galleries have been repainted a dozen times."

Dr. Rupert Sallow, Director of the Institute since 1951, thanked Mr. Brisk on behalf of the Board of Governors. "This gift secures the scientific heart of the Institute," Dr. Sallow said. "Our research departments have depended for too long on the generosity of a handful of individuals and on whatever could be spared from admissions. The Brisk endowment gives our scientists a foundation they can plan upon."

What the endowment will support

Under the terms agreed with the Trust, the Institute expects to direct the first years of income toward:

  • new recording tide gauges and current instruments for the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory at Brannock Bay;
  • a spectroscope and photographic equipment for the observatory at Harrow Point;
  • two junior research posts in the Department of Celestial Navigation;
  • a fund for field work, including a proposed return survey of the seabird colonies of the Isle of Graye.

The Trust will be administered by a board of three trustees, chaired by Mr. Brisk himself. The trustees will receive an annual accounting from the Institute's treasurer showing how the income has been spent.

A family of fishermen

Mr. Brisk, now 66, began work at the age of twelve gutting herring on the Port Calder quays. He founded Brisk Canneries in 1911 — the same year the Institute opened its doors — and today employs more than four hundred people in the city. He is a familiar figure at Institute lectures and is known to have supported the Institute's natural history purchases privately for many years.

"My father could not read a chart," Mr. Brisk told reporters. "I learned to read one at the Institute's Saturday classes when I was a boy. Whatever I can give back, I will."

ItemDetail
DonorWalter Brisk, Brisk Canneries
VehicleBrisk Family Trust
Principal$2,000,000
Permitted use of incomeScientific research; acquisition of scientific instruments
Signed30 September 1953

The Board of Governors will hold a reception for members of the Friends of the Meridian on 15 October in the central hall, beneath the whale skeleton brought back from the Isle of Graye in 1936.

Enquiries: Office of the Secretary, The Meridian Institute, 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder.

documents.title: Port Calder Gazette: Fire guts Meridian Institute east wing
documents.summary: Newspaper report two days after the 1962 fire, estimating that more than 3,000 objects were lost.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER GAZETTE
Friday, 16 March 1962

FIRE GUTS MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
"More than 3,000 objects" feared lost as east wing destroyed

By our Staff Reporter

The east wing of the Meridian Institute on Wrenfield Street lay in blackened ruins yesterday after a fire that burned through the night of Wednesday and into the early hours of Thursday morning, in what officials are already calling the worst blow suffered by the city's museum in its fifty-one years.

Institute staff, speaking as salvage work began, said that more than 3,000 objects are feared lost, among them large parts of the bird and shell collections, many of the dried plant specimens gathered by the Institute's first director, and nearly all of its store of historic photographs. "We will not know the full extent for months," said one senior curator, who asked not to be named. "Whole rooms are simply gone."

The alarm was raised shortly before midnight by the Institute's night watchman, Mr. Harold Pike, of Tanner's Row, who saw smoke in the east corridor and telephoned the fire brigade. Eight fire appliances attended. Chief Officer Dennis Marlowe of the Port Calder Fire Department said his men had fought "to hold the line at the central hall" and that their efforts had saved the main building and the west wing.

"The east wing was well alight when we arrived," Chief Officer Marlowe told the Gazette. "Our first job was to stop it reaching the roof of the central hall. If it had got into those timbers, we would have lost the lot." He said the cause of the fire was under investigation and declined to speculate, but confirmed that it had begun on the ground floor, near a darkroom.

Two firemen were taken to the Harbour Infirmary. One, struck by falling plaster, was released last night; the other is being treated for burns to his hands and is said to be comfortable. Mr. Pike was also treated for the effects of smoke.

The Gazette understands that Mr. Pike re-entered the building before the brigade arrived. Witnesses in Wrenfield Street said they saw him emerge from the west door carrying a bundle wrapped in his coat, which he handed to a constable. The Institute declined to comment.

The Director of the Institute, Dr. Rupert Sallow, who was called from his home in Crescent Hill at around midnight, spent the night at the scene. "This is a terrible loss for Port Calder," Dr. Sallow said. "But the building still stands, the great whale still hangs in the hall, and the library is safe. We will rebuild." He thanked the fire brigade and said the Institute would be closed to the public "for some weeks at least".

Among the objects reported damaged is the brass orrery which has stood in the central hall since before the First World War, and which was close to the burning wing. A number of charts and atlases in the west wing are said to have been soaked by water.

The Institute was founded in 1911 by the late shipowner Augustin Pell. Its east wing, added before the First World War, housed its natural history stores and workrooms.

Councillors last night called for an emergency meeting. Mayor Conrad Bellweather, who visited the scene yesterday morning, said: "The Meridian belongs to this city. The city will not let it fall." He said he would discuss "practical help" with the Institute's trustees next week.

Wrenfield Street remains closed between Anchor Lane and the Chapel steps. Motorists are advised to use Harbour Road.

PICTURE: Firemen damp down the ruins of the east wing yesterday morning. (Gazette photograph)

documents.title: Mayor launches Rebuild Meridian appeal
documents.summary: April 1962 news release announcing the public Rebuild Meridian appeal, the Friends' pledge and temporary storage at Vellmoor.
documents.body:
Mayor Launches "Rebuild Meridian" Appeal

News release issued by the Meridian Institute and the Office of the Mayor of Port Calder, 20 April 1962

The Mayor of Port Calder, Conrad Bellweather, today launched a public appeal to rebuild the Meridian Institute following the fire of 14 March, which destroyed the east wing of the Institute's building on Wrenfield Street.

Speaking on the steps of the Institute, the Mayor said: "For fifty years this building has belonged to the people of Port Calder - to every schoolchild who has stood beneath the great whale, every sailor who has come to look at the old charts, every family that has spent a wet Sunday afternoon in its galleries. Now it needs them. I am asking every household in this city to give what it can."

How the appeal will work

The appeal, to be known as Rebuild Meridian, will be administered by a committee chaired by the Mayor and including trustees of the Institute, representatives of the City Council and of the Port Calder Chamber of Commerce. Contributions may be made:

  • at any branch bank in Port Calder, to the "Rebuild Meridian" account;
  • in collecting tins at the Town Hall, the Harbour Office, the railway station and participating shops;
  • through schools and churches, many of which have already offered to hold collections;
  • by post to the appeal office at the Town Hall.

The committee has not yet set a final target, which will depend on the architects' assessment of the site, but the Mayor said the sum required would be "substantial - more than this city has ever raised for a single cause".

The Friends pledge their support

Friends of the Meridian, the Institute's membership society, has pledged to raise $185,000 towards the appeal through a programme of lectures, concerts, a summer fair and a door-to-door collection. A spokesman for the society said that members had begun organising "within a day of the fire".

The collections are safe

The Director of the Institute, Dr. Rupert Sallow, confirmed that the surviving collections are being moved to secure temporary storage at the Vellmoor Depository, in Vellmoor, where they will remain until new accommodation is ready. The first consignments left Wrenfield Street this week. "Everything that survived the fire will be looked after," Dr. Sallow said. "Nothing will be sold, and nothing will leave the care of the Institute."

The central hall and west wing will be closed while repairs and rewiring are carried out. The Institute hopes to reopen part of the central hall to the public before the end of the year.

What was lost

AreaStatus
East wing (natural history stores, herbarium, photographic archive, east gallery)Destroyed
Central hallSmoke and water damage; to be repaired
West wing (library, Map Room, offices)Smoke and water damage; to be repaired

Early estimates suggest that several thousand objects have been lost or damaged. A full assessment will take some time.

For further information contact the Appeal Office, Town Hall, Port Calder.

documents.title: New east wing opens: the Rautio Wing
documents.summary: October 1968 announcement of the opening of the Rautio Wing on the site of the fire-destroyed east wing, with Big Graye in its atrium.
documents.body:
The Meridian Institute Opens the Rautio Wing

Press release, 5 October 1968

Six and a half years after fire destroyed the east wing of its building on Wrenfield Street, the Meridian Institute today opened the Rautio Wing, a new east wing built on the same site and designed by the architect Selma Rautio.

The opening was performed by the Director, Dr. Margit Oster-Lind, in the presence of former Mayor Conrad Bellweather, who launched the Rebuild Meridian appeal in 1962, members of the Board of Trustees, and several hundred members of the public who had contributed to the appeal.

"This building was paid for by the people of Port Calder," Dr. Oster-Lind said. "It is theirs. We have built it so that it can never again burn as the old wing burned, and we have built it so that it is open, light and welcoming. From next Sunday, admission to the whole Institute on Sundays will be free."

The building

The new east wing is a four-storey structure of reinforced concrete and glass. Its principal features are:

  • a full-height, top-lit atrium, in which the fin whale skeleton known to generations of visitors as Big Graye has been re-hung, having been moved from the central hall;
  • two floors of galleries opening off the atrium, for natural history and for changing exhibitions;
  • sealed, air-conditioned collection stores on the lower ground floor, separated into fire compartments;
  • a complete automatic sprinkler system and fire detection linked to the Port Calder Fire Department;
  • new workrooms for the Conservation Studio, established in 1963;
  • a lecture theatre seating 220.

Mrs. Rautio, speaking at the ceremony, said the design had begun "with the whale". "Everyone I spoke to in Port Calder told me about the whale. So the building is a room for the whale, and everything else is arranged around it."

The return of the collections

Since the spring of 1962, the surviving collections have been kept in temporary storage outside the city. Their return has begun and will continue through the winter. The natural history galleries will open in stages between now and the spring of 1969.

Facts and figures

ItemDetail
ArchitectSelma Rautio
Construction beganSeptember 1965
Opened5 October 1968
Floor area6,400 square metres
Funded byRebuild Meridian public appeal, City of Port Calder, insurance settlement

The new east wing will be open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday to Saturday, and from 12 noon to 5 p.m. on Sundays.

documents.title: Stars Over Calder (1972 exhibition)
documents.summary: Exhibition page for Stars Over Calder (May-November 1972), curated by Dr. Miriam Castell around the restored Threlkeld Atlas.
documents.body:
Stars Over Calder

An exhibition of star maps, charts and instruments from the collections of The Meridian Institute.

Main Hall, Wrenfield Street — 6 May to 26 November 1972

Catalogue no. EXH-1972-04

About the exhibition

For sixty years the people of Port Calder have looked to the Institute on Wrenfield Street to explain the sky above the harbour. Stars Over Calder brings together, for the first time since the fire of 1962, the finest treasures of the Institute's astronomical and cartographic collections, many of them rescued, dried and painstakingly restored over the past ten years.

The exhibition is curated by Dr. Miriam Castell, Curator of Maps and Charts, with the assistance of the staff of the Department of Astronomy and Navigation and the Conservation Studio.

Highlights

  • The Threlkeld Atlas — the sixty-four hand-drawn plates of the southern skies, shown to the public for the first time since their restoration after the fire. Twelve plates will be displayed at a time, changed monthly.
  • The Calder Orrery — the eighteenth-century brass model of the solar system, newly restored and working again.
  • Charts of the Calder coast — manuscript and printed charts from 1790 to 1930, including the 1851 survey of Kittering Sound.
  • Instruments of the navigator — sextants, octants and chronometers used by the masters of Port Calder's merchant fleet.
  • The Harrow Point plates — a selection of photographs of the southern Milky Way taken at the Institute's observatory.

Opening hours and admission

DayHoursAdmission
Tuesday to Saturday10.00 – 17.0025 cents; children free
Sunday12.00 – 17.00Free (open doors Sunday)
MondayClosed—

Events

  • Curator's talk: "Drawing the Sky" — Dr. Castell, first Thursday of each month, 18.30.
  • Children's star-map workshop — Saturdays in July and August.
  • Lecture: "Navigating by the stars in the age of steam" — 14 September.

The Director, Dr. Margit Oster-Lind, writes in the catalogue foreword: "This exhibition is proof that what was damaged in 1962 was not lost. The Institute's treasures belong to the people of Port Calder, and we are glad to open our doors to them."

The illustrated catalogue (48 pages) is available at the front desk, price $1.50.

documents.title: Gazette clipping: Institute wins logbook case (1981)
documents.summary: Port Calder Gazette report of the June 1981 court ruling that the Corvina Logbook belongs to the Institute.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER GAZETTE — Friday, 12 June 1981 — Page 3

INSTITUTE KEEPS CAPTAIN'S LOG
Judge rules against Pell heiress after three-year battle

By Graham Tully, Staff Reporter

The Meridian Institute will keep the ninety-year-old logbook of Captain Josiah Harrow, a judge ruled yesterday, bringing to an end one of the most bitter legal disputes in the city's recent history, the case of Pell-Windham v. The Meridian Institute.

Judge Marcus Ashdown, sitting in the Port Calder District Court, rejected the claim of Mrs. Clarissa Pell-Windham, granddaughter of the Institute's founder Augustin Pell, that the four-volume log of the steamer Corvina was the property of the old Pell and Harrow shipping line and should have passed to her family when the company closed in 1974.

"These volumes are not a company record," the judge said. "They are a private journal, written by a man who loved the sea and wished to remember it. They were his to keep, his widow's to inherit, and hers to give."

Mrs. Pell-Windham, who was not in court yesterday, said through her solicitor, Mr. Ambrose Lisle, that she was "disappointed but not surprised" and would consider her position. Friends of the family said an appeal was unlikely.

Outside the court, the Institute's director, Dr. Margit Oster-Lind, said she was "relieved and grateful", and paid tribute to the Institute's counsel, Miss Harriet Dunne, who took the case without charge.

"The logbook has been in this city's museum for nearly seventy years," Dr. Oster-Lind said. "It survived the fire. It would have been a strange thing to lose it to a lawyer's argument. I hope now that the Pell family and the Institute can remember how much they have in common."

The log, kept between 1889 and 1894, is best known for Captain Harrow's description of the remote Isle of Graye, which inspired the Institute's expeditions there in the 1930s. It was given to the Institute by Captain Harrow's widow in 1912.

The case, which began in 1978, is believed to have cost the Institute more than $60,000 in expenses, despite Miss Dunne's free representation. Several members of the Institute's board had privately urged a settlement, the Gazette understands, but Dr. Oster-Lind insisted that the question of ownership be decided in court.

The judge declined to award full costs to the Institute, saying the claim had been "honestly brought, if mistaken". The logbook will go back on public view in the autumn.

documents.title: The Drowned Coast (exhibition, 1988)
documents.summary: Exhibition page for The Drowned Coast, Tobias Wren's 1988 exhibition on the sea-level history of the Calder coastline.
documents.body:
The Drowned Coast

An exhibition of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory
21 May – 30 October 1988
Rautio Wing, Ground Floor, The Meridian Institute, Wrenfield Street

Twelve thousand years ago you could have walked from the site of Port Calder to the Isle of Graye. The land you would have crossed now lies under forty to ninety metres of sea. The Drowned Coast tells how the rising ocean shaped the coastline we know today, and how scientists at the Institute's laboratory at Brannock Bay have pieced that story together.

About the exhibition

The exhibition has been curated by Dr. Tobias Wren, director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, with members of the laboratory's staff. It brings together sediment cores, fossil tree stumps dredged from the seabed off Brannock Bay, flint tools recovered by trawlers, and instruments used by the laboratory since its foundation in 1947.

Sections

  • The last ice. The Calder plain at the height of the last glaciation.
  • The flood. How and how fast the sea rose, told through radiocarbon-dated peat from the seabed.
  • Lost forests. Submerged oak and pine stumps from the drowned forest of the Brannock shelf.
  • People on the plain. Stone tools and animal bones brought up in fishing nets.
  • Measuring the sea. Tide gauges and current meters from the laboratory, including the bronze meter designed by the laboratory's founder in 1949.
  • The coast tomorrow. What continuing sea-level rise may mean for the Calder Estuary.

Opening hours

DayHoursAdmission
Tuesday–Saturday10:00–17:00Included with general admission
Sunday12:00–17:00Free
MondayClosed—

From the director

“This exhibition is the product of forty years of patient measurement at Brannock Bay,” said Dr. Felix Amberly, who became director of the Institute last year. “It shows what research and the public galleries can do together.”

A fully illustrated catalogue by Tobias Wren is available from the Institute shop, price 6 dollars.
