Interviewer: Dana Whitcombe
Date: 11 August 1998
Place: Interviewee's home, Tanner's Row, Port Calder
Duration: 1 hour 52 minutes
Transcribed by: project volunteers; checked by the interviewer

[Tape 1, side A]

WHITCOMBE: This is Dana Whitcombe for the Meridian Oral History Project, and it's the eleventh of August, 1998. I'm here with Mr. Harold Pike. Mr. Pike, thank you for having me.

PIKE: Harold, please. Nobody's called me Mr. Pike since I retired. Well, the doctor does.

WHITCOMBE: Harold. Could we start right at the beginning? Where were you born?

PIKE: Here. Not this house - my mother's house, two streets over, on Cooper's Lane. It's a car park now. Nineteen twenty-one. My father was a lighterman on the river, took barges up and down the estuary, and his father before him. So it was always the water with us. I was the eldest of five.

WHITCOMBE: What do you remember of the city when you were a boy?

PIKE: Smell of fish. Honestly that's the first thing. The canneries were going full tilt then - Brisk's was the big one, down at the end of the quay, and when the wind was wrong you'd get it all over the town. And horses. There were still horses pulling carts on the quay when I was small. And the ships. You'd go down on a Saturday and there'd be ten or twelve of them tied up along Lantern Quay, and the big ones out in the roads waiting for a berth.

WHITCOMBE: Did you go to the Institute as a child?

PIKE: Oh, everybody did. School took us. I remember the first time, I must have been eight or nine, and they took us into the big hall and there was the whale up there, and a lady - one of the teachers, not a museum lady - she said "that's a real whale, that is, boys, that swam in the sea", and one of the lads fainted. Clean away. I don't think it was the whale, I think it was he hadn't had any breakfast. But that's what we all said after: Billy Coombs fainted at the whale.

WHITCOMBE: [laughs] And after school?

PIKE: I left at fourteen, like you did then. Went to work for the Pell-Harrow Line, on the quay. Office boy first, running messages between the counting house and the ships, and then in the warehouses. Checking cargo in and out. They were still a big firm then, the Pell-Harrow Line - not what they had been, people said, but still big. Old Mr. Edmund Pell used to come down on the quay sometimes, in a grey coat, and everybody stood up straighter.

WHITCOMBE: What was it like to work there?

PIKE: Hard. Cold. Fair enough, though. They looked after their men better than some. You got a Christmas bonus, which a lot of places didn't give. And you learned things. I learned to read a bill of lading before I could hardly read a book. I stayed there till the war.

WHITCOMBE: And in the war?

PIKE: Navy. Stoker, then leading stoker. Minesweepers, mostly. I don't talk about that much, if you don't mind.

WHITCOMBE: Of course.

PIKE: I'll say this. I came back in forty-six and I couldn't settle to the quay again. Too many people I knew who weren't there. I did this and that - I was a lorry driver for a bit, I was on the docks casual. And then in fifty-five I saw the Institute wanted a night watchman. My wife saw it, really. She said, "Harold, you don't sleep anyway, you might as well be paid for it."

[laughter]

WHITCOMBE: So you joined the Institute in 1955.

PIKE: September fifty-five. Dr. Sallow was the director then. He interviewed me himself, which I didn't expect. He asked me if I was afraid of the dark and I said no, and he asked me if I was afraid of skeletons and I said not if they stayed still, and he laughed and gave me the job. He was all right, Dr. Sallow. People have said things about him since, but he was all right to me.

WHITCOMBE: What did the job involve?

PIKE: Rounds. You came on at nine at night and you went off at seven in the morning, and you did your rounds. The whole building, all three wings, every floor. There was a clock - a watchman's clock, it was called - you carried it on a strap and at each station there was a key on a chain in a little box, and you put the key in the clock and turned it and it punched the time on a paper tape inside. So they knew you'd been round. Twelve stations. It took me about twenty-five minutes, a round, and then you'd have ten minutes in the lodge with your tea and do it again.

WHITCOMBE: What was the building like at night?

PIKE: Beautiful. I'll say that. People think it must have been frightening and it was, a bit, the first few weeks. All those cases, and the birds with their glass eyes looking at you. But after that it was beautiful. The central hall with the moon coming in the high windows and the whale hanging there like a ship in the sky. The Map Room with all the old charts. I used to stop in the Map Room, if I'm honest, longer than I should have. There was a big book in a case in there - the star atlas, the Harrow Point Atlas we called it, because it was drawn out at the observatory - and they'd leave it open at a different page every week, and I used to look at the stars on it and then go out on the steps and try to find them. I never found half of them. It's all the southern sky, you see, and a lot of it's too low for us here.

WHITCOMBE: And the east wing?

PIKE: I didn't like the east wing. Never did. It was dark, and it smelled of chemicals - they used all sorts on the birds and the plants, arsenic and naphthalene and whatnot - and it creaked. The floors creaked and the pipes knocked. And there were rooms you weren't supposed to go in, only look in, because of the specimens. The stores. And the darkroom at the end, where the photographer worked, which always had a red light on the door and a smell of vinegar. I used to hurry through the east wing. I'm not ashamed to say it.

WHITCOMBE: Did you ever notice anything that worried you there, before 1962?

PIKE: I've been asked that before. People have asked me that. [pause] The lights used to flicker. In the east corridor, on the ground floor. Not all the time. And the switches were old brass ones and one or two of them got warm. I did mention it. I put it in the book - there was a book in the lodge where you wrote anything that needed seeing to - more than once. A man came and looked at it once, I think. I don't know. It wasn't my place. I was the watchman.

[Tape 1, side B]

WHITCOMBE: Could we talk about the night of the fire now? Take as long as you want.

PIKE: It's all right. I've told it enough times. It was a Wednesday. The fourteenth of March. There'd been a lecture in the hall - some gentleman about rocks - and they'd all gone by ten. I remember the photographer, Mr. Hask, he'd gone early, about six, said goodnight to me at the door. I did my rounds as usual. I did the east wing about five past eleven and there was nothing. Nothing at all. I've thought about that round a thousand times and there was nothing.

WHITCOMBE: And then?

PIKE: Then I did the west wing, and I had my tea, and I started the next round, and I came across the central hall - it would have been twenty to twelve, or near enough, because I'd just looked at the clock in the lodge - and I smelled it. Not wood smoke. Something sharp. Chemical. And I looked down the hall and under the doors to the east corridor there was a light. Orange. Moving.

WHITCOMBE: What did you do?

PIKE: I went and opened the doors. Which you shouldn't do, I know that now, they told me after, but I didn't know then. And the smoke came out at me like - I don't know what like. Like a wall. Yellow. It was the film burning, they said after, the old film. It gives off this yellow smoke and it's poison. I got a mouthful of it and I was on my knees. I shut the doors and I crawled back and then I ran to the lodge and telephoned the brigade. Nine-nine-nine. I remember my hands were shaking so I could hardly dial.

WHITCOMBE: How long before they came?

PIKE: Seven minutes, they said. It felt like an hour. And that's when I did the thing everyone asks about.

WHITCOMBE: Going back in.

PIKE: Going back in. [pause] I'll tell you what I was thinking, because people make it out to be brave and it wasn't brave. I was thinking about the Map Room. I'd been in that Map Room every night for seven years. I thought, the fire'll go right through the building, it'll go through the roof of the hall and down the other side and it'll all go. And I thought about what was in there. The atlas was too big - it's a great thing, you'd need two men. And the charts were in the drawers, dozens of drawers. But there was the old ship's logbook - Captain Harrow's - in the case by the window. Four books, leather, not so big. I knew what that was. I'd worked for his firm, you see. For the Pell-Harrow Line. We used to hear about Captain Harrow on the quay when I was a boy - he was a sort of legend, the old men talked about him. And I thought, I can carry that.

WHITCOMBE: So you went to the west wing.

PIKE: Through the hall and up the west stairs. The smoke was coming into the hall by then but not bad, not at the west end. I went into the Map Room and the case was locked and I didn't have that key - the curators had the case keys, not me - so I broke the glass with my torch. Cut my hand, look, you can still see it. [shows scar] And I took the four books out and I wrapped them in my coat, and I came back down and out the west door into the street. And there was a policeman there by then, a young one, and I gave them to him and I said "don't you let go of these, son, whatever happens", and he didn't. He stood there holding them all night, I heard. And then the engines came.

WHITCOMBE: Did you know at that point whether the west wing would burn?

PIKE: No. Nobody knew. I watched the whole thing from the street, with a blanket round me, and the ambulance men wanting me to go to the hospital and me saying no. I watched the east wing go. The roof went about one o'clock. You could see it from the harbour, they said, the glow. And the firemen - Mr. Marlowe, the chief, he was a big man with a voice like a foghorn - he had them all at the join, where the east wing meets the hall, pouring water on it, all night. And it held. The hall didn't go. The west wing didn't go. I needn't have gone in at all, as it turned out.

WHITCOMBE: But you couldn't have known that.

PIKE: No. That's what Dr. Sallow said. He came about midnight, in his overcoat over his pyjamas, and he stood with me, and when he found out what I'd done he shook my hand, and then he said, "Harold, never do that again," and I said, "I hope I won't have to, sir." [laughs]

WHITCOMBE: What happened in the days after?

PIKE: Oh, it was terrible. The smell. Everything wet and black. They had us all in - staff, volunteers, the Friends, anyone - carrying things out of the west wing and the hall to lorries. Everything that could be moved. They didn't know if the building was safe. I remember the atlas coming out, the Harrow Point Atlas, the star book - it had got wet, water through the ceiling from the hoses. It was all swollen, the pages. One of the curators, Dr. Castell, she was crying over it. Holding it in the back of the lorry and crying. And the brass thing, the orrery, the planets going round - that had got scorched, it was near the east end of the hall. The lacquer had all bubbled up like toffee.

WHITCOMBE: Where did the collections go?

PIKE: Out of town. To a depot inland, at Vellmoor. I drove one of the lorries, as it happens, because I'd done lorry driving. Up and down that road for weeks. And then I was out there for a bit as a watchman, too, the first winter. Cold! Cold as charity. But dry.

[Tape 2, side A]

WHITCOMBE: Let's talk about the people who came afterwards. Did you know Beatrix Nolan?

PIKE: Bea Nolan. Oh yes. She came the year after the fire, sixty-three, to start the conservation - fixing things, you know, properly, not just the curators having a go. Young woman, not much more than thirty-five, very quiet, very particular. Bea Nolan spent four years on that atlas. Four years! Page by page. She had them all laid out on blotting paper under glass weights, and she'd do a bit and then wait and then do a bit more. I used to go in and see her sometimes on my rounds - she worked late - and she'd show me. And when it was finished you'd hardly know. You could see a tide mark on some of the pages if you looked, but she said that should stay, that was part of its story now. And then she did the orrery. Took the whole thing to pieces.

WHITCOMBE: Did you stay on as watchman after the new wing opened?

PIKE: Till eighty-six. Thirty-one years. By then they had alarms and sprinklers and a control room with little lights, and the young fellows used to laugh at my clock. But I kept it. I've still got it. [pause] It's in the drawer there, if you want to see it.

WHITCOMBE: I'd love to. What did you think of the new wing?

PIKE: I liked it. I know some didn't - too modern, too much glass. But Mrs. Rautio came and walked round with me before it opened, because she wanted to know about the rounds, where a watchman would go, what he'd need to see. Nobody had ever asked a watchman anything before. And she put the whale in the middle where everyone could see him. That was right.

WHITCOMBE: You're remembered by a plaque in the entrance hall. How do you feel about that?

PIKE: Embarrassed. [laughs] Mrs. Oster-Lind put that up, the director after Dr. Sallow. I told her not to. She said, "Harold, it's not for you, it's for the children, so they know that ordinary people can do something." Well. I suppose that's all right, then.

WHITCOMBE: Is there anything else you'd like to say, for the record?

PIKE: Only that I was lucky. The brigade saved that building, not me. And everybody in this city put their hand in their pocket to build it back up. Dockers and schoolkids and old ladies. That's the story, really. Not me and a few old books.

WHITCOMBE: Thank you, Harold.

PIKE: Thank you. Would you like another cup of tea before you go?

[End of interview]

Notes by the interviewer: Mr. Pike showed me the watchman's clock after the recording ended. It is a brass Benzing-type clock with a leather strap and a partly used tape still inside. He indicated that he would like it to go to the Institute after his death. The logbook he describes is the Corvina Logbook of Captain Josiah Harrow. "Mr. Hask" is the Institute photographer Lionel Hask (employed 1949-1962). The lodge "book" Mr. Pike refers to has not survived.

documents.title: Oral history interview: Lottie Graves, docent and founder of Friends of the Meridian (1998)
documents.summary: Transcript of the 1998 oral history interview with Lottie Graves covering fifty years as a volunteer, the Friends, and the 1962 fire.
documents.body:
MERIDIAN ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
Interview transcript

Interviewee: Charlotte ("Lottie") Graves (born 1915)
Interviewer: Dana Whitcombe
Date: 2 September 1998
Place: Friends' Room, the Meridian Institute, Wrenfield Street
Duration: 1 hour 40 minutes
Transcribed by: project volunteers

[Tape 1, side A]

WHITCOMBE: It's the second of September 1998, and I'm with Mrs. Lottie Graves in the Friends' Room at the Institute. Lottie, you chose to be interviewed here rather than at home.

GRAVES: Well, I've spent more of my life in this building than in my own house, dear, so it seemed only right. And the chairs are better.

WHITCOMBE: [laughs] Let's start with your early life.

GRAVES: I was born in 1915 in Port Calder, in the Crescent Hill district, which was very respectable then and is very expensive now, which isn't the same thing. My father was a schoolmaster at the Grammar School - he taught Latin and, when they were short, mathematics, badly. My mother had been a nurse. There were three of us girls. I was the middle one and the one who was always getting lost.

WHITCOMBE: Getting lost?

GRAVES: In here, mostly. My father brought us every Saturday. He believed a child should be taken somewhere improving every week, and the Institute was improving and it was free on Saturday mornings for schoolchildren, which suited a schoolmaster's pocket. And I used to wander off. They'd find me in the Map Room looking at the old sea charts, or in the east wing looking at the birds. There was a hummingbird case in the east wing - dozens of them, all colours, like jewels - and I would stand in front of it for an hour. That case went in the fire. I minded that more than almost anything.

WHITCOMBE: Did you meet any of the staff as a child?

GRAVES: Dr. Aldane. The first director. He was a very old man by then - well, he seemed very old to me - with a white beard, and he used to walk through the galleries with his hands behind his back. And once he found me crying because I'd lost my sisters and he took me to his office and gave me a pressed flower from his collection. A sea-lavender, from the marsh up the coast. I kept it for years in my prayer book. I don't know what became of it. He said, "Every flower on the shore has a name, and most of them I gave them." I didn't know then that he meant it literally.

WHITCOMBE: What did you do after school?

GRAVES: I trained as a teacher, like my father, and I taught at the girls' elementary school on Harbour Road until I married in 1940. My husband was in the merchant navy. He was lost in 1943. [pause] I went back to teaching after that, and that's when I started volunteering here. They had very few staff after the war and they needed people to take the school parties round, and I was a teacher and I knew the building, so I simply offered. That was 1946.

WHITCOMBE: So you became a docent.

GRAVES: We didn't call it that then. We were "guide volunteers". Docent was an American word that came in later. Dr. Quayle was the director, the astronomer. She was a remarkable woman, very tall, very shy, not at all good with committees but wonderful with children. She'd come and take the older children up to the roof on a clear evening and show them Saturn through a little telescope she'd brought from home. She told me once that she'd only become director because nobody else wanted it, and that she would much rather be at Harrow Point with her telescope.

WHITCOMBE: Tell me about the founding of the Friends.

GRAVES: Well, that came out of the guides, really. By 1948 or so there were about twenty of us, and we were all doing it for love, and we started meeting for tea after the Saturday parties, and somebody - I think it was me, but I may be flattering myself - said, why don't we make this a proper society, with a subscription, and raise money for the Institute? Because it was very poor, then. Mr. Pell had died and his son was generous but not in the same way, and the government gave nothing. And Dr. Quayle said yes, please, anything. So in 1949 we founded the Friends of the Meridian. I was the first secretary and then chairman for a long time.

WHITCOMBE: What did the Friends do in those first years?

GRAVES: Lectures, mostly. We'd get one of the curators to give a talk on a Thursday evening, and charge a shilling, or whatever it was, and give the money to the Institute. And outings. We took members out to the Ocean Lab at Brannock Bay - the oceanographic laboratory, which Dr. Brandt had just started - and she would take them out in her boat and show them her instruments, and she'd always get somebody wet. It was a great favourite. And we bought things. Our first big purchase, I remember, was a set of display cases for the Graye gallery. We were so proud.

WHITCOMBE: What were the Institute's relations with the Friends like?

GRAVES: Oh, good. Mostly. There was a little friction under Dr. Sallow, because he was a very careful man and I think he felt that a lot of middle-aged ladies raising money for things he hadn't asked for was a nuisance. He liked big donors - he was very good with Mr. Brisk, for instance, the canning man, who gave the endowment. He was less good with small people. But he was always courteous to me.

[Tape 1, side B]

WHITCOMBE: Could we turn to 1962?

GRAVES: Yes. [pause] I was asleep, of course. It was nearly midnight. My telephone rang at about one in the morning - it was one of the other Friends, Mrs. Dorrance, whose husband was a trustee, and she said "Lottie, the Meridian's on fire", and I got dressed and went. Everybody went. By the time I got to Wrenfield Street there were hundreds of people, standing in the rain, and the police holding them back, and the whole sky over the east end of the building was orange. You could feel the heat on your face right across the street.

WHITCOMBE: What do you remember most?

GRAVES: The noise. People think a fire is quiet, like a bonfire. It isn't. It roars. And every so often there'd be a crash inside, as a floor went, and a great fountain of sparks would go up, and the whole crowd would make a sound - a sort of groan. And the firemen shouting. And then, about half past one I suppose, the roof of the east wing fell in, and I remember a woman beside me, a stranger, took hold of my hand. We stood there like that. I never knew her name.

WHITCOMBE: Did you know then about Harold Pike?

GRAVES: Not that night. We heard the next day that the night watchman had gone back in and saved the old logbook. Harold. Such a quiet man. He used to let me in early on Saturdays so I could set up for the school parties, and we'd have a cup of tea in his lodge. When I heard, I wasn't surprised at all. That was Harold.

WHITCOMBE: What happened in the days after?

GRAVES: Chaos. Wonderful, dreadful chaos. The Institute had nobody - no plan, no conservators, nothing. The curators were doing their best but there were hundreds of things wet or scorched and nobody knew what to do with them. So the Friends simply came. We carried things. We washed soot off things we probably shouldn't have washed. We made tea for the firemen and then for the removal men. We sat up with the wet books, turning pages with blotting paper between them - which, as it turned out, was the right thing, more by luck than judgement. And we packed. Everything was going out to the depository at Vellmoor, and it all had to be packed, and there weren't enough crates or enough hands.

WHITCOMBE: Why do you think people came?

GRAVES: Because it was theirs. That's the thing I've tried to explain to directors for fifty years. Before the Great Fire of Wrenfield Street, I think the trustees thought of the Meridian as their Institute - Mr. Pell's Institute, the scientists' Institute. And the people of Port Calder thought of it as theirs too, but nobody had ever asked them. The fire asked them. And they answered.

[Tape 2, side A]

WHITCOMBE: Tell me about the Rebuild Meridian appeal.

GRAVES: That was the Mayor's idea - Mr. Bellweather. He was a grocer, you know, before he went into politics, and he understood that you don't raise a million dollars from ten rich men, you raise it from a hundred thousand ordinary ones. He launched it on the steps in April, in the rain again - it always seemed to be raining in 1962 - and he asked every household to give something. And then he came to see me, and he said, "Mrs. Graves, the Friends know how to raise money in small amounts. Will you help?"

WHITCOMBE: What did you do?

GRAVES: Everything. We pledged, rather rashly, to raise a large sum ourselves, and then we had to find it. We had a fair on the green every summer for three years. We had concerts - the Harbour Male Voice Choir sang for us for nothing, and so did a very famous soprano who had grown up in Port Calder and whose name I'm not going to tell you because she made me promise. We went door to door. We had a stall at the fish market, would you believe - Mr. Brisk's men gave us a barrow. The schoolchildren collected pennies in jam jars. I had a map of the city on the wall of my dining room with pins in it for every street we'd done. By the end, the Friends had raised $185,000. Out of the million and a bit that the whole appeal raised. I'm still proud of that.

WHITCOMBE: That's a remarkable sum for the time.

GRAVES: It was. We had about three hundred members before the fire, and eleven hundred afterwards. That was the other thing the fire did. It made people join.

WHITCOMBE: What do you remember of Dr. Sallow's resignation?

GRAVES: It was sad. I think he was made to carry more than his share. There was a lot of talk about the wiring, and I believe there were decisions made that shouldn't have been, but the board made them with him. Then Dr. Oster-Lind came, and everything changed. She'd been at the Ocean Lab with Dr. Brandt for years and she was a scientist, but she understood the public. She came to a Friends meeting in her first month - no director had ever done that - and she said, "You rebuilt this place. From now on, you have a say in it." And she meant it. Free Sundays, the public lectures, a Friends seat on the exhibitions committee. That was the open doors policy. It started in that room, you know. The old Friends' Room, before the new building.

WHITCOMBE: And the new building itself?

GRAVES: The new east wing - the Rautio Wing, they call it now, after the architect. I didn't like it at first. Concrete! After our lovely old stone. But then they hung Big Graye in the middle of it, in all that light, and I came in the first Sunday it was open, and I stood underneath him and I cried. Because you could see him properly for the first time. In the old hall he was up in the gloom and you only saw his shape. Now you could see every bone. The children loved it. Well, they still do.

WHITCOMBE: What do you remember of the years after the new wing opened - the seventies and eighties?

GRAVES: Oh, they were good years for the Friends. Busy years. Dr. Oster-Lind wanted exhibitions that people would queue for, and she got them. The one I remember best is "Stars Over Calder", in 1972, which Dr. Castell put together - the lady who'd acted as director for that month. It was the first time the old star atlas was shown after it had been mended, and they had it open under glass in a darkened room with little lights, and a sky projected on the ceiling. We had queues round the block on Sundays. I trained forty new guides that year alone, just to cope. People would come out of that room and stand in Wrenfield Street and look up, as if they expected to see the stars in the daytime.

WHITCOMBE: And the guides - how did the training change?

GRAVES: It became proper. Before the fire we just learned things from each other. Afterwards Dr. Oster-Lind had the curators give us courses - twelve evenings, with a little examination at the end, which some of the older ladies found very insulting. [laughs] And Miss Nolan, from the conservation, gave us a talk every year on how to handle objects, and what not to touch, and why you must never, ever lean on a case. She'd show us slides of things that had been damaged by the fire and by the salvage afterwards - some of it by us, I'm sorry to say, in our enthusiasm. She was very kind about it. She said we'd done more good than harm. I'm not sure that was true, but it was kind.

WHITCOMBE: And more recently?

GRAVES: Well, the observatory closing, two years ago, that was a blow for us. The Friends used to run evening trips out to Harrow Point, to look through the big telescope. Hundreds of people went on those trips over the years. And then they said the sky was too bright now, with all the new houses and the motorway lights, and the scientists couldn't use it any more, and they shut it. I wrote to Dr. Amberly and said, the scientists may not be able to use it, but the public still can - a child doesn't care if the sky is a bit orange at the edges, a child just wants to see the moon. He wrote back very nicely and said he'd think about it. I'm still waiting. [laughs] Perhaps you can put that in your recording, dear, and somebody will listen to it one day.

WHITCOMBE: You've been here through, what, six directors?

GRAVES: Let me count. Quayle, Sallow, Oster-Lind, Amberly - he's the one now - and I knew Dr. Aldane, so that's five, and the one we don't mention because he was only acting for a month. [laughs] No, that was Dr. Castell, and she was lovely, she'd have made a very good director. I'm forgetting things.

WHITCOMBE: What would you like people to remember about the Friends?

GRAVES: That we were never just the ladies who make the tea. Although we did make a great deal of tea. We saved this Institute. Not by ourselves - the brigade saved the building, and the Mayor saved the appeal, and Dr. Oster-Lind saved the spirit of the place, if that doesn't sound too grand. But the Friends were the ones who were there. Every day. For fifty years.

WHITCOMBE: Thank you, Lottie.

GRAVES: Thank you, dear. Now, you'll stay for the Friends' tea, won't you? It's the second Wednesday. There's cake.

[End of interview]

Interviewer's note: Mrs. Graves donated her dining-room appeal map (a 1959 city street plan with approximately 900 pins) to the Institute archive at the end of the session. She remains an active volunteer. "Mrs. Dorrance" is Mrs. Agnes Dorrance, trustee 1952-1971, wife of the harbourmaster.

documents.title: Ossery Trench Expedition (1970)
documents.summary: Account of MOL's first deep-water expedition, which dredged the Ossery Trench to 2,900 m aboard the chartered trawler Bellrock in March–April 1970.
documents.body:
# Ossery Trench Expedition (1970)

The **Ossery Trench Expedition** was a six-week deep-water sampling voyage mounted by the **Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory** in March and April 1970. Led by Dr. Tobias Wren, it was the first attempt by any Port Calder institution to sample the floor of the Ossery Trench, a deep-sea trench about 120 km offshore.

*Not to be confused with the 2017 Ossery Trench Survey, a mapping project carried out nearly fifty years later.*

## Background

The Ossery Trench had been known to Port Calder fishermen since the nineteenth century as a place where lines "found no bottom." Soundings in the 1950s established depths below 2,500 metres, but nothing was known of its fauna. Wren, then a senior scientist at the laboratory, argued that the trench was "the one great unexplored habitat within a day's steaming of Port Calder."

The laboratory owned no vessel capable of deep trawling, so Wren chartered the stern trawler *Bellrock* from a Port Calder fishing company, together with her crew of nine.

## The voyage

The expedition sailed from Port Calder on 9 March 1970 with a scientific party of six. Over 41 days it made:

- 23 dredge and trawl hauls, the deepest reaching **2,900 metres**;
- 14 sediment grab samples;
- a line of temperature and salinity stations across the trench axis.

Bad weather cost eleven days, and a trawl warp parted during the deepest haul, losing a net and nearly 1,200 metres of wire. The *Bellrock* returned to port on 19 April 1970.

## Results

The expedition recovered around 3,100 specimens, including sea cucumbers, brittle stars, tube-dwelling worms and glass sponges. Several species were new to science. Wren's paper *Benthic Fauna of the Ossery Trench* (1971) described the collection and argued that the trench supported a distinct deep fauna rather than a sparse extension of the shelf community.

## Legacy

The expedition established deep-water work as a regular part of the laboratory's programme and helped secure Wren's appointment as director in 1972. The specimens remain the core of MOL's deep-water collection. When the trench was mapped in detail in 2017, researchers used the 1970 station positions to revisit several of the original dredge sites.

## Expedition members

- Dr. Tobias Wren (leader)
- Dr. Hanne Liss (sediments)
- Colm Ashby (technician)
- Dr. Reuben Tallis (hydrography)
- Grace Penhallow (research assistant)
- Ivo Marsh (photographer)

documents.title: Meridian Institute and Brisk Trust Reach Settlement
documents.summary: 2011 release announcing the settlement of the Brisk Trust's lawsuit, restoration of $3.4 million and new Brisk Research Fellowships.
documents.body:
Meridian Institute and Brisk Trust Reach Settlement

Joint statement, Port Calder, 29 March 2011

The Meridian Institute and the Brisk Trust today announced that they have settled Brisk Trust v. The Meridian Institute, the legal action brought by the Trust in 2009 concerning the use of income from the Brisk endowment. The settlement was approved by the Port Calder District Court on 25 March 2011.

Under the settlement:

  • the Institute will restore $3.4 million to the Brisk endowment account in five annual instalments, the last to be paid in 2016;
  • the Institute will establish the Brisk Research Fellowships, two-year posts for early-career scientists working in astronomy, oceanography or natural history, funded from endowment income;
  • a joint committee of the Trust and the Institute will review each year's use of Brisk income before the Institute's accounts are published;
  • neither party admits liability, and each will bear its own legal costs.

The action arose from the Institute's decision to apply Brisk endowment income toward the renovation of its public galleries in 2007 and 2008. The Trust argued that the 1953 deed of gift restricted that income to scientific research and scientific instruments.

Statements

Maud Brisk, chair of the Brisk Trust, said: "My father gave this money so that the Institute would always have scientists. We never wanted a quarrel with the Meridian; we wanted his wishes kept. Today they are, and the fellowships will carry his name forward in exactly the way he would have liked."

Dr. Nadia Corrow, Director of the Institute, said: "We made a mistake in how we read the deed, and we have put it right. The galleries needed the work, but we should have found the money elsewhere. I am glad this ends with something positive: new researchers at the Institute, in our centenary year."

Evelyn Marchbank, chair of the Board of Governors, said the Board had already adopted new controls on restricted funds, including a separate restricted-funds register and an annual external review.

Background

DateEvent
1953Walter Brisk endows the Institute with $2 million
2007–2008Public gallery renovation
2009Trust files suit in Port Calder District Court
March 2011Settlement approved

The first two Brisk Research Fellows are expected to be appointed in the autumn.

documents.title: The Meridian Institute Celebrates Its Centenary
documents.summary: News release on the 3 May 2011 centenary celebrations, including the launch of Nell Farris's history of the Institute.
documents.body:
One Hundred Years on Wrenfield Street: The Meridian Institute Celebrates Its Centenary

Port Calder, 3 May 2011

A hundred years to the day after Augustin Pell signed the charter founding what was then called the Pell Institute, the Meridian Institute today opened its doors free of charge to celebrate its centenary. More than eleven thousand visitors passed through the Wrenfield Street building between ten in the morning and ten at night, the busiest single day in the Institute's history.

The celebrations opened with the ringing of the ship's bell of the SS Corvina, lent for the day from the maritime gallery, and a short address by the Director, Dr. Nadia Corrow. "A hundred years ago this building was a shipowner's idea of what a curious city deserved," she said. "It has burned, it has been rebuilt, it has argued with itself about whether it is a laboratory or a museum, and it is still here, because Port Calder keeps coming through the door."

Centenary programme

  • Launch of Meridian at One Hundred, a history of the Institute by Port Calder Gazette journalist Nell Farris, with a reading in the lecture theatre.
  • Behind-the-scenes tours of the Conservation and Collections Care Division laboratories.
  • Open night at the Harrow Point Public Observatory, with shuttle buses from Wrenfield Street.
  • Family activities in the Rautio Wing atrium beneath Big Graye.
  • A centenary lecture by the Director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory on "Sixty-four years at Brannock Bay."

Evelyn Marchbank, chair of the Board of Governors, announced that the Board would publish a new strategic framework in the autumn and thanked the Friends of the Meridian, "who have carried this Institute through its hardest years."

A book for the centenary

Nell Farris's Meridian at One Hundred draws on the Institute archive, the Pell Papers and dozens of interviews with former staff. Farris, who has covered the Institute for the Gazette for more than twenty years, said she had tried to write "the history of an argument as much as the history of a building." Copies are available in the Institute shop.

Centenary facts
Founded3 May 1911
Directors to date6
Centenary-day visitors11,240

The Mayor of Port Calder, Alma Petrosyan, presented the Institute with a framed copy of the 1911 council resolution granting the Wrenfield Street site.

documents.title: First Graye Island Expedition (1934)
documents.summary: The 1934 expedition to the Isle of Graye, led by Captain Elias Venn aboard SS Kittiwake and funded by Edmund Pell.
documents.body:
# First Graye Island Expedition (1934)

The **First Graye Island Expedition** was a survey and collecting voyage to the Isle of Graye, a remote reef and island group south-west of Port Calder, undertaken by The Meridian Institute between June and September 1934. It was the Institute's first organised expedition.

## Background

The existence of the reef had been known in Port Calder since Captain Josiah Harrow recorded a landing there in his logbook in 1891, but it had never been properly charted. In 1933 **Captain Elias Venn**, a senior master with the Pell & Harrow Shipping Company, proposed a voyage to fix the reef's position and investigate its seabird colonies.

## Organisation

- **Leader:** Captain Elias Venn
- **Vessel:** SS *Kittiwake*, a Pell & Harrow coastal steamer of 640 tons, lent by the company
- **Funding:** Edmund Pell, chairman of Pell & Harrow, who met the costs of the charter, coal and crew
- **Members:** 11, including the leader, two Institute naturalists, a surveyor, a photographer and ship's officers seconded to the survey
- **Dates:** departed Port Calder 12 June 1934; returned 19 September 1934

## Results

The expedition fixed the position of the reef and produced the first reliable chart of its lagoon and passages. It collected 412 bird skins and eggs, a series of plant specimens, and several hundred photographs. Venn's narrative report, *Report of the Graye Island Expedition, 1934*, was published by the Institute in 1935.

## Assessment

The 1934 voyage has been criticised, then and since, for its narrow scientific programme; it was essentially a navigational survey with naturalists aboard. The Institute's Curator of Natural History, Percival Dunmore, argued that a second expedition was needed, leading to the larger 1936 voyage. The two expeditions are frequently confused. Key differences:

| | 1934 | 1936 |
|---|---|---|
| Leader | Elias Venn | Percival Dunmore |
| Vessel | SS Kittiwake | SS Merrow |
| Members | 11 | 17 |
| Headline result | Chart of the reef; bird collection | Fin whale skeleton |

## See also

- Isle of Graye
- Second Graye Island Expedition (1936)
- Pell & Harrow Shipping Company

documents.title: Second Graye Island Expedition (1936)
documents.summary: The 1936 expedition to the Isle of Graye, led by Dr. Percival Dunmore aboard SS Merrow, which recovered the whale skeleton Big Graye.
documents.body:
# Second Graye Island Expedition (1936)

The **Second Graye Island Expedition** was a scientific voyage to the Isle of Graye undertaken by The Meridian Institute from May to August 1936. It followed the smaller first expedition of 1934 and is remembered above all for recovering the fin whale skeleton now known as **Big Graye**.

## Origins

After the 1934 voyage, the Institute's Curator of Natural History, **Dr. Percival Dunmore**, argued that the reef had been charted but not studied. His proposal for a longer voyage with a full scientific party was approved by Director Hester Quayle in 1935.

## Organisation

- **Leader:** Dr. Percival Dunmore
- **Vessel:** SS *Merrow*, a Pell & Harrow steamer chartered for the season
- **Members:** 17 (Institute scientists, preparators, a surveyor, a doctor and a cinematographer, plus the ship's company)
- **Dates:** sailed 4 May 1936; returned 27 August 1936
- **Base:** a tented camp on the largest islet for ten weeks

## Work

The expedition carried out a botanical survey of the islets, a census of the seabird colonies, dredging in the lagoon, and tide observations. In July 1936 the party found a dead fin whale stranded on the outer reef flats. Dunmore halted other work for nine days while the carcass was flensed and the bones packed for shipment.

## Results

- The fin whale skeleton, accessioned in 1937 and displayed from 1939 as Big Graye
- About 3,000 invertebrate specimens from the lagoon
- A herbarium series of 280 sheets
- A 40-minute film of the camp and the whale recovery

Dunmore's *Second Graye Island Expedition: Final Report* was published in 1937.

## Comparison with the 1934 expedition

The first expedition (1934) was led by Captain Elias Venn aboard SS Kittiwake with eleven members, and its main output was a chart and a bird collection. The second was longer, larger, and led by a scientist rather than a mariner.

## Legacy

The whale made the 1936 expedition the best-known event in the Institute's pre-war history. The Graye gallery, opened in 1939 around the skeleton, remained one of the most visited parts of the Wrenfield Building until 1962.

## See also

- First Graye Island Expedition (1934)
- Big Graye
- Isle of Graye

documents.title: Exhibition: Fire and Recovery (2012)
documents.summary: Exhibition page for 'Fire and Recovery', marking the 50th anniversary of the Wrenfield Fire, curated by archivist Tamsin Rourke.
documents.body:
Fire and Recovery: The Wrenfield Fire at Fifty

14 March - 30 September 2012

Changing Exhibitions Gallery, Rautio Wing, first floor

Admission included with general entry

On the night of 14 March 1962, fire destroyed the east wing of the Meridian Institute. Fifty years later, Fire and Recovery tells the story of that night and of the years of rebuilding that followed - through the objects that were lost, the objects that were saved, and the voices of the people who were there.

About the exhibition

The exhibition is curated by the Institute Archivist, Tamsin Rourke, and draws extensively on her 2010 book Voices from the Fire. Throughout the galleries, visitors can listen to recorded recollections of the Wrenfield Fire from staff, volunteers and members of the public who witnessed it or took part in the salvage and the rebuilding appeal.

"The fire is usually told as a story of loss," says Rourke. "We wanted to tell it as a story about people - the watchman who went back into the building, the volunteers who dried books with blotting paper, the schoolchildren who collected pennies in jam jars. The recovery was as remarkable as the fire."

In the exhibition

  • The night: the fire department's investigation, press photographs, and the watchman's clock carried on his rounds that night.
  • What was lost: fragments recovered from the ruins of the east wing, including charred herbarium sheets and melted glass from the photographic archive.
  • What was saved: the ship's logbook carried out of the burning building, shown with its broken display-case lock.
  • Restoration: plates from the water-damaged star atlas and the story of their four-year restoration, shown with conservation notes and tools.
  • Rebuild Meridian: collecting tins, posters, the Friends' appeal map with its hundreds of pins, and a roll of donors.
  • A new wing: architect's drawings and models for the Rautio Wing, opened in 1968.

Key dates

DateEvent
14 March 1962Fire destroys the east wing
April 1962Rebuild Meridian appeal launched
1963Conservation Studio founded
1965Final loss assessment: 2,318 objects destroyed or damaged
October 1968Rautio Wing opens

Events

  • 14 March, 7 p.m.: Anniversary evening, with readings from Voices from the Fire.
  • Monthly: Curator's tour with Tamsin Rourke.
  • June: Conservation open days - see behind the scenes in the Conservation and Collections Care Division.

The exhibition is supported by Friends of the Meridian and the Port Calder Fire Department Benevolent Fund.

documents.title: The Wrenfield Fire of 1962
documents.summary: Full history of the March 1962 fire that destroyed the east wing of the Meridian Institute, its causes, losses and long aftermath.
documents.body:
# The Wrenfield Fire of 1962

*Compiled by the Institute Archive for the fiftieth anniversary, 14 March 2012.*

The Wrenfield Fire is the single most consequential event in the history of the Meridian Institute. It destroyed the east wing of the original building at 14 Wrenfield Street, cost the Institute a substantial part of its natural history holdings and its photographic archive, ended the directorship of Dr. Rupert Sallow, and set in motion a chain of changes - a professional conservation service, a new wing, a new public-facing philosophy - that still shape the Institute today. This article draws together the surviving documentary record: the fire brigade's investigation, the board minutes of 1962 to 1968, the final loss assessment of 1965, contemporary newspaper coverage, and the recollections gathered by later oral-history work.

## The building before the fire

When Augustin Pell's institution opened in 1911, it occupied a single three-storey stone building on Wrenfield Street, a short walk uphill from the docks. The building was extended almost immediately. Between 1912 and 1914 a long east wing was added to house the growing natural history collections, and a matching but smaller west wing followed in 1921 for the library, the offices and what became the Map Room. By the 1950s the plan of the building had settled into a pattern that older staff described as "the three houses": the west wing for books, charts and administration; the central hall for the great display spaces; and the east wing for the working collections.

The east wing was, by general agreement, the least loved part of the building. Its ground floor held the specimen stores for birds, shells and marine invertebrates, the sheet cabinets of the Aldane Herbarium, a packing room, and the photographic darkroom used by the Institute's photographer. The first floor held the east gallery, where natural history displays were rotated, and the second floor held staff workrooms and overflow storage. Wiring in the wing dated in large part from the 1914 fit-out, with additions made piecemeal in the 1920s and 1930s as electric lighting, heaters and darkroom equipment were introduced. The photographic archive - some 11,000 glass and film negatives documenting expeditions, specimens and Institute events since 1911 - was kept in a store room beside the darkroom. A significant part of that archive consisted of cellulose nitrate film, a material now known to be highly flammable.

None of this was unusual for an institution of the Meridian's age and size. Museums across the country were working in buildings fitted out before the First World War, and few had the money to rewire them. The Institute in 1962 was, by the standards of the day, busy and reasonably prosperous. Visitor numbers had risen through the 1950s; the Graye gallery in the central hall had been refitted; Big Graye, the fin whale skeleton brought back by the second Graye Island expedition, still dominated the central hall; and Dr. Hester Quayle's *A History of the Meridian Institute*, published only five months before the fire, had presented the Institute as a settled and confident body with half a century behind it.

## The evening of 14 March

Wednesday 14 March 1962 was, by every account, unremarkable. The Institute closed to the public at five o'clock. A lecture by a visiting geologist in the central hall ended at about half past eight, and the last members of staff left the building shortly before ten. The photographer, who had spent the afternoon printing plates for a forthcoming catalogue, later told investigators that he had switched off the enlarger and the darkroom lights when he left at about six, but that he could not remember whether he had unplugged the small electric heater used to keep the developing trays at temperature. The heater was not, in the end, found to be the cause.

The only person in the building overnight was the night watchman, Harold Pike, then aged forty. Pike had joined the Institute in 1955 after several years working on the docks. His rounds took him through all three wings on a fixed schedule, logging each circuit on a clock key. His log for the night shows a completed round of the east wing at 23:05, with nothing noted.

## The alarm and the response

At approximately 23:40 Pike, crossing the central hall on his next round, smelled smoke and saw light under the doors to the east wing corridor. He opened the corridor doors, found the ground floor filled with smoke, and ran to the porter's lodge to telephone the Port Calder Fire Department. The call was logged at 23:44. Pike then returned to the building, a decision for which he was later both praised and gently rebuked, and went to the west wing.

The first appliance arrived from the Harbour Road station at 23:51. By then fire had broken through the ground-floor windows of the east wing and was climbing into the east gallery. Chief Officer Dennis Marlowe, who took command on arrival of the second appliance, judged the east wing already lost and concentrated his crews on preventing the fire from crossing into the central hall, whose roof timbers would have carried it into the rest of the building. A water curtain was maintained along the junction of the east wing and the central hall for most of the night. Eight appliances attended in total, drawing on hydrants in Wrenfield Street and, later, pumping directly from the harbour.

The fire was declared under control at 04:20 on 15 March. No one was killed. Two firefighters were injured - one by a falling ceiling in the east gallery, the other with burns to the hands - and both recovered. Harold Pike was treated for smoke inhalation.

## Pike and the logbook

What Pike did when he went back into the building became, over the following decades, one of the Institute's founding stories. He went to the Map Room in the west wing, where the Corvina Logbook - the four-volume ship's log kept by Captain Josiah Harrow in the 1880s and 1890s, then one of the most valued items in the collection - lay in a display case. He broke the case with his torch, wrapped the volumes in his coat, and carried them out into Wrenfield Street, where he handed them to a police constable. The west wing, in the event, did not burn, but it was badly affected by smoke and by water from the hoses, and there was no way of knowing at the time that it would survive. Pike's action is commemorated by a small plaque in the entrance hall.

## Cause

The Port Calder Fire Department's investigation, reported to the Institute in April 1962, concluded that the fire began in the photographic darkroom on the ground floor of the east wing and was caused by faulty electrical wiring. Insulation on an old circuit running behind the darkroom's workbench had deteriorated, and a fault in that circuit ignited timber panelling and stored materials. The fire spread with exceptional speed because the adjoining store room contained nitrate film negatives, which burned fiercely and produced dense, toxic smoke. The report found no evidence of arson and exonerated the photographer's heater.

## Losses

The first public estimates of loss were high. The *Port Calder Gazette*, reporting two days after the fire, said that more than 3,000 objects had been lost; the figure was repeated in several national newspapers and in the early publicity of the rebuilding appeal. It proved to be an overestimate, reflecting the confusion of the first days and the fact that entire store rooms were inaccessible while the ruins cooled.

The Institute's final loss assessment, completed in June 1965 after three years of salvage, cataloguing and comparison with the pre-fire registers, recorded **2,318 objects destroyed or damaged, of which 1,406 were destroyed outright**. The distribution of loss followed the plan of the building closely:

- **Natural history stores (east wing ground floor):** the heaviest losses, including most of the bird skins and a large part of the shell collection.
- **The Aldane Herbarium:** roughly 40 per cent of its sheets were lost. The herbarium's founder's own type specimens had fortunately been separated into a steel cabinet in the late 1950s, and most of them survived.
- **The photographic archive:** almost entirely destroyed. The loss of the pre-1940 expedition negatives is still felt by researchers.
- **The east gallery:** all objects on display were lost or damaged beyond repair.

Several of the Institute's most important objects survived but were damaged. The Threlkeld Star Atlas, the hand-drawn atlas of the southern skies kept in the Map Room, was soaked by water that came through the ceiling from the hoses; its plates cockled and several suffered ink bleeding. The Calder Orrery, the eighteenth-century brass orrery which then stood at the east end of the central hall, close to the junction with the burning wing, was heat-damaged: its lacquer blistered, several of its ivory planet-spheres cracked, and part of its gearing was distorted. Big Graye, hanging in the centre of the central hall, survived untouched apart from soot, which took two years to clean.

## Salvage and storage

In the days after the fire, staff and volunteers worked through the west wing and the central hall, moving everything that could be moved out of the smoke- and water-affected rooms. Because the building could not be secured, and because the Institute had no spare storage of its own, the board arranged within a fortnight to lease space at the Vellmoor Depository in the inland town of Vellmoor, about forty kilometres from Port Calder. Surviving collections were moved there by lorry through April and May 1962. They remained at Vellmoor until 1968, when the new wing was ready. Staff who worked at Vellmoor in those years remember it as cold, dry and, for the most part, safe; it also meant that curators were separated from their collections by an hour's drive for six years.

## The Rebuild Meridian appeal

In April 1962 the Mayor of Port Calder, Conrad Bellweather, launched a public appeal under the name "Rebuild Meridian". The appeal was unusual for its time in reaching far beyond the Institute's traditional patrons: collections were taken in schools, at the docks and in churches, and the membership society, Friends of the Meridian, organised a long programme of events. By 1964 the appeal had raised $1.1 million, a figure that surprised the board and that fundamentally changed its sense of whom the Institute served.

## The Conservation Studio

The fire exposed the fact that the Institute had no trained conservators. Damaged objects in the first months were handled by curators and volunteers with more goodwill than expertise. In 1963 the board created a Conservation Studio and appointed Beatrix Nolan, then thirty-six, as its head. Nolan's first major project was the Threlkeld Star Atlas, which she worked on from 1963 to 1967, flattening, cleaning and stabilising each plate. Her restoration of the Calder Orrery followed in 1970. The studio she founded exists today as the Conservation and Collections Care Division.

## The resignation of Dr. Sallow

Dr. Rupert Sallow had been director since 1951. He was widely respected as a scientist and as a manager of the Institute's finances, and in the immediate aftermath of the fire he was praised for his energy. Over the following eighteen months, however, criticism grew - in the press, among some trustees, and among staff - over the Institute's handling of building safety in the years before the fire. Sallow resigned in February 1964. In March 1964 the board appointed Dr. Margit Oster-Lind as the fourth director of the Institute. She served until 1987, and her "open doors" policy - free Sunday admission and a public lecture series - is often read as a direct response to the public generosity shown after the fire.

## The Rautio Wing

The board resolved in 1963 not to rebuild the east wing in its original form. The commission for a new wing on the same site went to the architect Selma Rautio, whose design was deliberately modern: a concrete and glass structure with a tall top-lit atrium, sealed stores, compartmentalised fire zones and, for the first time in the Institute's history, a sprinkler system. The Rautio Wing opened in October 1968. Big Graye was moved from the central hall and suspended in the atrium, where it still hangs.

## Memory and commemoration

For many years the fire was spoken of inside the Institute mainly as a practical matter - a line in a registry entry, a reason why a series of photographs no longer existed. That began to change in the 1990s, when the Institute's oral history work recorded the memories of staff and volunteers who had been present, including Harold Pike and the docent and Friends founder Lottie Graves. The Institute Archivist, Tamsin Rourke, drew on these recordings for her 2010 book *Voices from the Fire*, and in 2012 the Institute marked the fiftieth anniversary with the exhibition "Fire and Recovery", which brought together salvaged objects, restored items and the recorded voices of witnesses.

## Chronology

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 14 March 1962, 23:40 | Fire discovered by night watchman |
| 14 March 1962, 23:44 | Fire Department called |
| 15 March 1962, 04:20 | Fire under control |
| 16 March 1962 | First press estimate of losses |
| April 1962 | Fire Department report; Rebuild Meridian appeal launched |
| April-May 1962 | Collections moved to Vellmoor |
| 1963 | Conservation Studio founded |
| February 1964 | Director resigns |
| March 1964 | New director appointed |
| June 1965 | Final loss assessment |
| 1967 | Restoration of the atlas completed |
| October 1968 | Rautio Wing opens; collections return from Vellmoor |
| 1970 | Restoration of the orrery completed |

## Assessment

Historians of the Institute tend to divide its story into "before the fire" and "after the fire", and the division is not merely rhetorical. Before 1962 the Institute was, in governance and outlook, a patron's foundation that happened to open its galleries to the public; its funding came from a small number of wealthy families and trusts, and its priorities were set by its scientists. After 1962 it depended - for the first time - on thousands of small donors, on the city council, and on the goodwill of people who had queued in the rain to drop coins into collecting tins. The Institute that emerged in 1968 was more professional in its care of collections, more cautious in its buildings, and more conscious of its public. It was also, some of its scientists felt, a little less sure of what it was for - a tension that has recurred in almost every decade since.

The fire also changed the physical record of the Institute's first fifty years. Researchers working on the early expeditions, the early herbarium or the Institute's own institutional history routinely encounter gaps where photographs, notebooks or specimens were lost. Many of the surviving objects bear the marks of that night: tide lines on paper, blistered lacquer, smoke staining in the grain of the display cases that were salvaged and reused. Rather than removing all such traces, the Institute's conservators have for several decades followed a policy of recording them, and in some cases deliberately leaving them visible, as part of each object's history.

## Sources

- Port Calder Fire Department, investigation report, April 1962.
- Minutes of the Board of Trustees, 1960-1968.
- Final loss assessment, June 1965.
- *Port Calder Gazette*, March 1962 to October 1968.
- Meridian Oral History Project recordings, 1998.
- Rourke, T., *Voices from the Fire* (2010).

documents.title: Brisk Trust v. The Meridian Institute (2009-2011)
documents.summary: History of the 2009 lawsuit in which the Brisk Trust challenged the Institute's use of restricted endowment income for gallery renovation.
documents.body:
# Brisk Trust v. The Meridian Institute

**Brisk Trust v. The Meridian Institute** (Port Calder District Court, case no. **2009-CIV-04417**) was a civil action brought in October 2009 by the Brisk Trust against the Meridian Institute over the Institute's use of income from the Brisk endowment. It was settled in March 2011.

## Background

In 1953 the canning magnate Walter Brisk endowed the Institute with $2 million through a family trust. The deed of gift provided that the income should be applied to "scientific research and the acquisition of scientific instruments." For more than fifty years the income was spent on research posts, field work, tide gauges, telescopes and laboratory equipment, and the arrangement caused no difficulty.

In 2006 the Institute began planning a major renovation of its Wrenfield Street public galleries, the first since the Rautio Wing was completed in 1968. The project's cost rose from an initial $9.1 million to $12.6 million. To close the gap, the Chief Financial Officer, **Gregory Stath**, proposed applying accumulated Brisk endowment income to the parts of the renovation that housed scientific displays, arguing that interpretation of science to the public was a form of "scientific research" within the meaning of the deed. The Director, **Dr. Nadia Corrow**, accepted the proposal, and the finance committee approved it without referring it to the full Board. Between 2007 and 2008, **$3.4 million** of Brisk income was spent on the galleries.

## The dispute

The Trust learned of the reallocation from the Institute's 2008 accounts. Its chair, **Maud Brisk** — the founder's daughter, who had chaired the Trust since 1988 — wrote to the Director in February 2009 asking for an explanation. The Institute's reply, defending the spending as within the deed, did not satisfy the trustees. After a failed mediation in the summer, the Trust filed suit on 14 October 2009, asking the court to declare the spending a breach of the deed and to order the money restored.

Maud Brisk's statement at the time of filing was widely quoted: "My father sat in the Institute's lecture hall as a boy. He knew exactly what a gallery was and exactly what a laboratory was, and he wrote down which one he was paying for."

## The Institute's position

The Institute's defence, led by the firm of Hollis Brandreth, argued that:

- the deed did not define "scientific research" and should be read in light of the Institute's charitable purposes as a whole;
- the renovated galleries included working displays of instruments and live data from the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory;
- the Trust had not objected to smaller uses of income for public lectures in earlier decades.

The Board chair, **Evelyn Marchbank**, commissioned an independent review of the Institute's restricted funds in early 2010. The review concluded that the gallery spending was "difficult to reconcile" with the deed and identified weaknesses in how restricted gifts were recorded. That finding made settlement likely.

## Settlement

The parties settled in March 2011, shortly before the centenary. Under the settlement the Institute agreed to:

1. restore $3.4 million to the endowment in five annual instalments ending in 2016;
2. create the **Brisk Research Fellowships** for early-career scientists;
3. submit its use of Brisk income each year to a joint review committee.

Neither side admitted liability. Gregory Stath remained CFO; the Institute's governance reforms, including a restricted-funds register and an external annual review, were credited by later auditors with preventing any repetition.

## Significance

The case is often cited as the sharpest episode in the Institute's long tension between its research mission and its museum mission. Commentators noted the irony that the renovated galleries were among the most successful in the Institute's history, while the research departments whose money paid for them had been quietly short of equipment for years.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 1953 | Brisk endowment established |
| 2007–2008 | $3.4 million of Brisk income spent on gallery renovation |
| Feb 2009 | Maud Brisk writes to the Director |
| 14 Oct 2009 | Suit filed |
| 2010 | Independent restricted-funds review |
| Mar 2011 | Settlement approved by the court |
| 2016 | Final restoration instalment paid |

Stars Above Calder

Harrow Point Public Observatory, Visitor Centre Gallery
14 June 2014 – 25 January 2015

How has the sky over Port Calder been watched, measured and imagined? Stars Above Calder tells the story of ninety years of astronomy on Harrow Point, from the opening of the observatory in 1925 to today's public viewing nights, through photographs, instruments, notebooks and original glass plates from the Institute's collection.

The exhibition is curated by Dr. Ines Halloran, Curator of Astronomy and head of the Department of Astronomy and Navigation, and is the first major exhibition to be held at the Harrow Point Public Observatory since the visitor centre opened in 2008.

What you will see

  • The discovery plates of Comet 1938b — the original glass photographic plates exposed at Harrow Point in November and December 1938, shown in public for the first time. Rediscovered during a survey of the plate archive, they record the only comet ever discovered from Port Calder.
  • A full-size facsimile of the Threlkeld Atlas — visitors can turn the pages of a high-resolution reproduction. The original manuscript atlas is too fragile to travel and is kept in a climate-controlled vault at Wrenfield Street.
  • The observers' notebooks — nightly records kept at the telescope between 1925 and 1996.
  • Light and dark — an interactive map showing how the growth of Port Calder brightened the night sky and ended research observing at the site.
  • The meridian line — the brass line in the transit room floor that gave the Institute its name.

Visiting

SessionTimesPrice
Daytime galleryWed–Sun, 11.00–16.00Free
Evening viewing and galleryFri–Sat, from dusk$12 adults, $6 children
School groupsBy arrangementFree

Related events

  • Opening night talk by Dr. Halloran: "Ninety Years on the Point" — 13 June 2014.
  • Comet-watching evening — 11 October 2014.
  • Family astronomy days — first Sunday of each month.

Observatory manager Dr. Leonie Farrant said: "Bringing these plates back to the place where they were exposed, after seventy-six years, is very special for us."

Supported by the Friends of the Meridian and the Brisk Research Fellowships programme.

documents.title: Pell-Windham v. The Meridian Institute (1978–1981)
documents.summary: History of the 1978–1981 lawsuit over ownership of the Corvina Logbook.
documents.body:
# Pell-Windham v. The Meridian Institute

**Court:** Port Calder District Court
**Case number:** CV-78-2291
**Filed:** 9 October 1978
**Decided:** 11 June 1981
**Plaintiff:** Clarissa Pell-Windham
**Defendant:** The Meridian Institute
**Outcome:** Judgment for the defendant

## Background

The Corvina Logbook, kept by Captain Josiah Harrow while master of SS Corvina from 1889 to 1894, was given to the Institute in 1912 by his widow, Constance Harrow. For sixty years its ownership was never questioned.

In 1974 the Pell & Harrow Shipping Company was wound up and its residual assets were distributed to its shareholders, principally the Pell family. **Clarissa Pell-Windham**, granddaughter of the Institute's founder Augustin Pell, argued that the logbook had been a company record, kept by a company master on a company ship, and that Constance Harrow had therefore had no right to give it away. On that view, title had remained with the company and passed to its shareholders in 1974.

## The parties

The plaintiff was represented by **Ambrose Lisle** of the Port Calder law firm **Vantry & Lisle**. The Institute was represented by **Harriet Dunne**, a Port Calder barrister who acted for it without fee. Director Margit Oster-Lind gave evidence on the Institute's behalf, as did the archivist Clement Hoy.

## The arguments

Lisle relied on the company's standing orders of 1886, which required masters to keep "a true log of every voyage" and to deliver it to the office "when called for", and on the fact that several P&H logs of the period were still among the company's papers.

Dunne's case rested on the character of Harrow's volumes. She showed that the official deck logs of the Corvina had been delivered to the office as required and later destroyed, and that the four volumes at the Institute were a separate, private journal: bound at Harrow's own expense, written in the first person, and full of natural-history notes and personal reflections that had no place in a company record. She also produced the 1912 deed of gift and letters showing that Augustin Pell himself had known of and welcomed the donation.

## Judgment

On 11 June 1981 Judge Marcus Ashdown found for the Institute. He held that the volumes were Harrow's personal journal and his personal property; that they had passed to his widow on his death; and that her gift of 1912 was valid. He added that it would be "a strange result" if the founder's own company could reclaim a gift the founder had welcomed. Costs were awarded against the plaintiff but later waived by the Institute.

## Aftermath

The case caused a long estrangement between the Pell family and the Institute. It ended in 1989–1990, when Clarissa Pell-Windham approached the new director, Felix Amberly, and subsequently gave the family's papers to the archive.

## Not to be confused with

This case is sometimes confused with the later dispute between the Brisk Trust and the Institute (2009–2011), which concerned the use of endowment funds rather than ownership of an object and was settled rather than decided.

documents.title: Ossery Trench Survey (2017)
documents.summary: Account of the 2017 multibeam mapping survey of the Ossery Trench co-led by MOL and Tollan College of Marine Science, funded by the National Maritime Heritage Board.
documents.body:
# Ossery Trench Survey (2017)

The **Ossery Trench Survey** was a joint mapping and sampling project carried out between August and October 2017 by MOL (the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory) and the **Tollan College of Marine Science**. It produced the first complete high-resolution bathymetric map of the Ossery Trench, about 120 km off the Calder coast.

*Not to be confused with the 1970 Ossery Trench Expedition, a dredging voyage led by Tobias Wren.*

## Leadership

The survey was co-led by **Dr. Rhea Oduya**, director of MOL, and **Professor Aurelio Banks** of Tollan College's department of marine geoscience. Oduya was responsible for the mapping programme; Banks led the sampling and sediment coring.

## Funding

The survey was funded principally by the **National Maritime Heritage Board** under grant **NMHB-2016-0772**, awarded in November 2016 for $740,000. The grant covered ship time, the charter of a remotely operated vehicle for eight days, and two years of data processing. Tollan College contributed staff time and laboratory analysis; the Meridian Institute contributed its vessel and a further $95,000 from its research budget.

## Vessel and methods

The work was carried out from MOL's research vessel *RV Tern*, fitted for the survey with a hull-mounted deep-water multibeam echo sounder. Over three legs totalling 46 days at sea, the survey:

- mapped some 2,300 square kilometres of seabed;
- recorded depths to **3,450 metres** at the deepest point of the trench, considerably deeper than the 2,900 metres reached by dredge in 1970;
- took 31 sediment cores and 18 targeted biological samples;
- revisited five of the 1970 dredge stations for comparison.

## Findings

The map revealed the trench as two basins separated by a sill at about 2,600 metres, explaining why earlier soundings had given inconsistent maximum depths. Sampling recovered specimens of several species first described from the 1970 material, as well as a stalked sea lily not previously recorded on the Calder margin. Some of the specimens and a large-format print of the new map went on display at the Institute in 2018.

## Outputs

- *The Ossery Trench Bathymetric Survey* (2018), final report by R. Oduya and A. Banks
- Public data release of the bathymetric grid (2018)
- Two doctoral theses at Tollan College (in progress)

documents.title: Deep Meridian: Seventy Years of Ocean Science (exhibition, 2018–2019)
documents.summary: Exhibition page for Deep Meridian, the 2018–2019 exhibition marking seventy years of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory.
documents.body:
Deep Meridian: Seventy Years of Ocean Science

14 April 2018 – 3 March 2019
Rautio Wing, Level 2 Galleries
Free with general admission

In 1947 a physicist with a borrowed boat and a converted lifeboat house set out to measure the sea around Port Calder. Seventy years later, the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory at Brannock Bay is one of the longest-running coastal research stations in the region. Deep Meridian tells its story, from the first tide gauge on the old slipway to the newest maps of the Ossery Trench.

What you will see

  • The founder's bench. A reconstruction of the workroom of Dr. Ottilie Brandt-Sayer, the laboratory's founder and director from 1947 to 1972, with her field notebooks, slide rule and the original current meter she designed in 1949.
  • Twenty years of weekly visits. A wall-sized chart of the laboratory's long-term temperature record, begun in 1949 and still running.
  • Into the deep. Specimens from Dr. Tobias Wren's 1970 dredging voyage, including glass sponges and a deep-sea holothurian displayed for the first time.
  • The new map. A six-metre floor projection of the bathymetric map produced by the 2017 Ossery Trench Survey, and specimens recovered on that survey, among them a stalked sea lily never before recorded off this coast.
  • Life at Brannock Bay. Oral histories from laboratory staff, boatmen and fishermen.

Timeline

YearEvent
1947Laboratory opens at Brannock Bay under Ottilie Brandt
1949Current meter and long-term moorings established
1970First deep-water expedition to the Ossery Trench
1972Tobias Wren becomes director
1974New laboratory building opens
1995Priya Sandoval becomes director; Ferrow Marsh field station founded
2015Rhea Oduya becomes director
2017Ossery Trench Survey maps the trench to 3,450 metres

Curator's note

“We wanted visitors to feel the patience of this work,” says Dr. Rhea Oduya, director of the laboratory. “Most of what we know about this coast comes not from one brave voyage but from people going back to the same mooring, week after week, for seventy years.”

Events

  • Family Ocean Day – Saturday 12 May 2018
  • Lecture: “Mapping the Invisible” – Thursday 7 June 2018, 18:30, Main Hall
  • Laboratory open weekend at Brannock Bay – 8–9 September 2018 (booking required)

Deep Meridian is supported by the Friends of the Meridian and the Oriel Foundation.

documents.title: Harrow Point Observatory to Close to Research
documents.summary: 1996 announcement that light pollution forces the Harrow Point Observatory to end research observing.
documents.body:
Harrow Point Observatory to Close to Research at the End of October

News release, The Meridian Institute, 1 October 1996

After seventy-one years of continuous observing, the Harrow Point Observatory will close as a research facility on 31 October 1996, the Meridian Institute announced today. The decision was taken by the Board of Governors at its September meeting on the recommendation of the Director, Dr. Felix Amberly, and the Department of Astronomy and Navigation.

The principal reason is light pollution. When the observatory opened on the Harrow Point headland in 1925 it stood six kilometres from a city of fewer than ninety thousand people, with nothing between the dome and the southern horizon but sea. Port Calder's southern suburbs now reach almost to the headland road, and the container terminal lights on the far side of the bay are visible from the dome on every clear night. Sky-brightness measurements taken by the department over the last five years show the background sky at the zenith has brightened by more than a full magnitude since 1970.

"We have fought this for a long time," Dr. Amberly said. "We shielded the car park, we persuaded the council to change the headland street lamps, and we moved our faint-object work to the small hours. But the honest assessment of our own astronomers is that Harrow Point can no longer do competitive research. It would be wrong to go on spending research money there."

What happens next

  • The 18-inch Pell Refractor will be cleaned, capped and left in place under the dome. It will not be removed or sold.
  • The photographic plate archive, about 31,000 plates dating from 1925, will be transferred to the Wrenfield Street building for cataloguing.
  • Department staff will move their observing programmes to remote time on telescopes operated by partner institutions.
  • The headland buildings will be kept weather-tight while the Board considers future uses. Public open evenings will end with the October programme.

The Institute stressed that the closure is not a reduction in its commitment to astronomy. The department's budget will be kept at its current level, with savings from building operations redirected to data analysis and to the plate digitisation work now being planned.

Reaction

The Friends of the Meridian expressed "deep regret" and asked the Board to keep the site available for public viewing in some form. A spokesperson for the Friends said that "generations of Port Calder schoolchildren saw Saturn for the first time through that telescope."

Several former staff attended an informal farewell observing night on 28 September. Among them was the retired curator Dr. Miriam Castell, who began her career as an assistant observer on the headland.

Harrow Point Observatory
Opened1925
Main instrument18-inch Pell Refractor
Distance from city centre6 km south
Research closure31 October 1996

Media contact: Communications Office, The Meridian Institute, Port Calder.

documents.title: Harrow Point Public Observatory Opens Its Doors
documents.summary: 2008 news release on the reopening of Harrow Point as a public observatory managed by Dr. Leonie Farrant.
documents.body:
Harrow Point Public Observatory Opens Its Doors

News release, 24 May 2008

Twelve years after it closed to research, the observatory on the Harrow Point headland reopened tonight as the Harrow Point Public Observatory, a visitor and education centre operated by the Meridian Institute. More than six hundred people queued along the headland road for the first public viewing night.

The observatory will be managed by Dr. Leonie Farrant, an astronomer and science educator who joins the Institute from a university outreach programme. "Harrow Point can't compete with mountain-top telescopes for research any more, and it doesn't need to," Dr. Farrant said. "What it can do is give people in Port Calder their own view of the sky, through a beautiful old telescope, in the building where their grandparents looked up at comets."

What visitors will find

  • Public viewing nights every Friday and Saturday, weather permitting, using the restored 18-inch Pell Refractor.
