The research departments have always wanted money that asks no questions; the galleries have always needed money that can be spent on the public; and the donors, from Augustin Pell onward, have always had views about which is which.

The lesson of a hundred years, if there is one, is that the Institute does best when it is honest about what its money is for. The Brisk lawsuit happened because that honesty lapsed. The Rebuild Meridian appeal succeeded because it was total: the city was told exactly what it was paying for and could walk into the result.

As the Institute begins its second century, its director and board are discussing a new campaign to double the endowment by 2030, with separate funds for research and for public programmes, each clearly labelled. Augustin Pell, who kept careful accounts and disliked surprises, would approve. Walter Brisk would want to read the small print. And the nine-year-old who walked in free on a Sunday afternoon would simply be glad the doors were open.

### A note on sources

The figures in this chapter are drawn from the Institute's annual reports, the minutes of the board and its finance committee, the Rebuild Meridian donor ledgers, and the Pell family archive. I am grateful to Tamsin Rourke, the Institute Archivist, for her patience with a journalist's questions, and to Gregory Stath, the Institute's chief financial officer, for explaining, more than once, the difference between restricted and unrestricted income.

Some older figures — especially the value of the Pell family's gifts in kind — are estimates, and I have said so where they appear. Readers who wish to check my arithmetic will find the board papers open to researchers by appointment in the Institute's reading room.

### Further reading

- Hester Quayle, *A History of the Meridian Institute* (1961)
- Tamsin Rourke, *Voices from the Fire* (2010)
- The Meridian Institute, *Annual Reports*, 1912–2010
- Tobias Wren, *Between Tides* (2001), especially chapter 4, on the funding of the laboratory at Brannock Bay

*The next chapter, "The Public's Museum," considers the Institute's visitors, from the Sunday crowds of the 1960s to the school parties of today.*

documents.title: Tidal Mixing in the Calder Estuary (1952)
documents.summary: Library catalogue record and abstract for Brandt and Hale's 1952 paper on estuarine mixing in the Calder Estuary.
documents.body:
# Tidal Mixing in the Calder Estuary (1952)

**Authors:** O. Brandt and W. Hale
**Published in:** *Journal of Coastal Hydrography*, vol. 7, no. 3 (1952), pp. 211–248
**Institutional affiliations:** Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, Brannock Bay; Department of Geography, University of Ashcombe
**Library shelfmark:** Periodicals, Reading Room
**Record type:** Journal article (Institute staff publication)

## Note on authorship

"O. Brandt" is Dr. Ottilie Brandt, founding director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, who retained this byline after her 1950 marriage. "W. Hale" is Professor Winifred Hale of the University of Ashcombe, then the leading estuarine hydrographer in the country. The collaboration began when Hale spent the summer of 1950 as a visiting scientist at Brannock Bay.

## Abstract

Observations of salinity, temperature and current made at thirty-two stations in the Calder Estuary between June 1949 and September 1951 are used to describe the mixing of river and sea water through the tidal cycle. The estuary is shown to alternate between a partially mixed state on spring tides and a strongly stratified, salt-wedge state on neap tides, with the transition controlled chiefly by river discharge. A simple budget of salt and fresh water is derived, from which a flushing time of between four and nine days is estimated. The implications for the dispersal of harbour effluent from Port Calder are discussed.

## Contents

1. Introduction
2. The Calder Estuary: topography and river regime
3. Observational methods
4. Salinity structure on spring and neap tides
5. Current observations
6. A salt budget for the estuary
7. Flushing and the dispersal of effluent
8. Conclusions

## Acknowledgments (from the paper)

"We are indebted to Dr. Margit Oster for the chemical titrations on which the salinity sections depend, to Mr. G. Sayer for the maintenance of the moorings, and to the Director and Board of the Meridian Institute for the use of the laboratory launch. Current records were obtained from moored self-recording instruments built in the laboratory workshop."

## Significance

The paper was the first quantitative description of the Calder Estuary and remained the standard reference for three decades. Its flushing estimate was cited in the 1958 public inquiry into the Port Calder harbour sewage outfall. It is also an early example of the Meridian Institute's collaboration with the University of Ashcombe, which continues today.

## Citations

Cited 214 times in the Institute's citation index (as of 2015), most frequently as "Brandt and Hale (1952)."

documents.title: The Ossery Trench Bathymetric Survey (2018) - executive summary
documents.summary: Executive summary of the final report of the 2017 Ossery Trench mapping survey by Oduya and Banks.
documents.body:
THE OSSERY TRENCH BATHYMETRIC SURVEY
Final Report

R. Oduya (Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, Meridian Institute)
A. Banks (Tollan College)

June 2018

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

1. Purpose

This report presents the results of a multibeam bathymetric survey and associated sampling programme carried out in the Ossery Trench between 14 August and 27 October 2017. The survey was a partnership between the Meridian Institute's oceanographic laboratory and Tollan College, and was funded principally by a grant from the NMHB under its Maritime Research and Heritage programme, with contributions from both partner institutions.

2. Coverage

Survey lines totalling 5,840 km were run from the research vessel RV Tern over three legs (46 days at sea). Coverage of the trench and its flanks is complete between the 1,000 m contour and the trench floor, an area of approximately 2,300 square kilometres. Grid resolution is 25 m on the trench floor and 10 m on the upper flanks.

3. Principal findings

- The deepest sounding recorded is 3,450 m, in the southern basin.
- The trench consists of two basins separated by a sill with a crest depth of about 2,600 m. This explains the inconsistent maximum depths reported in earlier soundings, which sampled one basin or the other.
- The northern basin is shallower (maximum approximately 3,020 m) and has a thicker sediment fill.
- Five dredge stations occupied in 1970 were relocated to within 200 m. The 1970 station at 2,900 m, previously described as "the trench floor," lies on the sill rather than in either basin.
- Slope failure scars on the eastern wall indicate at least three large submarine landslides; their age is unknown.
- Thirty-one sediment cores and eighteen biological samples were recovered. Preliminary identification confirms the persistence of several species described from 1970 material and adds a stalked crinoid not previously recorded on the Calder margin.

4. Data availability

The bathymetric grid, survey line data and sample catalogue are released with this report. Specimens are held at the Meridian Institute's deep-water collection at Brannock Bay; sediment cores are held at Tollan College.

5. Recommendations

(a) Repeat mapping of the eastern wall at five-year intervals to detect active slope failure.
(b) Dating of landslide deposits from cores.
(c) A dedicated biological survey of the southern basin floor, which was sampled at only four points.
(d) Continued collaboration between the two partner institutions and the NMHB in the management of the trench as a site of scientific and heritage interest, including two wrecks identified on the upper western flank.

6. Acknowledgments

We thank the master and crew of RV Tern; the ROV team; the NMHB grants office; and the many staff and students of both institutions who processed data ashore. The Meridian Institute's archive kindly provided the station logs and original charts of the 1970 expedition.

documents.title: Deed of Foundation of the Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy (1911)
documents.summary: Text of Augustin Pell's 1911 deed establishing the institute at 14 Wrenfield Street.
documents.body:
DEED OF FOUNDATION
THE PELL INSTITUTE OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
PORT CALDER

Dated this third day of May, nineteen hundred and eleven.

THIS DEED is made by AUGUSTIN PELL, merchant and shipowner, of Fennick Terrace in the City of Port Calder (hereinafter "the Founder").

WHEREAS the Founder desires to establish in the City of Port Calder an institution for the advancement of knowledge of the natural world and for the instruction and enjoyment of the people of the said City;

AND WHEREAS the Founder has acquired the freehold of the premises known as 14 Wrenfield Street, formerly a bonded warehouse, and has caused the same to be refitted with galleries, study rooms and laboratories at his own expense;

NOW THIS DEED WITNESSETH as follows:

1. NAME. There is hereby established an institution to be known as the Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy (hereinafter "the Institute").

2. OBJECTS. The objects of the Institute shall be the study of the sea, the sky and the living shore, and the display of the same to the people of Port Calder. In pursuit of these objects the Institute may:
   (a) collect, preserve and exhibit specimens, instruments, charts, books and records;
   (b) conduct observation and research, and publish the results;
   (c) mount voyages and field excursions;
   (d) provide lectures and instruction open to the public.

3. PREMISES. The premises at 14 Wrenfield Street, together with the fixtures and fittings thereof, are hereby conveyed to the Trustees to be held for the objects of the Institute and for no other purpose.

4. ENDOWMENT. The Founder hereby transfers to the Trustees four thousand ordinary shares in the Pell & Harrow Shipping Company, the income of which shall be applied to the maintenance of the Institute. The Trustees shall not sell the said shares save with the written consent of the Founder during his lifetime.

5. TRUSTEES. The first Trustees shall be the Founder; Mr. Lionel Darrow, solicitor; Mr. Silas Knapp, alderman of the City; and the Reverend Thomas Whitley. The Trustees shall constitute the Board of the Institute.

6. DIRECTOR. The Board shall appoint a Director who shall have charge of the collections, the staff and the scientific work of the Institute. The first Director shall be Dr. Cornelius Aldane, who has signified his willingness to act.

7. PUBLIC ACCESS. The galleries of the Institute shall be open to the public without charge on not fewer than one afternoon in each week.

8. NAME TO BE REVIEWED. The Founder records his wish that the Board may, at any future time and upon his request or after his death, adopt such other name for the Institute as it shall think fit, provided the objects in clause 2 are preserved.

9. AMENDMENT. The objects in clause 2 shall not be altered. The remaining clauses may be amended by resolution of three-quarters of the Board.

IN WITNESS whereof the Founder has set his hand and seal the day and year first above written.

SIGNED, SEALED AND DELIVERED by the said AUGUSTIN PELL
in the presence of:
    Lionel Darrow, Solicitor, Harbour Chambers, Port Calder
    Edith Marsh, clerk to the said solicitor

Accepted on behalf of the Institute:
    Cornelius Aldane, Director-designate

[Archivist's note, typed on a later card attached to the file copy: Original deed on vellum held in the Institute archive, strongroom shelf 1. Clause 8 was invoked in October 1928.]

documents.title: Board Resolution Renaming the Institute (October 1928)
documents.summary: Board minute recording the change of name from the Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy to The Meridian Institute.
documents.body:
PELL INSTITUTE OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
MINUTES OF A SPECIAL MEETING OF THE BOARD
Held in the Board Room, 14 Wrenfield Street, on Wednesday 17 October 1928 at 4 p.m.

PRESENT: Mr. Augustin Pell (Founder); Mr. Lionel Darrow (Chair); Alderman Silas Knapp; Mr. Edmund Pell; Mrs. Agnes Carrow; Professor Lucan Threlkeld (by invitation).
IN ATTENDANCE: Dr. Cornelius Aldane, Director; Mr. H. Tobin, Secretary.

1. APOLOGIES
Apologies were received from the Reverend Thomas Whitley.

2. LETTER FROM THE FOUNDER
The Chair read a letter from Mr. Augustin Pell dated 2 October 1928, invoking clause 8 of the Deed of Foundation and requesting that the Board adopt a new name for the Institute which does not bear his own. Mr. Pell stated that the Institute "belongs to the city and to the work, not to one family", and that he did not wish its reputation to rise or fall with that of his name or his firm.

Mr. Pell spoke briefly to the letter. He remarked that "a man's name wears out faster than a good idea."

3. PROPOSED NAME
The Director reported that the staff had been consulted informally. Several names had been suggested, including "The Calder Institute" and "The Wrenfield Institute". Professor Threlkeld proposed "The Meridian Institute", in reference to the brass meridian line set into the floor of the transit room at the Harrow Point Observatory, from which all the Institute's astronomical and navigational observations are reckoned. He observed that the name joined the sky and the sea, being equally a term of astronomy and of navigation.

Alderman Knapp asked whether the change would unsettle subscribers. The Secretary reported that the printers could supply new letterheads within a month at modest cost.

4. RESOLUTION
It was proposed by Mr. Darrow and seconded by Mr. Edmund Pell:

"That, in accordance with clause 8 of the Deed of Foundation and at the request of the Founder, the Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy shall henceforth be known as THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE, with effect from 1 January 1929; the objects of the Institute being in no way altered."

The resolution was CARRIED unanimously (six votes; Mr. Augustin Pell abstaining at his own request).

5. CONSEQUENTIAL MATTERS
(a) The Secretary to arrange new letterheads and signage. It was noted with some amusement that the Institute's magazine, Meridian Quarterly, founded in 1920, already bore the proposed name and would need no alteration.
(b) The carved stone name above the Wrenfield Street entrance to be retained as a historical feature, with a bronze plaque bearing the new name to be fixed beneath it.
(c) The Director to write to the Institute's correspondents and exchange partners announcing the change.

6. VOTE OF THANKS
The Board recorded its thanks to the Founder for his generosity and for his wishes in this matter.

The meeting closed at 5.10 p.m.

Signed as a true record:
L. Darrow, Chair          H. Tobin, Secretary

documents.title: Letter from Captain Venn to Director Aldane proposing a Graye voyage (1933)
documents.summary: Captain Elias Venn's 1933 letter to Dr. Cornelius Aldane proposing an expedition to relocate the reef recorded in Harrow's logbook.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE -- ARCHIVE, DIRECTOR'S CORRESPONDENCE, BOX 1933/2
Item: letter, 3 pp., manuscript. Received 7 February 1933.
Docket in Dr. Aldane's hand: "Captain Venn -- Graye proposal. Refer to Dr. Quayle & Mr. E. Pell. Ans'd 14 Feb."

                                        c/o Pell & Harrow Shipping Co.
                                        Lantern Quay, Port Calder
                                        6th February 1933

Dr. Cornelius Aldane,
Director, The Meridian Institute,
14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder

Dear Dr. Aldane,

You will perhaps remember me from the lecture on seabirds which I gave to your Friday evening audience two winters ago, when you were kind enough to lend me the lantern and the Institute's slides of petrels. I write now on a matter I have turned over in my mind for many years, and which I believe to be of real interest to the Institute.

In the year 1891 the late Captain Josiah Harrow, commanding the Corvina on the southern route, recorded in his log that he sighted breakers far to the south-west of any charted danger, sent a boat in, and landed upon "a low island white with birds". He gave it the name of his first mate, Graye. The log is, as you know better than I, in the Institute's keeping since Mrs. Harrow's gift. I have read the entry several times with your librarian's permission and I am satisfied that Harrow's reckoning, while rough, is honest.

No vessel of the company has since passed near enough to confirm the reef, for the good reason that no master wishes to find it by night. The Admiralty charts show nothing. It is my conviction that the island exists, that it lies within thirty miles of Harrow's position, and that a properly found vessel could fix it in a fortnight of summer weather.

I propose, therefore, that the Institute organise a voyage for this purpose in the summer of 1933 or, failing that, 1934. I would undertake to command and to direct the survey. I ask that the Institute provide two or three naturalists, for Harrow's "birds" deserve a better account than a sailor can give, and a photographer if one can be found who does not suffer at sea.

As to the vessel and the cost, I have spoken privately with Mr. Edmund Pell, who has succeeded his late father as chairman of the company. He tells me that he is well disposed to lending one of the smaller coastal steamers for a season and to bearing the cost of coal and crew, provided the Institute formally sponsors the undertaking and publishes its results. He felt that his father, who founded your Institute, would have wished it. I would not presume to speak for Mr. Pell beyond this, and he will no doubt write to you himself.

I am aware that you are soon to lay down your office, and that the decision may fall to your successor. I would be grateful if you would place this letter before whoever must decide. I am at sea until the 20th but my daughter Rosalind will forward any letters to me at the company's office.

With great respect, I remain,

Your obedient servant,

E. Venn
Master, S.S. Plover, Pell & Harrow Shipping Co.

----
[Attached note, typed, Director's office, 14 Feb. 1933:]
Replied to Captain Venn: the Director thanks him and has referred the proposal to Dr. Hester Quayle, who will take up the directorship in the summer, and to the Curator of Natural History. Mr. Edmund Pell has telephoned to confirm the offer of a vessel. No commitment made as to date.

documents.title: Letter from Ottilie Brandt to Director Hester Quayle proposing a coastal laboratory (1946)
documents.summary: Archived 1946 letter in which Ottilie Brandt proposes a permanent oceanographic station at Brannock Bay.
documents.body:
MERIDIAN INSTITUTE ARCHIVE
Director's correspondence, box 31, folder 7
[Typescript, two leaves, with pencil annotations by the recipient]

                                        Department of Natural History
                                        The Meridian Institute
                                        14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder
                                        4th November 1946

Dr. Hester Quayle
Director

Dear Dr. Quayle,

You asked me after last week's staff meeting to put in writing what I have been saying, rather too often, over tea. Here it is, as briefly as I can manage.

The Institute has sent men to the Isle of Graye twice, has a fine telescope on Harrow Point, and has a basement full of birds, shells and whale bone. It has no way whatever of measuring the sea. Every question I am asked by the harbour board, the fishermen's cooperative or the town engineer - how fast does the water leave the estuary, where does the sewage go, why did the herring move north - I answer from charts made by other people for other purposes, or I do not answer at all.

I propose that the Institute establish a small permanent station on the coast for the continuous observation of tides, currents, temperature and salinity. I have looked at four sites. The best is Brannock Bay, some thirty kilometres north. It has:

  1. deep water close inshore, so that moorings can be tended from a small boat;
  2. the old lifeboat house, empty since the new station opened at Kellet in 1939, which the harbour board would lease for a nominal sum;
  3. a sheltered anchorage;
  4. a road, if not a good one.

I estimate the cost of fitting out the lifeboat house as a laboratory at 2,400 dollars, and the running cost, with two assistants and a boatman, at about 5,000 dollars a year. A launch could be had second-hand. I would hope to recover part of the running cost by selling tide predictions to the cooperative, which has already asked.

I do not propose a grand institution. I propose a tide gauge, three moorings, and people who will visit them every week for twenty years. The value of such a record is small in its first year and very great in its twentieth.

Dr. Dunmore has kindly said he can spare me from the Department in the summer months. I would ask the Board to consider whether the station might become a separate unit reporting directly to you.

I should be glad to discuss this at any time, and I enclose a sketch plan of the lifeboat house.

Yours sincerely,

Ottilie Brandt
Research Associate

---
[Pencil annotation, top margin, in Quayle's hand:]
"To Board, Dec. meeting. Ask Treasurer re lease. Good. H.Q."

[Pencil annotation, foot of second leaf:]
"Approved in principle 11 Dec 46. Name? 'Oceanographic Laboratory' - O.B. prefers."

documents.title: Board of Trustees minutes, 11 June 1958
documents.summary: Board minutes renaming the Department of Celestial Navigation as the Department of Astronomy and Navigation and accepting a gift of a historic chart.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
MINUTES OF A MEETING OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
held in the Board Room, 14 Wrenfield Street, on Wednesday 11 June 1958 at 2.30 p.m.

Present: Mr. L. Carrick (Chair), Mr. E. Pell, Mrs. A. Dorrance, Mr. W. Brisk, Professor H. Tamblyn, Mr. S. Oakes, Alderman F. Rudd
In attendance: Dr. R. Sallow (Director), Mr. G. Petrie (Secretary and Bursar), Dr. M. Castell (Curator of Maps and Charts) for item 5

1. APOLOGIES
Apologies were received from Dr. H. Quayle (Honorary Trustee).

2. MINUTES
The minutes of the meeting of 12 March 1958 were approved and signed.

3. CHAIR'S REMARKS
The Chair noted that this was the last meeting to be attended by Mr. Edmund Pell, who will retire from the Board at the end of the month together with his retirement from the chairmanship of the shipping company. The Board recorded its warm thanks to Mr. Pell for twenty-nine years' service as a trustee and for his family's generosity since the foundation of the Institute.

4. DEPARTMENT OF CELESTIAL NAVIGATION - CHANGE OF NAME
4.1 The Director reported that the Department of Celestial Navigation had, since the death of Professor Threlkeld in 1939, moved steadily away from practical navigation towards astronomy, astrophysics and the history of astronomical instruments. Navigation instruction for merchant officers had ceased in 1947, when the Port Calder Nautical College assumed it. The present name was a source of confusion to correspondents and to university partners.
4.2 The Director proposed that the department be renamed the Department of Astronomy and Navigation, retaining "Navigation" in recognition of its history and its collections of charts and instruments.
4.3 Professor Tamblyn asked whether "Navigation" should be dropped altogether. The Director advised against, noting the importance of the chart and instrument collections to the Institute's maritime public.
4.4 RESOLVED: that with effect from 1 July 1958 the Department of Celestial Navigation shall be known as the Department of Astronomy and Navigation. Stationery, signage and the Meridian Quarterly masthead to be amended accordingly.

5. GIFT OF A CHART
5.1 Dr. Castell presented a report on a hand-drawn chart of Kittering Sound dated 1851, the work of the surveyor Josias Fell, which Mr. Brisk has offered to give to the Institute.
5.2 Dr. Castell described the chart as of first importance for the history of the survey of the northern coast, and in fine condition.
5.3 Mr. Brisk withdrew for the discussion of this item.
5.4 RESOLVED: that the gift be accepted with the thanks of the Board, and that the chart be placed in the Map Room.

6. FINANCE
6.1 The Bursar presented the accounts for the half-year. Income from the Brisk endowment was in line with forecast and has been applied, as required by the terms of the gift, to research and instruments. General income showed a small surplus.
6.2 Visitor admissions for the year to 31 May were 71,300, an increase of 9 per cent.

7. BUILDINGS
7.1 The Director reported that the refit of the Graye gallery in the central hall was being costed and he would bring proposals to a later meeting.
7.2 The Bursar reported that the roof of the west wing had been repaired.

8. ANY OTHER BUSINESS
None.

The meeting closed at 4.40 p.m.

Signed: L. Carrick, Chair

documents.title: Board of Trustees minutes, 23 November 1960
documents.summary: Board minutes in which the Director proposed deferring the $38,000 east-wing rewiring to fund the Graye gallery refit.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
MINUTES OF A MEETING OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
held in the Board Room, 14 Wrenfield Street, on Wednesday 23 November 1960 at 2.30 p.m.

Present: Mr. L. Carrick (Chair), Mrs. A. Dorrance, Mr. W. Brisk, Professor H. Tamblyn, Mr. S. Oakes, Alderman F. Rudd, Mrs. J. Vail
In attendance: Dr. R. Sallow (Director), Mr. G. Petrie (Secretary and Bursar)

1. APOLOGIES
None.

2. MINUTES
The minutes of the meeting of 14 September 1960 were approved and signed.

3. DIRECTOR'S REPORT
3.1 The Director reported that attendance in the year to date was 83,900, the highest in the Institute's history.
3.2 The Director reported that Dr. Hester Quayle's history of the Institute was expected to go to press in the spring, for publication in the autumn of 1961 to mark the Institute's fiftieth anniversary.

4. CAPITAL PROGRAMME 1961-62
4.1 The Bursar presented the capital programme. Two major items were before the Board: (a) the refit of the Graye gallery in the central hall, estimated at $41,500; and (b) the rewiring of the east wing, estimated by the City Electrical Engineer at $38,000. General reserves were sufficient for one of these items but not both in the coming year.
4.2 The Director proposed that the east-wing rewiring be deferred and that the Graye gallery refit proceed in 1961, to be ready for the fiftieth anniversary. He argued that the Graye gallery was the Institute's most visited space, that its present condition was "an embarrassment in an anniversary year", and that the east wing was not open to the public.
4.3 The Bursar noted that the City Electrical Engineer's report described the east-wing installation as "old but not at present dangerous" and recommended rewiring "within the next three to five years".
4.4 Mrs. Vail asked whether the east wing's stores of photographic film presented any particular risk. The Director replied that the matter would be reviewed with the photographer.
4.5 Professor Tamblyn said he was uneasy at deferring safety work in favour of display. Mr. Oakes said the Board should be guided by the Engineer's report.
4.6 RESOLVED (six in favour, Professor Tamblyn abstaining): that the Graye gallery refit proceed in 1961 at a cost not exceeding $41,500; that the east-wing rewiring be deferred and reconsidered in the capital programme for 1963-64.

5. BRISK ENDOWMENT
5.1 Mr. Brisk asked for confirmation that no part of the endowment income would be applied to the gallery refit. The Bursar confirmed that the refit would be met from general reserves and that endowment income continued to be applied to research and instruments only.

6. OCEANOGRAPHIC LABORATORY
6.1 The Director reported a request from Dr. Brandt-Sayer for a second launch for the laboratory at Brannock Bay. Deferred to the next meeting pending costs.

7. ANY OTHER BUSINESS
7.1 The Chair reported that Friends of the Meridian would hold its Christmas lecture on 14 December.

The meeting closed at 4.15 p.m.

Signed: L. Carrick, Chair

documents.title: Port Calder Fire Department investigation report PCFD-1962-118
documents.summary: Official fire department report locating the origin of the 1962 fire in the east-wing darkroom and attributing it to faulty wiring.
documents.body:
PORT CALDER FIRE DEPARTMENT
FIRE INVESTIGATION REPORT

Report No.: PCFD-1962-118
Premises: The Meridian Institute, 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder
Date of fire: 14-15 March 1962
Date of report: 9 April 1962
Investigating officer: Station Officer R. Albury
Approved: Chief Officer Dennis Marlowe

1. SUMMARY

1.1 At 23:44 on 14 March 1962 a call was received from the night watchman of the above premises reporting smoke in the east wing. The first appliance attended at 23:51. Eight appliances attended in total. The fire was brought under control at 04:20 on 15 March 1962 and was finally extinguished at 09:15.

1.2 The east wing of the premises (three storeys, masonry walls, timber floors and roof, constructed 1912-1914) was destroyed. The central hall suffered smoke damage and localised water damage. The west wing suffered smoke and water damage but no fire damage.

1.3 There were no fatalities. Two firemen were injured (Fireman J. Tully, head injury from falling ceiling; Leading Fireman P. Okoro, burns to hands). The watchman was treated for smoke inhalation.

2. ORIGIN

2.1 Examination of burn patterns, charring depth and the collapse sequence establishes the room of origin as Room E-108, the photographic darkroom on the ground floor of the east wing. The area of deepest charring was at floor level behind the fixed workbench on the north wall of Room E-108.

2.2 Room E-108 adjoined a store room holding photographic negatives on glass and on cellulose nitrate film. The nitrate film store was separated from the darkroom by a timber stud partition with a connecting door. The partition was consumed.

3. CAUSE

3.1 A lighting and power circuit ran in an unprotected timber batten behind the workbench in Room E-108. The installation was of mixed age; the original rubber-insulated cabling of c.1914 had been extended with later cable in at least two places.

3.2 Recovered sections of the circuit show perished and cracked insulation and evidence of arcing at a junction behind the workbench. It is the opinion of this Department that the fire was caused by an electrical fault in this circuit, which ignited the timber batten and adjacent panelling.

3.3 An electric tray heater in the darkroom was recovered and examined. Its switch was found in the OFF position and it is not considered to have been the cause.

3.4 No evidence of incendiary material or forced entry was found. Arson is ruled out.

4. SPREAD

4.1 The fire spread through the partition into the nitrate film store. Cellulose nitrate film burns rapidly, produces its own oxygen when decomposing and gives off large volumes of toxic smoke. Its involvement accounts for the speed at which the ground floor became fully involved and for the density of smoke reported by the watchman.

4.2 The fire travelled vertically through an open stair and service ducts to the first floor (east gallery) and roof. Crews were committed to a defensive water curtain at the junction of the east wing and central hall. This action is considered to have prevented spread to the central hall roof.

5. CONTRIBUTORY FACTORS

5.1 Age and condition of the electrical installation throughout the east wing. Inspection of surviving circuits in the central hall and west wing found similar cabling of c.1914 in several locations.

5.2 Storage of nitrate film adjacent to a room with electrical equipment and without fire separation.

5.3 Absence of automatic fire detection. Detection depended on the watchman's rounds, which were at approximately 35-minute intervals.

5.4 Absence of fire compartmentation between floors of the east wing.

6. RECOMMENDATIONS

6.1 Complete rewiring of the surviving parts of the premises before re-occupation.

6.2 Removal of all nitrate film to a detached, purpose-built store or its disposal after copying.

6.3 Installation of automatic fire detection linked to the Department.

6.4 Any rebuilding to incorporate fire compartmentation and, in collection stores, automatic sprinklers.

6.5 The Department commends the watchman for the promptness of his call.

Signed:
R. Albury, Station Officer
Dennis Marlowe, Chief Officer, Port Calder Fire Department

Copy to: The Trustees of the Meridian Institute; City Surveyor; Coroner's Office (for information).

documents.title: Board of Trustees minutes, 4 March 1964 (appointment of Director)
documents.summary: Board minutes containing minute BM-1964-03, appointing Dr. M. Oster-Lind as the fourth director of the Institute.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
MINUTES OF A SPECIAL MEETING OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
held in the Old Library, 14 Wrenfield Street, on Wednesday 4 March 1964 at 10.00 a.m.

Present: Mr. L. Carrick (Chair), Mrs. A. Dorrance, Mr. W. Brisk, Professor H. Tamblyn, Mr. S. Oakes, Alderman F. Rudd, Mrs. J. Vail, Mr. C. Bellweather (by invitation, as Chair of the Rebuild Meridian Committee)
In attendance: Mr. G. Petrie (Secretary and Bursar); Dr. M. Castell (Acting Director)

1. APOLOGIES
None.

2. RESIGNATION OF THE DIRECTOR
The Chair reported that the resignation of the Director, tendered on 17 February 1964, had taken effect on 29 February 1964. The Board recorded its thanks for thirteen years of service. The Chair reminded members that public comment on the circumstances of the resignation should be made only through the Chair.

3. APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR (Minute reference BM-1964-03)
The Chair reported on the work of the selection committee (Mr. Carrick, Mrs. Dorrance, Professor Tamblyn), which had interviewed three candidates on 26 and 27 February 1964.
The committee unanimously recommended the appointment of Dr. M. Oster-Lind as Director of the Institute.
Professor Tamblyn summarised the committee's reasons: Dr. Oster-Lind's scientific standing; her fourteen years' experience in the management of a research establishment; her record in public lecturing; and the committee's view that she had "the confidence of the staff and the ability to win back the confidence of the city".
Mrs. Vail asked about Dr. Oster-Lind's views on public access. The Chair read from her written statement to the committee, in which she proposed free admission on one day each week and a regular programme of public lectures, "so that the people who are rebuilding this Institute can see what they are rebuilding".
RESOLVED unanimously: that Dr. M. Oster-Lind be appointed fourth Director of the Meridian Institute with effect from 1 April 1964, on terms to be settled by the Chair and the Bursar.

4. ACTING DIRECTOR
The Board thanked Dr. Castell for acting as Director since 1 March and asked her to continue until 31 March.

5. REBUILD MERIDIAN
Mr. Bellweather reported that the appeal had passed $1 million and was expected to reach $1.1 million by the summer. Architects' drawings for the new east wing would be presented in May.

6. REWIRING
The Bursar confirmed that the rewiring of the central hall and west wing, recommended in the Fire Department's report, was complete.

7. ANY OTHER BUSINESS
None.

The meeting closed at 11.35 a.m.

Signed: L. Carrick, Chair

documents.title: Final loss assessment following the Wrenfield Fire (1965)
documents.summary: The Institute's definitive 1965 count of objects lost in the fire: 2,318 destroyed or damaged, 1,406 destroyed outright.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
Report to the Board of Trustees

FINAL ASSESSMENT OF COLLECTION LOSSES ARISING FROM THE WRENFIELD FIRE OF 14-15 MARCH 1962

Prepared by: The Registrar's Office, with the Conservation Studio (B. Nolan) and departmental curators
Presented: 30 June 1965
Director: Dr. M. Oster-Lind

1. PURPOSE

This report supersedes all earlier estimates, including the provisional figures circulated in March and April 1962 and the figures used in early publicity for the Rebuild Meridian appeal. It is based on a line-by-line comparison of the pre-fire accession registers (which survived in the west wing) with objects recovered, conserved or confirmed missing between March 1962 and May 1965.

2. METHOD

2.1 Each register entry for an object recorded as located in the east wing, the central hall or the Map Room on 14 March 1962 was checked against: (a) the salvage lists compiled in March-April 1962; (b) the inventories taken at the Vellmoor Depository; (c) condition reports prepared by the Conservation Studio since its foundation in 1963.

2.2 Objects were classed as DESTROYED (no recoverable material, or remains of no scientific or display value), DAMAGED (recovered with loss requiring conservation), or UNAFFECTED.

2.3 Where register entries describe lots (for example, a box of shells) the lot is counted as one object, consistent with the registers.

3. RESULTS

3.1 Total objects destroyed or damaged: 2,318
    of which destroyed outright: 1,406
    of which damaged: 912

3.2 The early estimate of "more than 3,000 objects" arose chiefly from double-counting of lots and from treating inaccessible store rooms as total losses. It should no longer be used.

3.3 By collection:

    Natural history (birds, mammals, shells, invertebrates)   destroyed 874   damaged 301
    Aldane Herbarium (sheets counted in lots of 20)            destroyed 212   damaged 96
    Photographic archive (negative series)                      destroyed 188   damaged 14
    East gallery display objects                               destroyed 97    damaged 22
    Library and archives (volumes)                             destroyed 21    damaged 311
    Maps, charts and atlases                                   destroyed 3     damaged 118
    Instruments                                                destroyed 11    damaged 50

3.4 The Aldane Herbarium has lost approximately 40 per cent of its sheets. The steel cabinet holding type specimens survived and its contents are largely intact.

3.5 Of the photographic archive, only negatives on loan for printing elsewhere at the time of the fire survive in any quantity.

4. OBJECTS OF PRINCIPAL IMPORTANCE

4.1 The Threlkeld atlas of the southern skies: DAMAGED (water). Conservation in progress since 1963 under B. Nolan; expected completion 1967.

4.2 The Calder Orrery: DAMAGED (heat). Blistered lacquer, three cracked ivory spheres, distorted gearing in the lunar train. Conservation deferred until the atlas is complete; provisional date 1970.

4.3 The Corvina Logbook: UNAFFECTED. Removed from the Map Room by the night watchman during the fire.

4.4 The fin whale skeleton in the central hall: UNAFFECTED except for soot deposits. Cleaning complete.

5. INSURANCE

The Institute's insurers have settled on the basis of the provisional valuation of 1963. No further claim will be made on the basis of this report. It is noted for the Board that the policy in force in 1962 covered the building at a value fixed in 1938 and covered the collections only at nominal values; the settlement therefore represented a small fraction of the true loss, and the rebuilding has depended overwhelmingly on the public appeal.

6. RECOMMENDATIONS

6.1 That the figure of 2,318 objects destroyed or damaged, of which 1,406 destroyed, be adopted as the Institute's official figure.

6.2 That registers be duplicated annually and a copy kept off-site.

6.3 That the Conservation Studio be established on a permanent footing with at least two further posts.

B. Nolan, Head of Conservation Studio
For the Registrar

documents.title: Letter from Clarissa Pell-Windham to Director Felix Amberly (1989)
documents.summary: Letter proposing reconciliation between the Pell family and the Institute and offering the family papers.
documents.body:
[Archive file: Director's correspondence 1989, folder P. Handwritten letter on blue paper, two sheets. Transcribed 2004.]

The Old Rectory
Holme Lane
Wrenfield, Port Calder

18th September 1989

Dr. Felix Amberly
Director, The Meridian Institute
14 Wrenfield Street
Port Calder

Dear Dr. Amberly,

You will, I expect, know my name, and perhaps not fondly. I hope you will forgive me for writing to you directly, and before we have met.

Eight years ago I lost a case against your Institute over Captain Harrow's logbook. I have not set foot in the Wrenfield Building since. I have had time to think about that case, and I no longer believe I was right to bring it — or, if I was right in law, and the judge said I was not, I was certainly wrong in spirit. My grandfather built that place so that the things in it would belong to everyone in the city. I made it a quarrel about who owned a book.

I am now fifty-eight. My father, Edmund, kept everything — every letter my grandfather wrote, every ledger of the company, the crew lists, the photographs of the ships, the correspondence with the captains. It is all in the attic here and in a store in town, some two hundred boxes, and none of it is catalogued. My sons have no interest in it. When I am gone it will be sold in lots or thrown away.

I would like it to come to the Institute, whole, and I would like to discuss with you how that might be done. I have no conditions except that it should be kept together and that researchers should be able to use it.

I will admit to a second motive. I should like my family's name back in the Wrenfield Building in some way that is not a court record. I understand that the quarrel may have left feelings among your staff and board, and I will not be offended if you need time.

I am generally at home in the mornings. My telephone number is on the enclosed card.

With kind regards, and I hope with the beginning of better relations,

Yours sincerely,

C. Pell-Windham

[Pencil note at foot in Amberly's hand: "Replied 21/9. Lunch 3 Oct. Tell Board. — F.A."]

documents.title: Oriel Foundation Awards $1.2 Million for Collections Digitisation
documents.summary: 1998 release announcing Oriel Foundation grant OF-1998-114 funding a digitisation project led by Joaquin Ferrer.
documents.body:
Oriel Foundation Awards $1.2 Million for Collections Digitisation

Port Calder, 16 February 1998

The Meridian Institute has received a grant of $1.2 million from the Oriel Foundation to photograph, catalogue and publish digital records of its principal collections over the next four years. The award, grant reference OF-1998-114, is the largest the Foundation has made to a cultural institution since it was established by the Oriel family in 1966.

The project will be led by Joaquin Ferrer, head of the Institute's Conservation Studio, working with the Department of Astronomy and Navigation, the Natural History department and the Institute Library. Mr. Ferrer said the first priority would be the objects most at risk from handling: "Every time a researcher turns a page of a two-hundred-year-old logbook or unrolls a chart, we lose a little of it. A good digital surrogate means the original can stay in the dark."

Scope of the project

PhaseYearsMaterial
11998–1999Maps, charts, ships' logs and manuscript atlases
21999–2000Aldane Herbarium sheets surviving from the 1962 fire
32000–2001Harrow Point photographic plates (about 31,000)
42001–2002Natural history catalogue cards and expedition field notebooks

The grant will fund two photographers, a cataloguer, a database developer and the purchase of a high-resolution copy stand and a flatbed scanner capable of handling glass plates. The Institute will contribute staff time and storage.

The Director, Dr. Felix Amberly, described the award as "a turning point in how we share what we hold. For most of our history, if you wanted to see the Institute's collections you had to come to Wrenfield Street and ask. By 2002, a schoolteacher in any town on the coast will be able to look at them."

Related work

The digitisation project will run alongside the Meridian Oral History Project, a volunteer effort beginning this spring to record the memories of former staff, docents and members. The oral history recordings are not funded by the Oriel grant, but the Institute hopes to include transcripts in the online catalogue once the database is in place.

  • Grant maker: The Oriel Foundation, Port Calder
  • Amount: $1,200,000 over four years
  • Project lead: Joaquin Ferrer
  • Expected completion: 2002

A spokesperson for the Oriel Foundation said the trustees had been impressed by "a clear plan, realistic costs and a genuine commitment to public access."

documents.title: Director's memorandum: renaming of the Conservation Studio (1999)
documents.summary: Internal memorandum renaming the Conservation Studio as the Conservation and Collections Care Division from February 1999.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
INTERNAL MEMORANDUM

To: All staff
From: Dr. Felix Amberly, Director
Copy: Board of Trustees; Joaquin Ferrer, Head of Conservation; Registrar
Date: 12 January 1999
Subject: Renaming of the Conservation Studio and transfer of collections management

1. With effect from 1 February 1999, the Conservation Studio will be renamed the Conservation and Collections Care Division.

2. The Division will continue to be led by Joaquin Ferrer, who will take the title Head of Conservation and Collections Care.

3. REASONS FOR THE CHANGE

3.1 The Conservation Studio was founded in 1963, in the aftermath of the fire, to repair damaged objects. Its name reflects that origin. Over the past decade, and especially since Mr. Ferrer succeeded to the headship, the emphasis of its work has moved steadily from treating individual objects to caring for the collection as a whole - controlling light, temperature and humidity, improving storage, reducing handling, and planning for emergencies.

3.2 The digitisation programme begun last year has made clear that documentation, storage and conservation cannot be managed separately. Objects are being moved, examined and imaged in large numbers and need a single team responsible for their safety.

3.3 The name "Studio" has caused some confusion with external partners, several of whom have assumed it is an art studio or a photographic studio.

4. TRANSFER OF STAFF

4.1 The collections management team (four posts), currently within the Registrar's office, will transfer to the new Division on 1 February. The Registrar will retain responsibility for acquisitions, accession registers and loans agreements.

4.2 No posts are affected other than by change of line management.

5. PRACTICAL MATTERS

5.1 Signage in the Rautio Wing lower ground floor will be changed during February.

5.2 Please use the new name in all correspondence, reports and publications from 1 February. The abbreviation CCCD may be used internally.

5.3 Existing stationery may be used until stocks run out.

6. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Mr. Ferrer and his staff for their exceptional work over the past year, and to acknowledge once again the legacy of the Studio's founder, whose standards remain the foundation of all that the Division does.

F. Amberly
Director

documents.title: Memo: Relocation of the Threlkeld Star Atlas to Vault C3
documents.summary: 2014 internal memo recording the move of the Threlkeld Star Atlas from the Map Room to climate-controlled Vault C3.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
INTERNAL MEMORANDUM

From:    Imogen Kells, Head, Conservation and Collections Care Division
To:      Dr. Nadia Corrow, Director
Copy:    Dr. Ines Halloran, Curator of Astronomy
         Tamsin Rourke, Institute Archivist
         Facilities Manager, Wrenfield Street
Date:    5 August 2014
Subject: Relocation of the Threlkeld Star Atlas to Vault C3 -- completion report

1. Summary

The Threlkeld Star Atlas was moved from its display case in the Map Room to Vault C3 on 29 July 2014. The move was completed without incident. The atlas will not return to open display. This memo records the reasons for the move, the procedure followed and the arrangements for access.

2. Background

Environmental monitoring in the Map Room over the past three years has shown relative humidity swings of up to 18 percent across a single day in summer, driven by the ageing west-wing air handling plant and by visitor numbers. The atlas is especially vulnerable. Its plates were water-damaged in the 1962 fire and, although the restoration carried out between 1963 and 1967 was excellent for its time, the repaired areas respond to humidity differently from the undamaged paper. Our condition survey in March found new cockling on eleven plates and slight lifting of the restoration tissue on plates 23 and 41.

The Director approved the move in May on the recommendation of this Division and the Curator of Astronomy.

3. Vault C3

Vault C3 is the smallest of the climate-controlled vaults built in the basement of the Rautio Wing during the 2007-2008 renovation. It is held at 18 degrees C and 45 percent relative humidity, with a tolerance of plus or minus 3 percent, and has independent monitoring and a gas fire-suppression system. Until now it has held photographic negatives and the most fragile herbarium sheets.

4. Procedure

- The atlas was assessed and photographed plate by plate on 21-25 July.
- It was packed in a custom-made archival box with a padded cradle supporting the binding.
- It was moved by lift and trolley on the morning of 29 July, before opening hours, accompanied by two conservators and a security officer.
- On arrival it was acclimatised for 48 hours in a buffer enclosure before being placed on the vault shelving.

5. Display

The Curator of Astronomy has asked to show the atlas in "Stars Above Calder" at the Harrow Point visitor centre. The Division cannot support loan of the original. A full-size facsimile has been produced from the 1998-2002 digitisation images, printed on archival paper and bound to match. The facsimile will be displayed in the exhibition and will then replace the original in the Map Room case with an explanatory label.

6. Access

Researchers may consult the original only with the written approval of the Curator of Astronomy and in the presence of a conservator, in the vault anteroom. For almost all purposes the digital images should be sufficient.

7. Other items

At the same time, the Harrow octant and two nineteenth-century charts from the Map Room were assessed. Both were found stable and remain on display. We recommend that the Map Room environmental controls be replaced in the next capital programme; until then, no further paper items should be added to the room.

I. Kells

documents.title: Rhea Oduya named director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory
documents.summary: 2015 news release announcing Dr. Rhea Oduya as MOL director, succeeding Dr. Priya Sandoval.
documents.body:
Rhea Oduya named director of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory

News release — The Meridian Institute, Port Calder — 1 July 2015

The Meridian Institute today announced the appointment of Dr. Rhea Oduya as director of MOL, the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory at Brannock Bay. She takes up the post immediately, succeeding Dr. Priya Sandoval, who retires after twenty years as director.

Dr. Oduya, a marine geophysicist, joined MOL in 2009 and has led its seabed mapping group since 2011. She is the laboratory's fourth director since its foundation in 1947, following Ottilie Brandt, Tobias Wren and Priya Sandoval.

“Rhea has built one of the most capable mapping teams on this coast in just a few years,” said Dr. Nadia Corrow, Director of the Meridian Institute. “She understands both the value of MOL's long records and the opportunities new technology is opening up. We are delighted.”

Dr. Oduya said: “I first came to Brannock Bay on a school trip, and I have never quite left. My priority is to keep MOL a place where research comes first, while opening our work to many more people in Port Calder.”

Dr. Sandoval's tenure

During Dr. Sandoval's directorship, from 1995 to 2015, the laboratory:

  • founded the Ferrow Marsh Field Station (1995);
  • acquired the research vessel RV Tern (2004);
  • expanded its work into coastal ecology and climate change;
  • established joint doctoral supervision with partner universities.

Dr. Sandoval will remain associated with MOL as an emeritus scientist.

Laboratory directors

DirectorTerm
Ottilie Brandt1947–1972
Tobias Wren1972–1995
Priya Sandoval1995–2015
Rhea Oduya2015–

About Dr. Oduya

Dr. Oduya grew up in Port Calder's harbour district and holds a doctorate in marine geophysics. Before joining MOL she held postdoctoral positions abroad working on continental-margin sediment systems. At Brannock Bay she introduced multibeam seabed mapping, led the 2011–2012 survey of the Brannock Bay approaches, and began the digitisation of the laboratory's archive of echo-sounder records dating back to the 1950s. She is a regular speaker in the Institute's public lecture programme and has served on the scientific committee of several national marine research bodies.

Media contact: Communications Office, The Meridian Institute, 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder.

documents.title: Annual Report 2016
documents.summary: The Institute's 2016 annual report, covering programmes, research, the final Brisk restoration payment, finances and 212,000 visitors.
documents.body:
The Meridian Institute: Annual Report 2016

For the year ended 31 December 2016. Presented to the Board of Governors and the members of the Institute, March 2017.

Contents

  • 1. Statement from the Chair
  • 2. The Director's review
  • 3. Exhibitions and public programmes
  • 4. Learning
  • 5. Collections and conservation
  • 6. Research
  • 7. Visitors and audiences
  • 8. People
  • 9. Finance
  • 10. Governance
  • 11. Supporters

1. Statement from the Chair

It is my privilege, for the ninth year, to introduce the Institute's annual report on behalf of the Board of Governors. 2016 was not a year of great openings or anniversaries. It was, instead, a year of steady work, and I want to begin by thanking the staff and volunteers who did it. Institutions like ours are judged by their big moments — a centenary, a new wing, a famous exhibition — but they are sustained by thousands of small ones: a conservator re-housing a box of herbarium sheets, a technician keeping a tide gauge running through a winter storm, a volunteer explaining for the hundredth time why the whale in the atrium has no teeth.

The Board met six times during the year. Its main business was the adoption of a revised investment policy for the endowment, the approval of a five-year capital programme for the Wrenfield Street building, and oversight of the final stage of our commitments to the Brisk Family Trust, which I describe below. The Board also agreed to begin the search, in due course, for a successor to our Director, Dr. Nadia Corrow, who has told us that she intends to retire within the next three years. There is no hurry, and Dr. Corrow has asked me to say that she is not going anywhere soon.

Finally, a word about governance. When I became chair in 2008, the Institute's Board had twenty-four members, no fixed terms and no register of the conditions attached to the gifts we hold. It now has fifteen members serving fixed terms, and every restricted gift the Institute has received since 1911 is recorded, with its conditions, in a register reviewed each year by our external reviewers. These are not glamorous reforms, but they are the reason I can report with confidence that every dollar of restricted income spent in 2016 was spent as its donors intended. — Evelyn Marchbank, Chair of the Board of Governors

2. The Director's review

Every year I try to answer one question in this review: is the Meridian Institute doing what Port Calder needs it to do? In 2016 I think the answer was yes, with some qualifications.

Our public programmes were strong. The two main temporary exhibitions of the year, described in section 3, drew larger audiences than we had forecast, and our schools programme reached more children than in any year since records began. The Harrow Point Public Observatory, now in its ninth year, continued to grow, and I am pleased to report that the Friends of the Meridian passed eight thousand member households for the first time.

Our research was productive. The Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory completed its second full year under Dr. Rhea Oduya and, as I report in section 6, secured the largest external research grant in its history late in the year. Our astronomers published eleven papers, and the two Brisk Research Fellows appointed in 2015 are both now well established.

The qualification is the building. Parts of the Wrenfield Street west wing, including the Map Room, still depend on heating and ventilation plant installed in the 1960s. Our conservators have been warning for several years that the environment in those rooms is not good enough for the most fragile objects, and in 2014 we had to move the Threlkeld Star Atlas into a climate-controlled vault for its own protection. The capital programme approved by the Board this year begins to address these problems, but it will take until the early 2020s to complete.

I also want to record the retirement, in December, of Dr. Marian Castel, our Curator of Ethnography since 1994. Marian built the Calder Coast Collection almost from nothing, and she was, for twenty-two years, the Institute's conscience on the question of whose history we tell. We will miss her in staff meetings, where she never let a discussion of galleries pass without asking who the galleries were for. — Dr. Nadia Corrow, Director

3. Exhibitions and public programmes

The Institute presented two major temporary exhibitions and five smaller displays in 2016.

"Salt and Silver: Photographs of the Calder Coast, 1880–1960" (February–August) drew on the photographic holdings of the Calder Coast Collection and on loans from families along the coast. It included the earliest known photographs of the Lantern Quay warehouses and a series of portraits of cannery workers from the 1930s. The exhibition was curated by Dr. Marian Castel and was her last major project for the Institute.

"Weather Makers" (September 2016–February 2017) explored the history of weather observation on the Calder coast, from the handwritten barometer readings in nineteenth-century ships' logs to the automated stations operated today by the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory. It was designed as a family exhibition and included a working weather station on the Rautio Wing roof, with live readings displayed in the gallery.

Smaller displays included a case of recent acquisitions in the entrance hall, a display on the history of the Friends of the Meridian, and a small show at the Harrow Point Public Observatory on the planets visible during the year.

The public lecture series, which dates back to the 1960s, continued on the first Thursday of each month. The best-attended lecture of the year, by Dr. Ines Halloran, Curator of Astronomy, was on the history of comet hunting at Harrow Point. More than four hundred people attended, and the talk was repeated in November.

Free Sunday afternoon admission to the Wrenfield Street galleries, a policy that dates back to the directorship of Dr. Margit Oster-Lind, was maintained. About 19 percent of our visitors at Wrenfield Street came on free Sundays.

4. Learning

We welcomed 38,200 schoolchildren on organised visits across our three sites, an increase of 6 percent on 2015. Every primary school in Port Calder visited at least once. The learning team also ran holiday workshops, a teachers' summer institute and a new programme of "science on the shore" sessions at Brannock Bay for secondary students.

The online collections catalogue, first created with the help of an Oriel Foundation grant in the late 1990s, was used by more than 1,400 teachers. We began work on a new version, to be launched in 2018, which will include lesson plans for every major gallery.

The Harrow Point Public Observatory ran 92 public viewing nights, of which 61 had clear enough skies for telescope viewing. Daytime solar sessions reached 4,100 schoolchildren.

5. Collections and conservation

The Conservation and Collections Care Division treated 1,212 objects during the year, of which 186 were full treatments and the remainder surveys, re-housing or minor stabilisation. Major projects included:

  • the re-housing of about 2,600 sheets from the Aldane Herbarium into new acid-free folders, completing a project begun in 2013;
  • conservation of the cannery wage books transferred to the Calder Coast Collection;
  • a full condition survey of the fin whale skeleton in the Rautio Wing atrium, which recommended that the skeleton be lowered and re-hung on a new armature within the next three years;
  • continued environmental monitoring of the Map Room.

We acquired 214 objects by gift or purchase. The most significant were a group of fourteen letters written by Captain Josiah Harrow to his wife between 1889 and 1893, purchased at auction with the support of the Friends of the Meridian, and a collection of 320 photographic negatives of the Brisk Canneries, given by a former employee.

Loans out included two charts to a national maritime exhibition and three Graye seabird specimens to a university study of historic plumage.

Storage remains the Division's greatest concern. The basement vaults built beneath the Rautio Wing during the 2007–2008 renovation are now almost full, and the off-site store on the city's industrial estate is not climate-controlled. The Division has prepared a ten-year collections storage plan, which the Board will consider in 2017, recommending a new purpose-built store shared with other Port Calder heritage organisations.

6. Research

The Institute's research departments published 34 peer-reviewed papers during the year.

Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory. Under its director, Dr. Rhea Oduya, the laboratory maintained its long-running tide, temperature and salinity records at Brannock Bay and in the Calder Estuary, and continued its salt-marsh monitoring at Ferrow Marsh. In December 2016 the laboratory was awarded a grant of $740,000 by the National Maritime Heritage Board for a survey of the Ossery Trench, to be carried out in 2017 jointly with Tollan College of Marine Science. It is the largest external research grant the laboratory has ever received, and the first return to the trench by an Institute team since the 1970s.

Department of Astronomy and Navigation. The department continued its programme on the history of navigation, including a study of the Corvina logbook's astronomical observations, and its contemporary work on sky brightness and light pollution over the Calder coast. Dr. Ines Halloran's team completed the cataloguing of the Harrow Point plate archive.

Natural History. The department published a revised checklist of the birds of the Isle of Graye, comparing specimens collected in the 1930s with modern surveys and documenting the loss of two breeding species.

Brisk Research Fellowships. The two current Brisk Research Fellows, Dr. Tomasz Rendell (seabird ecology) and Dr. Ayesha Quarrie (history of astronomy), both completed the first year of their two-year fellowships. The fellowships are funded from the income of the Brisk endowment and were created in 2011.

7. Visitors and audiences

Visitor numbers are counted by our ticketing system at Wrenfield Street and at Harrow Point, and by head count at Brannock Bay open days. Free-entry visitors are issued zero-price tickets and are included in the totals.

The Institute welcomed a total of 212,000 visitors across its three sites in 2016, the highest number in its history and an increase of 7.4 percent on 2015.

Site20152016
Wrenfield Street galleries160,900171,300
Harrow Point Public Observatory30,10033,900
Brannock Bay open days6,4006,800
Total197,400212,000

Our visitor survey found that 58 percent of visitors lived in Port Calder or within 30 km of it, 29 percent came from elsewhere in the country, and 13 percent from overseas. Satisfaction remained high, with 91 percent of respondents rating their visit good or excellent. The most common complaint was the queue for the cafe.

Online, the Institute's website received 1.3 million visits, and the collections catalogue recorded 410,000 object views.

8. People

At the end of 2016 the Institute employed 203 staff (full-time equivalent) and was supported by 412 active volunteers, who gave more than 41,000 hours of their time.

Dr. Leonie Farrant, who has managed the Harrow Point Public Observatory since it reopened in 2008, was appointed Deputy Director in October, with responsibility for public programmes, learning and visitor services. She is succeeded at Harrow Point by Owen Petrakis, formerly the observatory's education officer.

Dr. Marian Castel retired as Curator of Ethnography in December after twenty-two years. The Calder Coast Collection has been placed in the care of the Institute Archivist, Tamsin Rourke, while the curatorial structure is reviewed.

Gregory Stath completed his eleventh year as Chief Financial Officer.

We record with sadness the deaths during the year of two long-serving volunteer guides, and of a former member of the Board of Governors.

9. Finance

The Institute recorded a small operating surplus of $186,000 on total income of $15.9 million. The surplus has been transferred to the building reserve.

Income$ thousands
Admissions and memberships4,880
Trading (shop, cafe, events)2,140
Grants for research2,960
Gifts and donations1,730
Endowment income2,990
Municipal support1,200
Total15,900
Expenditure$ thousands
Research5,120
Exhibitions and public programmes3,310
Collections and conservation2,470
Learning1,090
Buildings and operations2,860
Administration674
Total15,714

Endowment. The market value of the endowment at 31 December 2016 was $54.2 million. The Board adopted a revised investment policy during the year, setting a spending rate of 4 percent of a three-year rolling average of the endowment's value.

The Brisk Family Trust. In June 2016 the Institute paid the fifth and final instalment of the $3.4 million it agreed in 2011 to restore to the Brisk endowment. With this payment the Institute has met every financial obligation under the settlement. The joint review committee of the Trust and the Institute met in November and confirmed that all Brisk income in 2016 had been spent on scientific research and scientific instruments, principally the Brisk Research Fellowships, new sensors at Brannock Bay and a camera for the Harrow Point Pell Refractor. Maud Brisk, chair of the Trust, attended the committee's meeting and afterwards wrote to the Director that the Trust considered the matter "closed, and closed well."

10. Governance

The Board of Governors at 31 December 2016:

  • Evelyn Marchbank (Chair)
  • Rafael Quint (Vice-chair; Chair, Finance and Investment)
  • Dr. Hana Lowry
  • Colm Aspinall
  • Prof. Aurelio Banks
  • Judith Carrow-Mayne
  • Dr. Emeka Salt
  • and eight further governors listed on our website

The Institute's statutes limit governors to three consecutive terms of four years.

11. Supporters

The Institute is grateful to all those who supported its work in 2016, including the Port Calder Municipal Council, the Oriel Foundation, the National Maritime Heritage Board, the Brisk Family Trust, the Friends of the Meridian and more than two thousand individual donors.

Looking ahead. Three priorities will shape the Institute's work in 2017. First, the Ossery Trench Survey: the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory will spend the first half of the year preparing equipment, recruiting a sea-going team and planning stations, with the voyage itself scheduled for late summer. Second, the exhibition marking seventy years of the laboratory, planned for 2018, will move from outline to detailed design; its working title is "Deep Meridian." Third, the capital programme for the Wrenfield Street building will begin with surveys of the west wing roof and the environmental plant serving the Map Room and the adjacent galleries.

The Board also expects to consider, during 2017, whether the Department of Astronomy and Navigation and the physical oceanography work at Brannock Bay should be brought closer together. Our scientists increasingly work across that boundary — on coastal weather, on sea level and on light over the water — and several have suggested that a joint structure would help them compete for grants. No decision has been taken, and the Director has asked both groups to consult widely before any proposal comes to the Board.

A note on the Harrow Point Public Observatory. 2016 marked a change of leadership at the observatory, which has grown under Dr. Farrant's management from an experimental Friday-night programme into a year-round education centre. Its visitor centre now hosts a permanent display on the history of observing on the headland, including a replica of the brass meridian line in the dome floor from which the Institute takes its name, and a small gallery of photographic plates from the observatory's research years. The observatory's success has been one of the clearest demonstrations that a site no longer suited to research can still serve the Institute's scientific mission by sharing it with the public.

The Friends of the Meridian gave $265,000 during the year, including $48,000 toward the purchase of the Harrow letters and $120,000 for the schools programme. Their volunteers staffed the information desk every day the galleries were open.

The Meridian Institute, 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder.

documents.title: Annual Report 2017
documents.summary: The Institute's 2017 annual report: the Ossery Trench Survey, 231,500 visitors and a revised 2016 visitor figure of 208,400.
documents.body:
The Meridian Institute: Annual Report 2017

For the year ended 31 December 2017. Presented to the Board of Governors and the members of the Institute, March 2018.

Contents

  • 1. Statement from the Chair
  • 2. The Director's review
  • 3. Exhibitions and public programmes
  • 4. Learning
  • 5. Research
  • 6. Collections and conservation
  • 7. Visitors and audiences
  • 8. People
  • 9. Finance
  • 10. Governance and supporters

1. Statement from the Chair

For much of the Institute's history, the phrase "going to sea" meant something quite literal to the people who worked here. The founder was a shipowner; the first great expeditions sailed in his company's ships; the oceanographic laboratory at Brannock Bay was founded by a scientist who spent her early career on survey vessels. In 2017 the Institute went to sea again, in the most ambitious research voyage it has undertaken in almost fifty years, and I want to begin by congratulating everyone who made it possible.

The Board met six times during the year. Its main business was oversight of the first stage of the capital programme for the Wrenfield Street building, the approval of the budget for the exhibition that will open in April 2018 to mark seventy years of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory, and preparation for the leadership transitions that lie ahead of us. In particular, the Board noted with regret the decision of our Chief Financial Officer, Gregory Stath, to leave the Institute in the summer of 2018, and it has begun the search for his successor.

I also wish to draw members' attention to a correction to last year's report, explained in section 7. We found during the year that our ticketing system had counted some visitors twice in 2016, and we have revised the figure we published. I would rather report a smaller number accurately than a larger one wrongly, and I am grateful to the staff who found and fixed the problem. — Evelyn Marchbank, Chair of the Board of Governors

2. The Director's review

The Institute's work in 2017 fell, as it usually does, into two halves that do not always sit comfortably together. On one side, a museum on Wrenfield Street and a public observatory on Harrow Point that between them welcomed more visitors than in any previous year. On the other, research laboratories whose work is largely invisible to those visitors, which this year produced some of the most exciting results in the Institute's recent history.

I have spent much of my directorship arguing that these two halves are one institution, and that each needs the other. Our visitors come, in large part, because we are not just a museum: because the tide gauge readings on the screen in the atrium are real and live, because the astronomer giving the Thursday lecture has just come back from the telescope. And our scientists benefit, more than they sometimes admit, from an institution that can explain their work to the public, and from the political and financial support that public affection brings. But the tension is real. Every dollar spent on a gallery is not spent on a laboratory, and the Institute has not always been careful about the difference. We have learned from that, and in 2017 I think we got the balance right.

My thanks go to all our staff and volunteers, and in particular to the crew and scientists of the Ossery Trench Survey, whose work I describe in section 5. — Dr. Nadia Corrow, Director

3. Exhibitions and public programmes

The main temporary exhibition of the year was "The Map and the Territory" (March–October), which paired charts from the Institute's collection with modern satellite images of the same coasts. It included a nineteenth-century chart of Kittering Sound, several of the Institute's ships' logs, and the facsimile of the Threlkeld Star Atlas produced in 2014. It was curated by the Department of Astronomy and Navigation with the Institute Archivist, Tamsin Rourke.

From November, the galleries hosted "Seventy Years at Brannock Bay: A Preview," a small display introducing the major exhibition planned for 2018 on the history of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory. The preview included a replica of an early current meter and a film about the laboratory's founding in 1947.

The Harrow Point Public Observatory ran a special programme for the total lunar eclipse in the autumn, which was watched by 1,900 people on the headland lawns, the largest crowd in the observatory's history.

The public lecture series continued on the first Thursday of each month. Free Sunday afternoon admission was maintained.

4. Learning

We welcomed 40,100 schoolchildren on organised visits across our three sites. The "science on the shore" programme at Brannock Bay, piloted in 2016, was expanded to twenty secondary schools. During the Ossery Trench Survey the learning team ran live video links from the research vessel to eleven Port Calder classrooms, in which students questioned scientists at sea about their work.

Work continued on the new online collections catalogue, now due to launch in the second half of 2018.

5. Research

The Ossery Trench Survey. Between August and October 2017, the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory carried out the first detailed survey of the Ossery Trench, the deep-sea trench that lies about 120 km off the Calder coast. The survey was co-led by Dr. Rhea Oduya, Director of the laboratory, and Professor Aurelio Banks of Tollan College of Marine Science, and was funded by a $740,000 grant from the National Maritime Heritage Board, awarded at the end of 2016.

Working from the research vessel RV Tern, the team used multibeam sonar to map about 1,900 square kilometres of the trench and its walls, reaching depths of 3,450 metres. They also collected water samples, sediment cores and, with a small remotely operated vehicle, more than 600 biological specimens. Early results suggest that the trench floor supports a richer community of amphipods and sea cucumbers than had been expected, and that its northern wall has been shaped by large submarine landslides.

The survey was the first Institute expedition to the trench since the dredging voyage led by Dr. Tobias Wren in 1970. Several of the stations sampled in 1970 were re-occupied to allow comparison between the two sets of results. A full report will be published in 2018, and selected specimens will feature in next year's exhibition.

Life aboard the RV Tern was not always comfortable. The survey lost six days to an autumn gale in late September, when the vessel sheltered in the lee of the Isle of Graye, and one of the two sediment corers was damaged beyond repair on its fourth deployment. The team adapted by extending the sonar mapping into the gale-lost days as soon as the sea allowed, and by borrowing a replacement corer from Tollan College, which was flown to the nearest port and brought out by the vessel's tender. Dr. Oduya wrote afterwards that "the trench was generous and the weather was not," and that the survey's success owed a great deal to the ship's crew and to the graduate students from both institutions who kept the laboratory running around the clock.

The survey's data are being shared openly. Bathymetric grids will be deposited with national data centres once the report is published, and the biological specimens will be divided between the Institute's collections and those of Tollan College under an agreement signed before the voyage. The Institute's share will be accessioned into the natural history collections in 2018.

Department of Astronomy and Navigation. The department continued its sky-brightness monitoring and published a study of the astronomical observations recorded in nineteenth-century Port Calder ships' logs. Dr. Ines Halloran was elected to the council of a national astronomical society.

Natural History. The department completed the re-identification of the bird collections from the 1934 and 1936 Graye expeditions.

Brisk Research Fellowships. Dr. Tomasz Rendell and Dr. Ayesha Quarrie completed their fellowships in the autumn. Two new Brisk Research Fellows will be appointed in 2018.

6. Collections and conservation

The Conservation and Collections Care Division treated 1,340 objects. It began planning the lowering and re-hanging of the fin whale skeleton in the Rautio Wing atrium, now scheduled for 2019, and completed the conservation of the fourteen Harrow letters purchased in 2016. The Division also supported the Ossery Trench Survey by preparing preservation protocols for specimens collected at sea.

We acquired 187 objects, including a ship's chronometer from a Port Calder trawler and a collection of drawings of Brannock Bay by a local artist.

7. Visitors and audiences

Correction to the 2016 figures. In reviewing ticketing data during 2017, our visitor services team discovered that combined tickets, which allow a visitor to enter both the Wrenfield Street galleries and the Harrow Point Public Observatory on the same day, had been counted once at each site and once again when the combined ticket was sold. As a result, 3,600 visits to Harrow Point in 2016 were double-counted. The corrected total for 2016 is 208,400, not the 212,000 published in last year's report. The error has been fixed and the counting method has been independently checked.

In 2017 the Institute welcomed 231,500 visitors across its three sites, an increase of 11.1 percent on the corrected 2016 figure and the highest total in its history.

Site2016 (as published)2016 (revised)2017
Wrenfield Street galleries171,300171,300186,200
Harrow Point Public Observatory33,90030,30037,400
Brannock Bay open days6,8006,8007,900
Total212,000208,400231,500
