Visitor satisfaction remained at 91 percent. The lunar eclipse evening and the school holidays in August produced the busiest days of the year at Harrow Point and Wrenfield Street respectively.

8. People

At the end of 2017 the Institute employed 207 staff (full-time equivalent) and was supported by 438 active volunteers.

Gregory Stath, Chief Financial Officer since 2005, announced that he will leave the Institute in the summer of 2018 to become finance director of a hospital trust. Over thirteen years he oversaw the Institute's finances through the 2007–2008 gallery renovation, the centenary and the growth of the endowment. The Board and the Director thank him for his service.

Dr. Leonie Farrant completed her first full year as Deputy Director. The review of curatorial structure following the retirement of the Curator of Ethnography was completed, and the Board agreed to create a new post of Curator of Coastal History from 2018.

9. Finance

The Institute recorded an operating surplus of $242,000 on total income of $16.8 million.

Income$ thousands
Admissions and memberships5,260
Trading (shop, cafe, events)2,310
Grants for research3,420
Gifts and donations1,580
Endowment income3,030
Municipal support1,200
Total16,800

The market value of the endowment at 31 December 2017 was $56.9 million. Income from the Brisk endowment was spent entirely on research posts and scientific instruments, as confirmed by the joint review committee.

10. Governance and supporters

Evelyn Marchbank continued as Chair of the Board of Governors, with Rafael Quint as Vice-chair. Two new governors joined the Board during the year.

The Board's committees met regularly throughout the year. The finance and investment committee, chaired by Rafael Quint, reviewed the performance of the endowment each quarter and began the handover planning for the Chief Financial Officer's departure. The collections committee approved all acquisitions above $10,000 and reviewed the Conservation and Collections Care Division's plans for the fin whale skeleton. The nominations and governance committee, chaired by Evelyn Marchbank, began to consider the skills the Board will need as the Institute approaches a change of Director in the next few years, and recommended that at least one future governor should have direct experience of running a scientific research organisation.

The restricted-funds register, introduced in 2011, was reviewed by our external reviewers in February 2018. They found that every restricted gift received in 2017 had been recorded with its conditions and that all restricted income had been spent in accordance with those conditions. They made two minor recommendations about the recording of gifts in kind, both of which have been adopted.

11. The Friends of the Meridian

The Friends of the Meridian, the membership society founded in 1949, ended the year with 8,410 member households, a new record. Friends volunteers staffed the information desk at Wrenfield Street every day the galleries were open, ran the Saturday children's club and provided the stewards for every public viewing night at Harrow Point. The Friends gave $282,000 to the Institute during the year, including $90,000 toward the classroom video links used during the Ossery Trench Survey, $60,000 for the conservation of the Harrow letters and $110,000 for the schools programme.

The Friends' annual lecture, given in October by Professor Aurelio Banks, described the first results of the survey to an audience of more than five hundred members in the lecture theatre and a further overflow room. Many members will remember that the Friends were founded by volunteer guides who wanted to do more for the Institute than simply visit it; seventy years later, that spirit is undiminished.

12. The year in numbers

Measure2017
Visitors, all sites231,500
Schoolchildren on organised visits40,100
Public viewing nights at Harrow Point96
Peer-reviewed papers37
Objects treated by conservators1,340
Objects acquired187
Active volunteers438
Friends of the Meridian households8,410

13. Looking ahead to 2018

The year ahead will be one of the busiest in the Institute's recent history. In April we will open "Deep Meridian," the largest exhibition we have staged since the centenary, telling the story of seventy years of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory from its founding at Brannock Bay in 1947 to the Ossery Trench Survey. The exhibition will fill both temporary galleries and part of the Rautio Wing atrium, and it will be accompanied by a programme of lectures, family days and a new learning resource for secondary schools.

The full scientific report of the Ossery Trench Survey will be published in the middle of the year, and the first papers describing the specimens collected are expected to follow. The laboratory is already planning follow-up work, including a proposal for long-term instrument moorings on the trench wall.

The first phase of the Wrenfield Street capital programme, the replacement of the roof over the west wing, will begin in the summer. The Map Room and adjacent galleries will close for part of the work, and the most sensitive objects on display there will be moved temporarily into store. The second phase, the replacement of the west wing's environmental plant, is planned for 2019 and 2020 and will, we hope, allow some of the most fragile paper collections to return to public view in better conditions than they have ever had.

A new Chief Financial Officer will join the Institute in the summer, and two new Brisk Research Fellows will begin their fellowships in the autumn. The Board will also begin, in consultation with the Director, the process of planning for her eventual succession.

We are grateful, as always, to the people of Port Calder, whose support has carried the Institute for more than a century.

The Institute's supporters in 2017 were as generous as ever, and we record our thanks here.

The Institute thanks the National Maritime Heritage Board, Tollan College of Marine Science, the Port Calder Municipal Council, the Oriel Foundation, the Brisk Trust, the Friends of the Meridian and all our individual donors and members.

The Meridian Institute, 14 Wrenfield Street, Port Calder.

documents.title: Dr. Idris Palk Appointed Director of the Meridian Institute
documents.summary: May 2019 announcement that Dr. Idris Palk will succeed Dr. Nadia Corrow as the Institute's seventh director.
documents.body:
Dr. Idris Palk Appointed Director of the Meridian Institute

Port Calder, 20 May 2019

The Board of Governors of the Meridian Institute today announced the appointment of Dr. Idris Palk as the Institute's seventh Director. Dr. Palk succeeds Dr. Nadia Corrow, who retires at the end of this month after fifteen years in the post. He takes up the appointment on 1 June 2019.

Dr. Palk, 52, is a geophysicist by training. He comes to Port Calder from the Halvard Museum of Science in Easterly, where he was Director of Collections and Research for eight years and led the museum's move to a new storage and research centre. Before that he spent a decade at sea as a marine geophysicist, including three seasons mapping continental shelf sediments.

"The Meridian is one of the few institutions of its size that still does real science alongside its public work," Dr. Palk said. "I want to keep both halves strong, and I want them to talk to each other more. The laboratory at Brannock Bay and the galleries on Wrenfield Street should feel like one place."

Search process

The appointment follows an international search led by a committee of the Board chaired by Evelyn Marchbank. The committee interviewed six candidates, including two internal applicants. Ms. Marchbank said the Board had been looking for "someone who can lead a research organisation and run a museum, and who can explain to Port Calder why it needs both."

Tributes to Dr. Corrow

The Board paid tribute to Dr. Corrow, whose tenure included the reopening of the Harrow Point site as a public observatory, the centenary in 2011, the "Deep Meridian" exhibition and a near-doubling of school visits. "Nadia steadied the Institute through some difficult years and handed it over in better shape than she found it," Ms. Marchbank said.

documents.title: Rafael Quint Elected Chair of the Board of Governors
documents.summary: July 2020 announcement that Rafael Quint succeeds Evelyn Marchbank as chair of the Institute's Board of Governors.
documents.body:
Rafael Quint Elected Chair of the Board of Governors

Port Calder, 1 July 2020

The Meridian Institute announced today that Rafael Quint has been elected chair of its Board of Governors, succeeding Evelyn Marchbank, who has chaired the Board since 2008 and steps down after completing the maximum of three terms allowed under the Institute's revised statutes.

Mr. Quint, 61, is the former chief executive of the Port Calder Harbour Authority, where he oversaw the expansion of the southern container terminal and the conversion of the old Lantern Quay warehouses into housing and shops. He joined the Board in 2014 and has chaired its finance and investment committee since 2016.

"I grew up two streets from Wrenfield Street and I have been coming to the Institute since before I could read the labels," Mr. Quint said. "The coming years will be hard for every museum. We have closed our doors for three months this spring, our income has fallen sharply and we have to plan for a reopening that will look very different. My job is to make sure the Institute comes out of this with its science and its public mission intact."

Tribute to Evelyn Marchbank

The Director, Dr. Idris Palk, thanked Ms. Marchbank for twelve years of service. "Evelyn chaired this Board through the centenary, through a painful dispute over restricted funds and through two leadership changes. She rebuilt our governance so that the kind of mistake we made in 2007 cannot happen again."

Ms. Marchbank will remain an honorary governor.

documents.title: Institute creates Department of Earth and Sky Sciences
documents.summary: 2022 announcement merging the Department of Astronomy and Navigation with MOL's physical oceanography group into a new Department of Earth and Sky Sciences.
documents.body:
Institute creates Department of Earth and Sky Sciences

News release — The Meridian Institute — 1 February 2022

The Meridian Institute today announced a reorganisation of its research departments. From 1 April 2022, the Department of Astronomy and Navigation and the physical oceanography group of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory will be combined in a new Department of Earth and Sky Sciences.

The new department will be headed by Dr. Ines Halloran, currently Curator of Astronomy. It will bring together the Institute's work on astronomy, navigation, tides, currents and climate, and will be responsible for the historic instrument collection, the Harrow Point public programme, and the long-term tide and current records begun at Brannock Bay in 1949.

MOL — the Ocean Lab at Brannock Bay, as it is known locally — will continue under its director, Dr. Rhea Oduya, with a renewed focus on marine biology, seabed mapping and the deep-water specimen collection. Staff of the physical oceanography group will remain based at Brannock Bay.

Why the change?

  • The two groups already share instruments, historic records and a common interest in measurement of the natural world.
  • The Department of Astronomy and Navigation, founded in 1914, has shrunk to five staff since research observing at Harrow Point ended.
  • A single department will be better placed to compete for climate and environmental research funding.

“This is about putting our strengths together, not about cutting,” said Dr. Idris Palk, Director of the Meridian Institute. “The sky and the sea have been studied side by side at this Institute since 1911. Now they will be in the same department.”

Some staff have expressed concern. In a letter to the board, a group of MOL scientists said the change risked “splitting the laboratory in two.” Dr. Oduya said she supported the reorganisation but would “watch closely that research capacity at Brannock Bay is protected.”

The Meridian Institute: Annual Report 2021

From the Chair

2021 was a year of reopening. Our galleries were closed for eleven weeks at the start of the year and operated under timed entry until September. Through it all our staff kept the collections safe, our scientists kept their long-running measurements going, and our learning team taught more than eight thousand children online. I thank every one of them. — Rafael Quint, Chair of the Board of Governors

From the Director

This year the Board approved the most significant change to the structure of our science in half a century. From 2022, the Department of Astronomy and Navigation and the physical oceanography group of the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory will come together as a single department covering the atmosphere, the ocean surface and the sky. The laboratory at Brannock Bay will continue as the home of our marine biology. We have made this change because our scientists increasingly work across those boundaries — on sea level, on coastal weather, on light pollution over the water — and because a single department can compete better for grants.

We also completed the first year of the reassembled whale skeleton in the atrium, reopened the Harrow Point Public Observatory in June, and welcomed our first two Brisk Research Fellows since the pandemic began. — Dr. Idris Palk, Director

documents.title: Strategic Plan 2023–2028: One Institute, Sea and Sky
documents.summary: The Institute's 2023–2028 strategic plan, addressing research versus museum priorities, the department merger and finances.
documents.body:
THE MERIDIAN INSTITUTE
STRATEGIC PLAN 2023–2028
"ONE INSTITUTE, SEA AND SKY"

Approved by the Board of Trustees, 8 November 2022
Rafael Quint, Chair of the Board
Dr. Idris Palk, Director

-----------------------------------------------------------------
CONTENTS
1. Foreword from the Chair
2. Introduction from the Director
3. Where we are now
4. What we heard
5. Our purpose and our two missions
6. Five strategic aims
7. Organisation
8. Finance
9. Risks
10. Measuring progress
Appendices A-C
-----------------------------------------------------------------

1. FOREWORD FROM THE CHAIR

When Augustin Pell signed the deed that created this Institute in 1911, he gave it a double purpose: to study the sea, the sky and the living shore, and to show them to the people of Port Calder. More than a century later those two purposes are still the heart of what we do. They are also, if we are honest, the source of many of the hardest choices this Board has had to make.

This plan is the first to be prepared since the closures of 2020 and 2021, which tested every part of the Institute. It is also the first since the Board and the Director agreed to reorganise our scientific departments. I want to thank the staff, volunteers, Friends, partners and members of the public who took part in the consultation that shaped it — more than 1,900 people in all.

I commend the plan to everyone who cares about the Institute.

Rafael Quint
Chair of the Board of Trustees

2. INTRODUCTION FROM THE DIRECTOR

I came to the Institute in 2019 knowing its reputation: a museum that people in Port Calder love, and a research institute whose marine science is respected well beyond the coast. What I did not fully appreciate, until I had been here a while, was how often those two identities have been set against each other — in budgets, in buildings, in who gets the space and who gets the credit.

This plan tries to stop treating that tension as a problem to be managed and start treating it as the thing that makes us distinctive. A visitor who stands under the whale skeleton in the Rautio Wing is looking at the result of an expedition, a piece of research, and a conservation project. The research gives the museum its stories; the museum gives the research its public. We want to be "one Institute" in fact as well as in name.

Dr. Idris Palk
Director

3. WHERE WE ARE NOW

3.1 Audiences. After two difficult years, visitor numbers in 2022 are recovering and are forecast to reach about 190,000 by year end — still well short of the record levels of 2017 and 2018. Membership of the Friends of the Meridian has held up well at just over 11,000 households. Online audiences grew by more than 300% during the closures, and many of those users have stayed with us.

3.2 Research. MOL continues to publish strongly, with 41 peer-reviewed papers in 2021, many of them in partnership with the University of Ashcombe and Tollan College of Marine Science. The Ossery Trench data of 2017 are still yielding results. Research in astronomy and navigation, by contrast, has become small and mostly historical since the Harrow Point observatory closed to research in 1996.

3.3 Collections. We care for about 1.1 million objects, specimens and archival items. Around 22% are catalogued to modern standards and about 9% are digitised. The collections stores in the basement of the west wing are full, and several are below the environmental standard we would want.

3.4 Buildings. The Rautio Wing is now more than fifty years old. Its roof and services need major renewal within the plan period. The west wing — the oldest part of the Wrenfield Building — is in reasonable condition following the gallery works of 2007–2008. The MOL building at Brannock Bay needs a new seawater system.

3.5 Staff and volunteers. We employ about 235 people and rely on around 400 volunteers. Staff surveys show strong commitment to the Institute and weaker confidence in how decisions are made across departments.

4. WHAT WE HEARD

The consultation ran from March to June 2022. Among the things we heard most often:

- Visitors want to see more of the science happening now, not only historic objects.
- Scientists want the public galleries to reflect their work, but worry that time spent on exhibitions and outreach is not recognised.
- Staff in the museum departments feel that research gets the prestige and the grant money, while the museum earns the income.
- Members and donors want to know how their money is spent — and in particular that restricted gifts are used as intended.
- Partners value the Institute's long-term data records, especially the tide and current series from Brannock Bay.
- Many people mentioned the history of the building, and the 1962 fire in particular, as part of what makes the Institute matter to them.

5. OUR PURPOSE AND OUR TWO MISSIONS

Our purpose remains unchanged since 1911: the study of the sea, the sky and the living shore, and the display of the same to the people of Port Calder.

We have two missions — research and public engagement — and this plan commits us to treating them as equal and interdependent. The history of the Institute is full of moments when one was allowed to crowd out the other. Some of those moments did lasting harm.

- In 1960 the Board deferred the rewiring of the east wing in order to refit a public gallery. The 1962 fire began in that wing two years later. Whatever the exact chain of cause and effect, the lesson the Institute drew — that safety and care of the collections must never be traded for display — is one we reaffirm.
- In the 1960s and 1970s the "open doors" policy brought the public in as never before, but left research underfunded for a decade.
- In 1996 the observatory at Harrow Point was closed to research, and for twelve years the Institute had no public presence there either.
- In 2007–2008 research income restricted by the Brisk Trust was spent on gallery renovation. The dispute that followed, settled in 2011, cost the Institute money, time and trust. The restitution payments were completed in 2016. We are determined that nothing like it happens again.

Each of these was a case of treating research and museum as competitors for the same resources. This plan sets out a different approach.

6. FIVE STRATEGIC AIMS

AIM 1: SHOW THE SCIENCE
By 2028, every permanent gallery will include a "current research" element, refreshed at least annually, and at least one major temporary exhibition every two years will be built around current Institute research. The model is "Deep Meridian" (2018–2019), which presented seventy years of MOL's work and drew some of our highest visitor figures.
Targets: visitor satisfaction with "learning something new" above 85%; 12 public research events per year at each site.

AIM 2: ONE INSTITUTE, SEA AND SKY
We will complete the reorganisation begun in 2022, in which the Department of Astronomy and Navigation and MOL's physical oceanography group were brought together as the new Department of Earth and Sky Sciences, led by Dr. Ines Halloran. MOL continues at Brannock Bay as the home of our marine biology and ecology research. The new department brings together our work on tides, currents, climate, navigation and the sky — subjects that were never as separate as our old structure suggested — and gives our astronomy collections a research home again. We will review the new structure in 2025.
Targets: joint grant applications between departments; shared seminar series; a single research strategy by 2024.

AIM 3: CARE FOR THE COLLECTIONS
We will create a new collections centre to replace the basement stores, bringing the most vulnerable collections up to modern environmental standards. We will catalogue to modern standards 40% of the collections by 2028, and digitise 20%. The Conservation and Collections Care Division will lead a programme of condition surveys, starting with the manuscripts and the Aldane Herbarium, the latter still carrying the scars of the 1962 fire.
Targets: collections centre business case to Board by 2024; catalogue and digitisation figures reported annually.

AIM 4: A PLACE FOR EVERYONE
We will extend free admission from one Sunday a month to every Sunday, restoring in full the "open doors" principle of Dr. Oster-Lind's directorship. We will expand school programmes at Harrow Point and Brannock Bay, and work with community groups whose histories are under-represented in our galleries and in the Pell Papers and other archives.
Targets: 30% of visitors from the most deprived areas of Port Calder by 2028; 25,000 school visits per year.

AIM 5: A SUSTAINABLE INSTITUTE
We will put the Institute's finances on a footing that protects both missions: see section 8.

7. ORGANISATION

From 2023 the Institute's work will be organised in six units: the Department of Earth and Sky Sciences; the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory; the Department of Natural History; Collections, Archive and Conservation (combining the Map Room, manuscripts, ethnography and the Conservation and Collections Care Division); Public Engagement; and Finance and Operations.

A new Research and Public Programmes Committee, jointly chaired by a head of a scientific department and the head of public engagement, will decide on major exhibitions and the allocation of shared gallery space.

8. FINANCE

8.1 Income. In the year to December 2021 the Institute's total income was $31.8 million, from admissions and trading (about 29%), grants and contracts (about 34%), endowment income (about 17%), the city council (about 9%) and donations and membership (about 11%).

8.2 The endowment. The Institute's endowment funds stood at $61.5 million at 31 December 2021, compared with $48 million at the centenary in 2011. This growth reflects the success of the centenary campaign, the completion of the Brisk restitution, several large bequests and strong investment returns. Around 38% of the endowment is restricted by donors to particular purposes; the largest single restricted element is the capital held by the Brisk Trust, which is separately managed and whose income may be spent only on research and scientific instruments.

8.3 Policy on restricted funds. Following the Brisk dispute, the Board adopted in 2011 a policy that every restricted fund is tracked separately, reported to the Audit Committee each quarter, and confirmed in writing to the donor or their trustees each year. This plan reaffirms that policy and extends it to all grants.

8.4 Spending rule. We will draw no more than 4% of the three-year average endowment value each year.

8.5 Fundraising. We will seek to raise $25 million over the plan period, of which $15 million is for the new collections centre and the Rautio Wing roof, $6 million for research (including new Brisk Research Fellowships to be matched by other donors), and $4 million for free admission and community programmes.

9. RISKS

- Visitor recovery is slower than forecast.
- Capital costs of the building programme rise.
- The reorganisation of departments disrupts research or damages morale.
- Major grants, including from the National Maritime Heritage Board and the Oriel Foundation, are not renewed.
- A collections emergency — fire, flood or environmental failure — in stores that are known to be below standard. The Institute has direct experience of what such an emergency can do.

Each risk has a named owner on the senior management team and is reviewed quarterly by the Board.

The collections risk deserves particular comment. The fire of March 1962 began in a darkroom in the old east wing and destroyed or damaged more than two thousand objects in a single night. The Institute's response — a dedicated conservation unit, a new wing built to the highest fire standards of its time, and a culture of care for the collections that runs through every department — has served it well for sixty years. But the basement stores of the west wing were never rebuilt, and they now hold a large share of the collections in conditions that the Conservation and Collections Care Division has repeatedly described as inadequate. Flood risk in these stores has also increased with rising sea levels and more intense rainfall; the Calder Estuary burst its banks in the Wrenfield district twice in the last decade. For these reasons the Board has placed the new collections centre at the top of the capital programme, ahead of the Rautio Wing roof, and has asked for a costed interim plan to move the most vulnerable material — the manuscripts, the herbarium and the works on paper in the Map Room — to temporary accommodation that meets the current standard before the end of 2024.

10. MEASURING PROGRESS

The Director will report to the Board each year against the targets in this plan, and a summary will be published in the Annual Report. A mid-term review will take place in 2025.

APPENDIX A: SUMMARY OF CONSULTATION RESPONSES

The consultation gathered 1,912 responses: 1,340 online survey responses from members of the public and Friends; 214 staff survey responses; 96 volunteer responses; 31 written submissions from partners, community groups and donors; and notes from 14 public meetings held in Port Calder, Brannock Bay and Vellmoor.

A.1 Public and Friends. Asked what they valued most about the Institute, respondents most often named the whale skeleton and the Rautio Wing atrium (38%), "the feeling of history" in the west wing (27%), family activities (22%) and stargazing at Harrow Point (19%). Asked what they would change, the most common answers were admission prices (31%), more to see about current research (24%), more seating and better cafe facilities (17%), and better public transport to Harrow Point and Brannock Bay (12%). A number of older respondents wrote about the 1962 fire, the Rebuild Meridian appeal and the years when the collections were kept at Vellmoor, and said that the Institute's survival had made it "the city's museum" in a way it had not been before.

A.2 Staff. Staff responses were generally positive about the Institute's mission and colleagues, and more critical about communication between departments and about workloads. Scientists said that time spent on public programmes was not counted in performance reviews; museum staff said that their contribution to the Institute's income was not reflected in their influence. Several respondents from the former Department of Astronomy and Navigation welcomed the merger as a way of reconnecting the astronomy collections with active research; some MOL staff worried that the division of their laboratory would weaken it. Conservation staff pressed for the collections centre as the highest priority of all.

A.3 Volunteers. Volunteers asked for better training, more recognition, and a clearer role in exhibition planning. Many are also members of the Friends of the Meridian, whose volunteer tradition goes back to 1949.

A.4 Partners and donors. The University of Ashcombe and Tollan College of Marine Science both emphasised the importance of the long-term data series at Brannock Bay and asked for commitments that they would be maintained. The Brisk Trust welcomed the Institute's restricted-funds policy and signalled willingness to consider matching funds for new research fellowships. The Oriel Foundation encouraged the Institute to put digitisation and public access at the centre of its collections plans. Community groups asked for greater representation of the fishing and dock communities of the Calder coast in the galleries.

APPENDIX B: HOW THE PLAN WAS PREPARED

The plan was prepared by a working group of the senior management team, chaired by the Director, with two trustees and two staff representatives elected by their colleagues. Drafts were discussed at three Board meetings (March, July and October 2022) and at an all-staff meeting in September 2022. The working group commissioned an independent review of the Institute's buildings, which informed the capital priorities in Aim 3 and section 8.5, and an independent financial review, which informed the spending rule in section 8.4.

APPENDIX C: KEY DATES IN OUR HISTORY
1911  Pell Institute of Natural Philosophy founded at 14 Wrenfield Street
1925  Harrow Point Observatory opens
1929  Institute takes the name The Meridian Institute
1934, 1936  Expeditions to the Isle of Graye
1947  Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory founded at Brannock Bay
1953  Brisk Trust established
1962  Fire destroys the east wing
1968  Rautio Wing opens
1996  Harrow Point Observatory closes to research
2008  Harrow Point reopens as a public observatory
2011  Centenary; Brisk settlement
2017  Ossery Trench Survey
2022  Department of Earth and Sky Sciences formed

documents.title: Dr. Leonie Farrant Becomes Director of the Meridian Institute
documents.summary: September 2023 announcement that deputy director Dr. Leonie Farrant succeeds Dr. Idris Palk as the eighth director.
documents.body:
Dr. Leonie Farrant Becomes Director of the Meridian Institute

Port Calder, 4 September 2023

Dr. Leonie Farrant today took up office as the eighth Director of the Meridian Institute. She succeeds Dr. Idris Palk, who stepped down in July for health reasons after four years as Director.

Dr. Farrant has been Deputy Director of the Institute since 2016, with responsibility for public programmes, learning and visitor services, and has acted as Director since Dr. Palk's departure. The Board of Governors confirmed her appointment at a special meeting on 31 August after what the chair, Rafael Quint, called "a short search that kept coming back to the person already doing the job."

"Leonie knows every corner of this Institute," Mr. Quint said. "She has run our public programmes through a pandemic, she led the planning for the new Department of Earth and Sky Sciences with Idris, and she has the trust of the scientists and the front-of-house staff alike. That combination is rare."

Priorities

In a message to staff, Dr. Farrant set out three priorities for her first year:

  • completing the capital plan for the Wrenfield Street west wing, whose roof and environmental controls date largely from the 1960s;
  • securing long-term funding for the research departments so that they do not depend on year-to-year grants;
  • widening access, including a free-entry evening each week and a new partnership with Port Calder schools.

"Idris set us on a good course and I intend to keep to it," Dr. Farrant said. "The strategic plan the Board adopted last year still stands. My job is to deliver it."

Dr. Palk

The Board thanked Dr. Palk for his leadership through the pandemic years and the 2022 reorganisation of the science departments. He will remain an adviser to the Director on the research programme until the end of the year.

RoleHolder
DirectorDr. Leonie Farrant (from 4 September 2023)
Chair of the BoardRafael Quint
Deputy Director (acting)To be announced

queries.text: How did the way the Meridian Institute is funded change over its history?
queries.answer: It began as one man's patronage: Augustin Pell's endowment of shipping shares and gifts (e.g. the Pell Refractor), with Edmund Pell lending ships for the Graye voyages. Walter Brisk's 1953 $2 million endowment introduced money restricted to research and instruments; after the 1962 fire the city-wide Rebuild Meridian appeal (the Friends raising $185,000) paid for rebuilding. From the 1990s project grants from the Oriel Foundation and the NMHB funded digitisation and research, while the endowment grew to $61.5 million by 2021; the 2009-2011 Brisk lawsuit over $3.4 million spent on galleries led to strict restricted-funds controls.

queries.text: How has the tension between the Institute's research mission and its public museum role played out over time?
queries.answer: The 1911 deed gave the Institute a double purpose of research and display, and the two have repeatedly competed for money and space: in 1960 a gallery refit was preferred to east-wing rewiring, Oster-Lind's 'open doors' policy was criticised for diverting staff from research, and Harrow Point closed to research in 1996 before reopening as a public observatory in 2008. The sharpest episode was the 2009-2011 Brisk lawsuit over research income spent on galleries. The 2022 merger into the Department of Earth and Sky Sciences and the 'One Institute, Sea and Sky' plan try to treat the two missions as equal and interdependent.

queries.text: What were the lasting effects of the 1962 fire on the Institute?
queries.answer: The fire destroyed the east wing and 2,318 objects (1,406 outright), including about 40% of the Aldane Herbarium and almost all the photographic archive; collections spent six years at Vellmoor. It led to the founding of the Conservation Studio (1963), Director Sallow's resignation (1964), the fire-safe Rautio Wing (1968) paid for largely by the public Rebuild Meridian appeal, and Oster-Lind's 'open doors' policy. It turned the Institute from a patron's foundation into the city's museum and remains central to its memory through oral histories, Voices from the Fire and the 2012 Fire and Recovery exhibition.

queries.text: Trace the story of the Isle of Graye from its first recorded sighting to the whale skeleton in the atrium.
queries.answer: Captain Josiah Harrow recorded landing on an uncharted, bird-covered reef in his 1891 Corvina logbook, naming it after his mate Graye. Captain Elias Venn proposed a voyage in 1933, and his 1934 expedition on SS Kittiwake fixed and charted the reef. Percival Dunmore's larger 1936 expedition on SS Merrow recovered a stranded fin whale, which became Big Graye, hung in the central hall from 1939 and the Rautio Wing atrium from 1968, and was re-measured in 2019 at 19.8 m rather than 21.3 m.

queries.text: How did ocean science at the Brannock Bay laboratory develop from 1947 to the present?
queries.answer: Ottilie Brandt founded MOL in a converted lifeboat house in 1947 around long-term measurement of tides, currents and estuarine mixing (her 1949 current meter, the 1952 Brandt and Hale paper). Tobias Wren took it into deep water with the 1970 Ossery Trench Expedition and a new 1974 building; Priya Sandoval broadened it into coastal ecology and climate with the Ferrow Marsh station. Under Rhea Oduya it moved to high-resolution seabed mapping, including the 2017 Ossery Trench Survey, celebrated in the 2018 Deep Meridian exhibition; in 2022 its physical oceanography group joined the new Department of Earth and Sky Sciences.

The architect of the Rautio Wing, built after the 1962 fire, also designed MOL's 1974 laboratory building at Brannock Bay.
The Corvina Logbook was written by a co-founder of Pell & Harrow, and the granddaughter of the other co-founder (Augustin Pell) sued the Institute over it.
The conservator who restored the atlas made by the first head of the Department of Celestial Navigation was Beatrix Nolan.
The designer of the Brandt Current Meter co-authored 'Tidal Mixing in the Calder Estuary' with University of Ashcombe professor Winifred Hale.
The curator of the 1972 'Stars Over Calder' exhibition had earlier worked as an assistant under the discoverer of Comet 1938b.
The donor of the Kittering Sound Chart was the father of the Brisk Trust chair who sued the Institute in 2009.
A co-leader of the 2017 Ossery Trench Survey succeeded her own doctoral advisor as MOL director.
The watchman who raised the alarm in the 1962 fire rescued the logbook that records the 1891 sighting off the Isle of Graye.
The director who deferred the east-wing rewiring in 1960 resigned in 1964 after the fire, which was caused by faulty east-wing wiring.
The 1998 Oriel-funded digitisation project was led by the successor of the conservator who restored the Calder Orrery.
The fourth director, appointed by board minute BM-1964-03, had previously been deputy at the Meridian Oceanographic Laboratory.
Comet 1938b was discovered with a telescope paid for by the Institute's founder, Augustin Pell.
The 'Deep Meridian' exhibition featured specimens from a survey co-led with Tollan College of Marine Science.
After the 1962 fire, surviving collections were stored in a former Pell-Harrow Line warehouse (the Vellmoor Depository).
The curator of the 2012 'Fire and Recovery' exhibition drew on oral histories recorded by Dana Whitcombe.
The director appointed in 2023 had been the first manager of the reopened Harrow Point Public Observatory.
The 1970 Ossery Trench Expedition was led by a former student of Brandt's co-author Winifred Hale.
The board chair during the 2009 Brisk lawsuit had been a partner at the law firm that represented the plaintiff in the 1978 logbook lawsuit.
The plaintiff in the 1978 logbook lawsuit was the daughter of the man who funded the 1934 Graye expedition.
The Calder Orrery's maker had his workshop on the site later occupied by the Pell & Harrow head office.
Herbarium type sheet HERB-AL-0457 came from the marsh that since 1995 hosts MOL's field station.
The membership society founded by Lottie Graves raised $185,000 for the Rebuild Meridian appeal.
The 2014 'Stars Above Calder' exhibition showed the original plates of a comet discovered by Arlo Fenwick.
MOL's founder married the chief engineer of the ship that carried the 1936 Second Graye Island Expedition.
The 2014 'Stars Above Calder' exhibition showed a facsimile of the Threlkeld Atlas because the original had moved to Vault C3.

confusablePairs.distinction: 1934 First Graye Island Expedition: led by Captain Elias Venn aboard SS Kittiwake, 11 members, funded by Edmund Pell, mapped the reef. 1936 Second expedition: led by Dr. Percival Dunmore aboard SS Merrow, 17 members, recovered the Big Graye fin whale skeleton.
Dr. Miriam Castell (1918-2001) was Curator of Maps and Charts 1955-1980 and curated Stars Over Calder; Dr. Marian Castel (b. 1956) was Curator of Ethnography 1994-2016.

Stars Over Calder (1972) was curated by Miriam Castell at Wrenfield Street and showed the restored original Threlkeld Atlas; Stars Above Calder (2014-15) was curated by Ines Halloran at the Harrow Point Public Observatory and showed a facsimile plus the Comet 1938b plates.
1970 Ossery Trench Expedition: Tobias Wren, trawler Bellrock, dredging to 2,900 m. 2017 Ossery Trench Survey: Rhea Oduya and Aurelio Banks, RV Tern, multibeam mapping to 3,450 m, NMHB-funded.

Pell-Windham v. The Meridian Institute (1978-1981) was about ownership of the Corvina Logbook and was won by the Institute; Brisk Trust v. The Meridian Institute (2009-2011) was about misuse of restricted endowment income and was settled.

The Venn Sextant belonged to Captain Elias Venn and was donated in 1951 by his daughter Rosalind; the Harrow Octant belonged to Captain Josiah Harrow and was donated in 1912 by his widow Constance with the Corvina Logbook.
The 2016 report gives 212,000 visitors for 2016; the 2017 report revises 2016 to 208,400 and gives 231,500 for 2017.
Idris Palk was appointed 7th director in May 2019 succeeding Nadia Corrow; Leonie Farrant was appointed 8th director in September 2023 succeeding Palk.
1996: Harrow Point Observatory closed to research because of light pollution; 2008: reopened as the Harrow Point Public Observatory for outreach, managed by Leonie Farrant.
